fit: unspecified coriander preparation in a Parkinson menu

fit: mixed curry containing dried seed powder

fit: coriander in anesthetized-rat hypotension title

assessment: The combined methanolic almond, peanut and watermelon seed extract favored less block catalepsy and greater activity. It did not test peanut oil, an isolated seed arm or a resting-tremor outcome.

fit: oral corn oil comparator and unstimulated salivary flow

fit: curry leaf extract and motor tasks in rotenone mice
assessment: The publisher figure shows shorter beam and pole times and a partial increase in open-field distance after leaf extract. These tests do not measure clinical freezing episodes after cooked curry leaf.

fit: isolated isolongifolene and toxin-model rat behavior
assessment: A separate isolated-compound study assessed open-field and rotarod performance. Neither cooked leaf nor clinical freezing episodes were measured.

fit: curry leaf extract and fly climbing or jumping
assessment: Climbing and jumping favored an extract arm in the fly toxin model. The test does not measure human freezing events or cooked leaf.

fit: intralaryngeal almond oil carrier and hoarseness
assessment: A laryngeal case reports hoarseness resolving after a course including menthol in almond oil and surgery; no oral exposure, cold pressing, Parkinson diagnosis or measured vocal intensity.

fit: Rat leaf extract with contradictory charcoal transit direction

fit: Human mixed decoction and irritable bowel symptoms
assessment: The completed trial used three botanical ingredients and found an inconclusive bowel severity contrast. The registration and article did not measure OFF time or levodopa.

fit: Clinical iron tablet with levodopa drug exposure

fit: Hydroalcoholic leaf extract and rat transit

fit: Measured iron in a ground curry leaf food formulation
assessment: The report gives compositional iron in finished idli, with no medication exposure or OFF measure. Food matrix and pharmaceutical iron are distinct exposures.

fit: Ferrous-sulfate-fortified curry-leaf product in laboratory study
assessment: The formulation adds ferrous sulfate and reports in vitro iron handling. It does not test ordinary ground curry leaf use with levodopa or measure daily OFF time.

fit: Overlapping mouse charcoal transit experiments
assessment: Five arm means and SDs match across the original reports. The full series adds distinct verapamil and atropine comparisons without gastric emptying, levodopa or OFF time.

fit: oat bran in a multi-ingredient meal and mobility measures
assessment: The protocol includes balance and chair stands, and excluded diagnosed neurodegenerative disease. It supplies no Parkinson falls outcome for rolled oats.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits

fit: habitual oats and pooled cereal intake in celiac disease or IBS

fit: cayenne frequency and combined anxiety and depression scores

fit: oral related pepper extract and DASS anxiety in students

fit: oral cinnamon capsules and blood pressure in type 2 diabetes
assessment: Blood pressure fell with capsules relative to placebo. Symptomatic lightheadedness on standing was unmeasured.

fit: ground cinnamon capsule and repeated post-meal supine blood pressure

fit: dried cinnamon powder capsules and ambulatory blood pressure in hypertension
assessment: Day-90 24-hour pressure comparisons were inconclusive. No standing challenge or Parkinson symptom score.

fit: cinnamon use and cardiovascular nonmotor domain in a Parkinson survey

fit: ground cassia beverage and acute blood pressure in middle-aged adults

fit: topical piperine rinse and composite of pronunciation difficulty and worsened taste

assessment: The original report includes a chocolate group and several biochemical, microbiota and histology outcomes. It has no scored anxiety behavior or clinical anxiety measure.

assessment: The seed extract reduced induced excess orofacial movements in rats. Dried culinary leaf and reduced facial expression were not studied.

fit: coriander in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome
assessment: The menu lists coriander without specifying the plant part and the motor examination includes facial expression. Dried cilantro exposure and facial expression item changes are unavailable.

fit: freeze-dried cherry powder in a formulated drink and self-rated mood

fit: oral and injected almond oil in rat forced-swim behavior

fit: olive and coconut oil in the same Parkinson dietary survey

fit: coconut oil in mixed oral feeds and mouse rotarod retention

fit: healthy human salivary effect of three mixed cumin-ginger sprays
assessment: The study concerns spray formulation, salivation and safety. It supplies no swallowing test or isolated toasted-cumin exposure.

assessment: Cumin intake was recorded and exploratory nonmotor comparisons were inconclusive after correction. No preparation or cumin-specific dysphagia estimate is reported.

fit: case of acute allergy after fried mixed food containing ground cumin
assessment: The report records acute anaphylaxis and sensitization to cumin. It supplies no toasted-seed or Parkinson swallowing assessment.

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking

fit: rocket salad beverage and blood pressure in healthy adults
assessment: The post-beverage systolic pressure declined at 150 minutes. The beverage, posture, population, and endpoint leave fall frequency after raw leaves unmeasured.

assessment: The article measures a global motor outcome without an arugula or fall-frequency contrast.

fit: fresh arugula in a nitrate-rich vegetable crossover

fit: daytime protein regimens and clinical dyskinesia in severe fluctuations

fit: chives on a Parkinson pilot diet menu and composite motor score

fit: oral dried dill aerial-part and black rice extract, open-field movement after stroke

fit: oral dill and black rice extract and aggregate stroke neurological score in adults

fit: maternal oral dill extract and developmental motor reflexes in offspring
assessment: The abstract describes better developmental righting, rotation and cliff avoidance following maternal extract exposure. These motor reflexes provide no Parkinson bradykinesia or fresh-leaf comparison.

fit: oral sowa extract and rotarod motor performance during withdrawal
assessment: The two extract arms had longer retention than withdrawal alone. This motor coordination task supplies no fresh leaf or clinical bradykinesia estimate.

assessment: Investigators report no clear comparative PBA-s change without numerical results or the apathy item. Its direction is unresolved.

fit: developmental safflower exposure and novelty exploration

fit: isolated safflower pigment and depression-like measures in a Parkinson mouse model
assessment: Higher sucrose intake and lower immobility after the purified pigment are an opposite-direction clue at the level of depression-related measures. Neither the tested exposure nor endpoint is the frozen claim.

assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes speech, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: crushed fennel seed infusion and unsolicited fatigue mention
assessment: Among ten women reporting on a seed infusion, the other-effects item rose from 0 to 8 points. The narrative mentions fatigue without reporting its direction or count. Controls did not complete the questionnaire. The seeds were crushed and steeped, and the population had menopausal symptoms.

fit: oral fennel oil and categorical fatigue severity in primary dysmenorrhea
assessment: The fatigue distribution favored oil at both strengths. Overall p=.08, with rescue medication and differential discontinuation. Oral oil, cyclic menstrual fatigue and toasted seed in Parkinson differ.

fit: fennel extract and fatigue-specific comparison in primary dysmenorrhea
assessment: The primary abstract gives p=.058 with no fatigue arm means or relative direction. The full Persian results table remains open.

fit: fennel soft capsules and menstrual weakness versus no medication
assessment: The table reports weakness falling 6.65 to 2.88 for fennel and staying at 6.39 for control. It disagrees with the abstract control value. Menstrual weakness, a capsule and an unblinded comparator limit transfer.

fit: fennel seed in a honey mixture evaluated in people with Parkinson disease
assessment: The preparation was unspecified. Survey fatigue counts are pooled across 150 people and cannot be linked to the mixture recipients.

fit: oral Parkinson trial corn vehicle and seated cardiovascular monitoring
assessment: The trial measured seated wrist blood pressure and found no significant contrast. Standing changes and symptoms were not measured as an endpoint.

fit: self-reported cooking corn oil and seated blood pressure
assessment: Predominant corn-oil users had lower seated pressure than people mainly using animal fats. Self-reported exposure, seated monitoring and absence of a symptom endpoint limit the finding.

fit: Parkinson CBD trial dizziness reporting with oral corn vehicle
assessment: The associated thesis reports dizziness in the active arm. Posture and an oil-specific comparison are unavailable.

fit: oral corn oil comparator and blood pressure in seated treated hypertensive adults
assessment: Seated pressure is a distinct outcome from standing lightheadedness. The study neither specifies refining nor compares corn oil against randomized no-oil use.

fit: Scrambled egg offered within both Parkinson diet plans; one visual hallucination event occurred in the ketogenic arm
assessment: Individual intake and event timing are unknown. Hallucinations resolved after pramipexole reduction. The trial did not compare egg-specific visual hallucination frequency.

fit: Mixed diluted Avena formulation with measured sleep efficiency planned
assessment: Completed 81-person short-term insomnia trial with no posted results. It tests a combination tablet and does not isolate oat grain.

fit: Mixed oat-based beverage protocol with sleep quality secondary
assessment: The planned trial in older adults has no posted results. The formulation, comparison and outcome do not identify a rolled-oat effect.

fit: Oat-milk products and planned toddler sleep outcomes
assessment: The recruiting study compares different dairy and oat product regimens. The sleep records are pending and the exposure and population differ from the frozen claim.

fit: habitual oats and pooled cereal intake in celiac disease or IBS
assessment: P0156 (p. 350) reports habitual gluten-free oats during a different acute gluten challenge. P0157 (pp. 350–351) compares persistent celiac symptoms without a difference in reported oat use. P0590 estimates pooled gluten intake in irritable bowel syndrome. None gives a rolled or cooked oats and Parkinson falls, insomnia or rigidity comparison.

fit: Mixed oat straw extract and adult sleep complaints
assessment: Final PSQI favored the combination containing oat straw extract, melatonin, valerian and other ingredients. No separate oat arm or Parkinson cohort.

fit: Whole grains and prevalent versus incident insomnia in a cohort
assessment: Fully adjusted odds ratio for highest versus lowest whole-grain quintile was 0.93 for prevalent insomnia and 1.00 for incident insomnia. Whole grains were pooled and no rolled-oat or Parkinson effect was estimated.

fit: Mixed granola and inconsistent subjective versus EEG sleep outcomes
assessment: In the uncontrolled UMIN000053189 cohort, subjective insomnia scores fell from baseline at weeks four and eight and EEG sleep outcomes did not change significantly. The test recipe does not establish rolled oats.

fit: Personalized granola and uncontrolled insomnia scores
assessment: Overall Athens Insomnia Scale change was inconclusive. A subgroup of 19 improved from baseline. The recipe supplement and any isolated oat contrast remain unavailable.

fit: Breakfast oat products with glycemic outcomes
assessment: The published UMIN000048192 breakfast experiments report glucose and no sleep results. Their relationship to the registry's oatmeal lunch and sleep narrative is unresolved.

fit: Extracted oat fiber doses and exploratory daily sleep duration
assessment: Two-week NCT06739941 study found no significant change in sleep duration over time or between three open doses. No inactive control, rolled-oat preparation or clinical Parkinson insomnia endpoint.

fit: Oat flour and bran products with a sleep item inside GHQ-12
assessment: NCT06393114 randomized 56 analyzed adults with mild metabolic deterioration to crossover oat gurt and porridge periods. Both used oat flour, bran and faba protein. Supplement Table 11 reports an inconclusive direct GHQ-12 comparison (P=.569). No sleep item estimate, plain rolled oat contrast or Parkinson population. The journal and EPO6_170 describe one trial.

fit: Oatmeal challenge shared by both randomized enzyme periods
assessment: In NCT06628869, sleep quality did not differ significantly between fructanase and placebo (P=.91). Both periods used the same oatmeal and inulin. The trial estimates an enzyme effect rather than an oat effect.

fit: rolled oats as the food comparator in chronic insomnia
assessment: For rolled oats the diary mean sleep time changed from 359 to 376 minutes in one week. Within-arm changes and the week-by-condition comparisons were inconclusive. There was no randomized no-oat control and no Parkinson cohort.

fit: Parkinson insomnia and diet-pattern scores
assessment: The pattern analysis reported no significant insomnia association and no individual rolled-oat comparison.

fit: wild green oat extract and actigraphic sleep in smokers
assessment: Wake after sleep onset changed by −0.7 minutes versus +5.4 with placebo at eight weeks (p=.047). The preparation, population and outcome differ from rolled oats and Parkinson insomnia severity.

fit: Oatmeal-rice lunch with numerical sleep estimates unavailable
assessment: The registry and DOI 10.11402/ajscs.36.0_58 report OSA-MA measurement with discordant sample counts. The sleep estimates and participant overlap remain open.

fit: Measured aflatoxins in retail dried fig samples from Rabat-Salé
assessment: Original Table 2 confirms six of twenty dried fig samples with detectable total aflatoxins and one with aflatoxin B1. Maximum values were 32.9 and 0.28 micrograms per kilogram respectively. Separate Jan–Oct 2006 purchases do not overlap with the 2005 ochratoxin campaign. Individual ingestion and Parkinson visual outcomes were outside the design.

fit: combined dried fig oral exposure and maze behavior in a scopolamine memory model
assessment: The oral mixture included dried fig and olive oil. Maze behavior and hippocampal markers in rats provide no clinical visual hallucination frequency estimate.

fit: pediatric PRES case with EEG and visual hallucinations
assessment: The observed visual episodes tracked seizure activity in the selected case. The clinical setting, age group and mechanism differ from the frozen exposure and population.

fit: epilepsy and non-epilepsy randomized-trial safety summary
assessment: Two placebo visual hallucination reports and two differently coded psychotic-disorder reports in active epilepsy trial arms are subject to selected coding and context. These data do not involve dried fig intake or Parkinson disease.

fit: Primary abstract; shared RECOVER extension group
assessment: The paper reports general hallucinations in 13 percent of 84 participants and the registry reports 11 affected participants and 22 events. These describe the same single-arm extension and neither source reports a dried-fig comparison.

fit: fig intervention against active fiber in a 20-person meeting abstract
assessment: At two weeks the fig arm improved in transit and defecation frequency from baseline. The authors report no clear arm difference across defecation symptoms. Earlier publication than the 40-person registry recruitment and a different cohort size and outcome window distinguish the records. The report has no Parkinson visual outcome.

fit: walnut–fig syrup against active lactulose in older adults
assessment: The randomized 90-person functional constipation study reports responses in 43/45 on the combination versus 41/45 on lactulose (P=.677). Parkinson was exclusionary. It cannot isolate either ingredient. IRCT20200714048108N1 describes the same study with a two-week treatment scheme, while the paper describes four weeks.

fit: single-cohort caplet pilot combining flaxseed and fig extract
assessment: The 15 participants received flaxseed powder with extracted fig fruit and reported several bowel changes. The before–after pilot lacks a concurrent comparison and cannot isolate fig. The early DOI 10.17795/jjnpp-40069 and the later DOI identify one report family.

fit: multisensory hallucination categories and functional brain connectivity
assessment: The full preprint analyzes 53 people with Parkinson disease and differentiates minor, structured and absent hallucination groups. Structured symptoms combine visual, auditory and other modalities. The model and induced sensed-presence task do not measure dried fig intake or separately count visual episodes after exposure.

fit: medication crossover and robot-induced sensed presence in Parkinson disease
assessment: Twenty people completed the analyzed crossover. A stronger induced presence response during prescribed dopaminergic treatment was reported in the 11 with prior spontaneous hallucinations. This is an experimentally provoked phenomenon, distinct from spontaneous visual episode frequency following food. Participant overlap with the July preprint remains unverified.

fit: mixed dried sweet fruit category in author observations
assessment: Dried figs appear in a pooled row listing cognitive complaints, without item-specific observation counts. Hallucinations are named in other rows. No dried-fig visual episode or Parkinson diagnosis is established.

fit: fresh or harvest-period fig exposure and an attributed intoxication metaphor
assessment: The travel account reports an impression of greater excitement during the harvest and a local saying. It does not identify a dated eater, fermented preparation, measured alcohol, Parkinson disease or visual disturbance.

fit: DLB diagnosed in surveillance series, differential history
assessment: Reports five prospectively seen DLB cases. Distinguishes diagnostic labels and reported symptoms. Possible overlap with the 2001 Tschampa article. No standardized visual recurrence or culinary fig measure.

fit: Idiopathic Parkinson matched groups, longitudinal cognition by hallucination onset
assessment: Fifty-four patients contributed repeated motor, cognition and affect measures. Early-onset history had similar cognitive change to matched controls. Late-onset history was associated with greater cognitive and affect decline. No counted visual episode outcome or dried-fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson medication case series, broad symptoms and mixed adverse observations
assessment: Seventeen admissions for broad acute psychiatric symptoms received combined medication changes. The report describes global mental improvement and one evening hallucination adverse event. Visual modality and recurrence rate unspecified. No dried-fig exposure.

fit: Lewy body dementia case with formed visual symptoms
assessment: Conference member subarticle832 distinguishes visual hallucinations and clinical parkinsonism in a Lewy body dementia case. The diagnosis and case trajectory do not give repeated visual episodes after fig consumption.

fit: regulatory tables and maintenance adverse-event narrative
assessment: Open conversion and randomized maintenance have distinct denominators and coding. The 2015 label includes a composite; the full approval package has an explicitly visual maintenance withdrawal.

fit: analytical composition of the named food preparation
assessment: The authoritative food-composition record FDC 174665 (NDB 09094) identifies dried uncooked figs. The pantothenic acid result is 0.434 mg per 100 g, with eight analytical data points and a reported range of 0.350–0.531 mg per 100 g. This establishes that the ordinary dried fruit contains the nutrient under study. It provides no clinical exposure assessment, brain-tissue response or visual hallucination outcome.

fit: immediate clinical fig reaction with separate fresh and dried skin tests
assessment: The original poster summarizes an immediate reaction to fig ingestion with unspecified prepared form. Separate skin tests show sensitization to fresh and dried material. The controlled intake challenge did not occur; neither visual episodes nor clinical Parkinson effects were measured.

fit: authentic 1872 first edition distinguishes fresh from dried practice
assessment: Printed page 439 assigns reported excitement to heavy fresh fig intake during harvest. The dried-fruit discussion concerns customary use and preservation. The 2003 printing repeats this account, so it contributes no second independent observation. No diagnosed Parkinson or visual symptom outcome is documented.

fit: inspected historical edition separates heavy fresh intake and dried storage
assessment: The written account attaches excitement to heavy fresh fruit consumption during the harvest. Sun-dried figs and some dipped in oil are described separately, with no comparable reported experience. The literary account gives no clinical visual hallucination or Parkinson outcome.

fit: fresh and sun-dried culinary preparations in simulated digestion
assessment: The original summary reports differences by fig variety and compound in a dialysed in vitro digestion fraction. Several measures increase after drying, while the examined anthocyanins are undetected in the dried fraction. The exposure is a food matrix assay and clinical effects remain unmeasured.

fit: new postoperative visual hallucination in a Parkinson stimulation cohort
assessment: The 36-person pre-post surgical study lists one person with a new visual hallucination after subthalamic stimulation. Symptom onset for one patient does not establish a repeated visual episode frequency or a dried fig exposure effect.

fit: patient and caregiver recognition of a visual symptom
assessment: The visual item was recognized by 40.6% of 32 patients and 39.3% of 28 caregivers. These are responses on Parkinson disease knowledge, with no assessment of food exposure or observed episodes.

fit: inhaled levodopa safety and occurrence of hallucination
assessment: Short studies report hallucination adverse-event participants in 1.5% with inhaled levodopa versus 1.3% with placebo. The longer study includes a nonrandom observational comparison, 2.2% versus 1.6%. A visual hallucination appears among treatment discontinuation reasons. These figures are participants with events and no food was compared.

fit: pimavanserin chart review and global clinical impressions
assessment: Six medicated patients included four with Parkinson disease and two with dementia with Lewy bodies. The chart review reports an overall improvement in the hallucinations and delusions clinical impression at three months. It gives no comparator or separate visual episode rate.

fit: amantadine switch and hallucination adverse event
assessment: An open-label subgroup of 24 Parkinson deep brain stimulation patients switched from immediate-release to extended-release amantadine. The report gives hallucination adverse events in 25% and contains no separate count of visual episodes. NCT02202551 is the parent study.

fit: visual hallucinations and place misidentification in dementia
assessment: The Lewy body dementia case describes visual hallucinations as well as a separate misidentification delusion and cognitive fluctuations. It lacks a timed food comparison or count of visual episodes.

fit: Registration for the 71-participant randomized STEPS trial
assessment: The sham-controlled registration confirms the distinct trial and has no posted summary results. Its primary report does not give disaggregated visual counts at abstract depth.

fit: Randomized phase registry safety counts
assessment: The official results list one serious visual-hallucination event in one participant among 191 in the rotigotine safety group and zero among 96 in placebo. These denominators describe safety follow-up. The parent article's randomization was 190 versus 97. The comparison concerns a transdermal medication and reports no dried fig intake.

fit: Single-arm extension registry event term
assessment: Eleven of 84 participants had 22 events recorded under a general hallucination term. The open-label extension drew from the RECOVER parent trial and has no parallel placebo group. Counts combine events within an individual and do not specify visual modality or a dried-fig contrast.

fit: Registration for the six-person unilateral pilot
assessment: The registry identifies one nonrandomized group of six and lacks posted summary outcomes. The separately published adverse-event narrative supplies the visual observations.

fit: refractory visual hallucination trial eligibility and severity outcomes
assessment: The US and EU registries identify the same proposed drug comparison. Eligibility requires visual hallucinations more than three times per week and primary assessment concerns a global severity score after four weeks. The registry does not supply measured results or a culinary exposure. This study is separate from TOLEDO.

fit: registered Lewy body dementia medicine comparison and pooled neuropsychiatric outcome
assessment: The parent trial posted total NPI measures. Hallucinations contribute to a composite but stand-alone visual frequency is unavailable. The medicine comparison does not test dried figs.

fit: registered 12-week hallucination scale comparison without posted outcomes
assessment: TOP HAT registers an ondansetron-versus-placebo comparison with a hallucination endpoint at 12 weeks. The sponsor describes the SAPS hallucinations score as assessing frequency or severity. The official registry does not supply results. This prescription trial is separate from food exposure and earlier uncontrolled case series.

fit: Parkinson cohort protocol with dietary diaries and nonmotor phenotyping
assessment: DUPARC specifies vision and other nonmotor phenotyping in de novo Parkinson disease and planned a three-day dietary diary for nutrient intake. It also identifies diet as a potential confounder in the microbiome analysis. The protocol reports no separate dried fig measure, fig comparison or exposure-linked visual hallucination outcome. Registry NCT04180865 identifies this cohort.

fit: Parkinson visual symptoms, PET and questionnaires within a specific meeting member
assessment: The ePresentation compares 11 Parkinson patients with visual symptoms and nine without using FDG PET and perceptual or clinical ratings. Relative hypermetabolism and a questionnaire association without multiple-comparison correction have no food exposure or visual episode-rate estimate.

fit: resting EEG microstate transition in Parkinson hallucination phenotype
assessment: The poster compares 19 patients with hallucinations and 20 matched patients. Some transition probabilities differ and duration, occurrence and coverage are broadly similar. Microstate occurrence is an EEG outcome, without a dried fig comparison.

fit: evoked visual EEG in Parkinson minor hallucination phenotype
assessment: The separate poster compares 23 Parkinson patients with minor hallucinations and 23 without. Early visual categorization and later processing responses belong to a stimulus task. The participants' food exposure and spontaneous visual episode frequency are not measured.

fit: multiethnic dietary habits and broad perception domain
assessment: The observational analysis includes fresh fruit as a food class and describes its combined NMSS perception and hallucination domain. Its author-reported corrected comparisons concern selected patterns, supplements and herbs or beverages and provide no result by dried fig and visual episode frequency.

fit: Conference partial scope, seizure visual symptom context
assessment: Review covers all 337 archived pages. The only hallucination lexical match is a seizure-imaging poster. The archived object skips printed p. 1010. The missing page remains open.

fit: task-based differences between Parkinson visual hallucination groups
assessment: BNA poster P-W082 measures attention-task behavior and fitted drift rate in groups defined by hallucination status. It supplies neither a fig exposure nor a change in symptom frequency.

fit: original 1870 print correspondence showing a mismatched historical citation
assessment: The correspondence cited by the later walnut–fig syrup paper discusses iron and aloes. Two unrelated clinical reports on the same page compare anatomical findings to walnut size. The page does not measure consumption or its reported effect, and it supplies no source for a historical fig or walnut response.

fit: original source context with different preparation, outcome, attribution or population
assessment: The study measures visual misperception task errors and imaging in Parkinson disease. It does not estimate spontaneous hallucination frequency or assess dried figs.

fit: visual hallucinations and attributed pain in a Parkinson case
assessment: Author abstract reports resolution of hallucinations and pain after gabapentin in an uncontrolled stage IV Parkinson case. The patient attributed pain to perceived insects. No dried fig exposure or episode-frequency estimate is reported.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy without the frozen food preparation
assessment: Parkinson visual hallucination status stratifies diffusion imaging groups. The comparison does not estimate episode frequency or a dried-fig effect.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy without the frozen food preparation
assessment: A Parkinson case-control cohort records visual hallucination features across population groups. The study did not use dried figs to compare episode frequency.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy without the frozen food preparation
assessment: The drug trial reports affected participants with visual hallucinations in its adverse-reaction table. This is an event category under medication strategies without a dried-fig exposure or episode rate.

fit: original clinical measurement or case context without a matched ingredient comparison
assessment: The complete pathology paper recounts episodic visual hallucinations during delirium in an earlier pseudo-Huntington case. No frequency measure or dried-fig exposure.

fit: primary dopamine agonist sleep attack case series
assessment: The primary abstract confirms a nine-person sleep case series. The visual case detail comes from the later table, and original case body access remains open.

fit: Diagnostic review and formed visual features
assessment: Clinical review uses formed visual histories as diagnostic context. It reports neither a separate episode-rate study nor dried-fig intake.

fit: visual hallucinations during unrelated medication intoxication
assessment: The exact letter reports visual hallucinations during acute intoxication in an individual with parkinsonism. The food hypothesis and episode frequency are outside the report scope.

fit: Author abstract of autopsy-linked clinical imaging case
assessment: A single dementia case showed low presynaptic tracer uptake and was confirmed as Lewy body dementia at autopsy. Whether that case appears in the later series remains unverified. The abstract records no separately assessed visual symptoms or dried-fig intake.

fit: Pathology-confirmed Parkinson or MSA, broad medication-related psychiatric outcome
assessment: The pathology-confirmed comparison uses broad medication-associated psychiatric effects for diagnostic grouping. No dedicated visual episode measure or dried-fig exposure.

fit: Clinical Parkinson mimic and temporally linked visual symptoms
assessment: The clinical conference describes hallucinations after a medication change in a patient whose final diagnosis differed from the initial Parkinson diagnosis. No fig exposure or visual episode rate.

fit: banana pulp enzyme and in vitro substrate reaction
assessment: The original abstract measures salsolinol oxidation in banana pulp enzyme assays. It distinguishes a reaction in vitro from diet and clinical outcomes. No dried fig composition or human visual symptom observations are reported.

fit: Pathology-confirmed diagnostic groups and visually guided drawing
assessment: The original criteria give acceptable copies in 2 of 17 Lewy body and 16 of 27 Alzheimer participants (p=0.002). The relaxed criteria give 8 of 17 and 20 of 27 (p=0.11). Two Parkinson dementia cases were excluded. The outcome provides diagnostic task context without food intake or episode frequency.

fit: Cardiac diagnostic imaging and clinical hallucination status
assessment: The full author copy compares 11 people with Lewy body dementia, 10 with Alzheimer disease and 10 controls. Ten of the 11 have a positive entry in the general hallucination column. The diagnostic comparison estimates cardiac tracer uptake. It measures no visual episode rate or fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson drug-use review, mixed clinical visual observations
assessment: Table 1 reports visual symptoms emerging, resolving or absent during apomorphine exposure. The source synthesizes original cohorts with heterogeneous event labels and concurrent drugs. There was no common visual episode rate or fig exposure.

fit: Retrospective atypical dementia diagnostic groups, visual symptom history
assessment: Table 2 records visual hallucinations in 9/25 CJD, 2/19 Alzheimer and 7/12 DLB patients over their course. This is symptom occurrence in selected diagnostic groups with no dried-fig intake or visual episode count.

fit: Parkinson narrative differential, visual symptom history
assessment: The review discusses visual hallucinations as a differential diagnosis clue. It presents no original visual event frequency or dried-fig comparison.

fit: DLB and Alzheimer imaging groups, visual symptom history
assessment: The official 303-page DOI object was reviewed. Poster PS_51 records a visual history in 25/34 probable DLB and 0/28 probable Alzheimer-type patients. No fig exposure or visual episode rate. NLM-listed pages 1264–1298 remain an explicit scope discrepancy.

fit: Cardiac diagnostic imaging and visual clinical feature
assessment: The original comparison enrolls 14 people with probable Lewy body dementia and 14 with probable Alzheimer-type dementia. Table 2 records visual hallucination presence. The finding is a clinical characteristic and supplies no within-person episode frequency or fig exposure. The exact body-review disposition was already recorded on November 16.

fit: longitudinal Parkinson hallucination interviews
assessment: The primary abstract identifies Rush Hallucination Inventory interviews at four visits over 48 months. The full methods for modality and frequency remain open. No dried fig intake is reported.

fit: Open rivastigmine trial abstract
assessment: In the 12-person Parkinson study the authors describe improvement in hallucinations and sleep disturbance. The abstract lacks a comparator, visual item count and fig exposure.

fit: Open tacrine or donepezil cognition and motor comparison
assessment: The 11-person study uses cognitive and motor scales. A reported change in cognition is a separate endpoint from a visual symptom. Distinct from the rivastigmine cohort.

fit: Visual orientation scoring critique and response
assessment: The letter reports clear rotation errors in 7 of 134 patients with Alzheimer disease and disputes the earlier drawing interpretation. The reply reuses the Ala sample and shows the original models for the contested copies. These are drawing observations with no fig comparison or reported hallucination rate.

fit: Clinicopathological cohort with visual phenotype
assessment: The study used longitudinal clinical records and regional pathology in 63 cases with Lewy bodies, including 29 DLB cases, 18 Parkinson dementia cases and 16 with parkinsonism without dementia. Well-formed visual hallucinations were associated with Lewy body burden in the amygdala and parahippocampus. The visual phenotype and its timing differ from an event-frequency response to food.

fit: Primary abstract; isolated multiple system atrophy case
assessment: The case labels infestation delusion as a possible early manifestation of multiple system atrophy. It cannot supply a separately assessed visual event frequency in Parkinson disease or a food comparison.

fit: DLB and Alzheimer imaging groups, likely linked to PS_51
assessment: The primary abstract reports 26 DLB patients with visual hallucinations and 15 with bilateral hypoperfusion. The conference reports 25 with visual histories and the same 15. Participant linkage and full article remain pending.

fit: banana pulp and peel chemistry by ripeness
assessment: The original banana assay finds salsolinol in later-stage pulp and peel with markedly different table values by preparation. It does not measure Ficus carica or a neurological endpoint. Avoid transferring the measured analyte across fruit species.

fit: Parkinson medication cohort and unresolved visual adverse-event detail
assessment: The publisher abstract reports retrospective motor outcomes in 64 Parkinson participants, 45 of whom converted to daytime infusion monotherapy. Visual adverse-event detail and possible reuse of the earlier 19-person Colzi cohort remain unverified. This is a medication comparison without fig exposure.

fit: postoperative visual hallucination events in an advanced Parkinson series
assessment: Two of seven developed visual hallucinations several weeks after bilateral stimulation. These are adverse events in a surgery and medication context, without per-person hallucination frequency or assigned dried fig intake.

fit: Parkinson clinical review with medication-related visual history
assessment: The review describes reported visual hallucinations as part of psychosis and discusses different medication contexts. It does not measure a new clinical comparison, a visual episode rate, or dried-fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson perfusion and visual reasoning with symptom exclusion
assessment: The full eligibility methods explicitly excluded people with visual hallucinations. The 28 Parkinson participants without dementia and 17 controls were compared on perfusion; subsets of 25 and 14 completed visual reasoning. The results give visual processing context without a visual episode rate or food exposure.

fit: Population diagnostic prevalence and bounded symptom coding
assessment: The 601 examined participants included 20 probable and 10 possible Lewy body dementia diagnoses and two separately classified Parkinson dementia diagnoses. The 5.0% measures diagnostic prevalence. The Table 4 signs in the rendering remain unverified. The study gives no within-person episode rate or fig exposure.

fit: clinical fig allergy and dried-fig extract cross-reactivity
assessment: Five patients had allergic symptoms after fig ingestion. The laboratory separates fresh and dried extract inhibition. Reported percentages reflect IgE binding, with no hallucination outcome or preparation-specific clinical rate.

fit: Uncontrolled dementia follow-up, Parkinson subgroup of three
assessment: Behavioral ratings improved over follow-up in the Parkinson dementia subgroup. The published 45% visual figure has no compatible affected-patient numerator at the recorded subgroup size of three. This is a drug follow-up without a separately enumerated visual episode rate or dried figs.

fit: severe postoperative deficiency and route-dependent magnesium response
assessment: The two surgical cases involve losses, seizures and confusion. Orange juice carried oral magnesium sulfate in one case, while oral salts failed during recurrence in the other before parenteral replacement helped. No visual hallucination frequency or Parkinson diagnosis was documented.

fit: injected derivative and rat striatal receptor expression
assessment: The rat experiment measured striatal receptor transcript levels after systemic N-methyl-norsalsolinol exposure. Serotonin 5-HT2A and delta-opioid transcripts rose; mu-opioid expression fell. The clinical hallucinosis link is the authors' interpretation. The abstract provides no measurement of food-derived salsolinol, fig ingestion or observed visual episodes.

fit: Expert synthesis of Lewy body and Parkinson disease dementia
assessment: The report describes overlap of clinical and pathological presentations and reviews drug sensitivity and neuropsychiatric outcomes. No exact visual episode comparison or dried-fig exposure.

fit: Primary six-month account from the unilateral pilot
assessment: The six-person pilot paper gives six-month motor and safety findings but no separate visual count. The same pilot's later primary paper reports three affected participants. These publications are one study family.

fit: Diagnostic review of young-onset dementia
assessment: The differential table describes visual hallucinations as a feature of one dementia phenotype. The review has no original visual-frequency or dried-fig comparison.

fit: Uncontrolled quetiapine follow-up in Parkinson disease
assessment: The open-label cohort of 35 had improved psychiatric measures over 12 months. Dopaminergic regimens changed in many participants. The abstract distinguishes hallucinations and delusions without a separately reported visual episode rate.

fit: Clinical dementia and Parkinson group imaging comparison
assessment: The 164-person cohort measures scan readings against clinical diagnosis. The imaging differentiation between Lewy body and Alzheimer dementia does not measure visual episodes or a response to food.

fit: Statistical imaging analysis across clinical groups
assessment: FP-CIT image maps show binding reductions in Parkinson and Lewy body dementia groups. The endpoint is imaging, and overlap with the other 2004 imaging paper remains unverified.

fit: EXPRESS randomized medication trial
assessment: General hallucination adverse-event term was recorded in 17 of 362 on rivastigmine and 17 of 179 on placebo. Modality and per-person event count are unspecified. No food exposure arm.

fit: Longitudinal Parkinson hallucination and sleep cohort
assessment: The authors followed 89 deliberately stratified Parkinson participants at five assessments. At six years 49 were interviewed and 40 were deceased or too ill to participate. Nightmares and vivid dreams were associated with concurrent hallucinations but did not predict subsequent hallucinations in initially unaffected participants in the abstract (OR 0.94, p=.51). The cohort does not test dried figs. The exact visual modality ascertainment and full outcome tables remain open.

fit: central Italian fieldwork on mixed dried fig decoction and other parts
assessment: The original tables place dried figs with other ingredients in a respiratory decoction and report separate latex and veterinary uses. The neighboring mallow entry is the one describing mild laxative use. Counts represent localities reporting customs. The fieldwork does not document changes in Parkinson visual episodes.

fit: hospital case series after Ficus insipida latex
assessment: A child in the index case had unconsciousness and edema after a nonculinary latex preparation. The report does not attribute recurrent formed visual episodes to edible dried fig flesh.

fit: Conference archive with a distinct alternate visual symptom etiology
assessment: Member 136013 describes tremor and visual hallucinations with thyroid dysfunction and amiodarone exposure. The case does not evaluate Parkinson disease or dried figs. The complete DOI extent is 25–279. The additional NLM pages remain separately unresolved.

fit: Measured mycotoxins in Turkish export and retail dried figs
assessment: Ochratoxin A and aflatoxin B1 were measured in two export-year groups and in a separate retail group. Both toxins occurred in some export samples. The study measured food products and provides no individual ingestion, Parkinson diagnosis or visual episode frequency.

fit: reanalysis of the earlier ceremonial pharmacokinetic cohort
assessment: Fourteen of 15 earlier volunteer profiles underlie the reanalysis. Time profiles for another mixed botanical exposure do not establish a clinical Parkinson event frequency.

fit: neuropathology with exclusions for established Parkinson motor onset
assessment: The clinicopathologic comparison includes 106 autopsy-confirmed dementia cases, 89 with Alzheimer pathology alone and 17 with Lewy body variant. It excludes Parkinson motor onset more than 12 months before dementia. Visual hallucination history predicted Lewy body pathology in the fitted model (OR 7.3, 95% CI 1.71–31.08). The model predicts neuropathology from a clinical feature and provides no fig exposure or exposure-linked episode rate.

fit: Consensus classification and management synthesis
assessment: The report describes diagnostic weighting and summarizes earlier medication observations on attention, visual hallucinations and sleep. It is not an independent symptom comparison or a dried-fig study.

fit: Diagnostic neuropathology review
assessment: The Lewy body section discusses clinical overlap between Lewy body dementia and Parkinson disease dementia. It describes diagnostic history and pathological findings without a new measured visual event rate or any tested dried-fig intake.

fit: Parkinson perfusion grouped by dementia status
assessment: Thirty participants with Parkinson dementia and 22 without dementia were compared with 10 controls. The result concerns occipital perfusion and cognitive scores. It does not report counted visual episodes or a fig comparison.

fit: Primary follow-up of the six-person unilateral pilot
assessment: The adverse-event section reports three new visual cases within six months. One resolved after medication reduction and two resolved spontaneously. The 2008 wording groups them under resolution after medication reduction. No separately measured culinary exposure or frequency.

fit: Parkinson visual-status SPECT comparison
assessment: The investigators compared 24 Parkinson participants who reported visual hallucinations with retained insight and 41 without prior visual hallucinations. The right fusiform signal was lower at a corrected cluster threshold. Higher right superior and middle temporal signals were described at an uncorrected threshold. These are group perfusion comparisons, without a dried-fig intervention or repeated visual episode counts.

fit: Cross-sectional clinical interviews at primary abstract depth
assessment: The study assessed 35 Parkinson dementia and 21 DLB participants already experiencing recurring visual hallucinations. Patients described episode frequency, typical duration and perceived content through a structured interview. Caregivers completed a separate neuropsychiatric inventory. Most patients described complex experiences daily, usually lasting minutes. This recruited sample addresses episode characteristics, with no estimate across all Parkinson patients or comparison by fig intake.

fit: Clinical chart association with fall status
assessment: Table 2 shows hallucination history in 53.3% of Parkinson fallers and 37.5% of nonfallers. Methods mention visual hallucinations. The study's outcome is falls and fractures and the exposure comparison does not measure dried figs.

fit: DLB visual symptom rating and uncontrolled pre-post donepezil exposure
assessment: The NPI hallucination score decreased from 6.4 to 1.4 in 20 patients. The visual symptoms were identified separately from the imaging endpoint. The occipital peaks did not pass correction. There was no placebo group or fig exposure.

fit: Postmortem tissue comparison with one recorded visual history
assessment: The study compared complex I in brain samples from 10 Parkinson and 12 control donors. The clinical table records visual hallucinations in one donor with seizures. It does not systematically measure visual recurrence or culinary fig exposure.

fit: Animal movement model and distinct cited historical human observation
assessment: The article studies movement abnormalities in a mouse model. Its introduction separately recounts a previously published human case of acute illness with visual hallucinations and parkinsonian features, attributed to Richter and colleagues. The human observation is a citation in the background. It adds no independently observed Parkinson cases, food exposure or visual episode rate to the animal paper.

fit: Neuropharmacology review with cited visual symptom and medication reports
assessment: The review discusses visual modality, vivid dreams and drug response evidence. It cites overlapping hallucination and illusion categories and distinct uncontrolled treatment trials. These are cited observations and no dried-fig comparison.

fit: Alzheimer autopsy and symptom history by pathology group
assessment: Hallucinations are documented in 10/24 with amygdala Lewy bodies and 9/30 without, using item-specific chart denominators and undifferentiated modality. The study gives no significant contrast or fig exposure.

fit: Original diagnostic imaging educational review
assessment: The review names visual hallucinations as a symptom of Lewy body dementia and describes diagnostic imaging patterns. No new visual comparison is measured. Figures are scan illustrations and the review does not assess figs.

fit: formed visual hallucination history in low vision
assessment: A low-vision rehabilitation cohort asked 225 first-time referrals about formed visual hallucinations. Seventy-eight (35%) reported them. Worse measured contrast sensitivity retained an association after adjustment for acuity and other covariates. The outcome is presence in a vision-clinic population. The study does not compare fig intake or Parkinson episode rates.

fit: Original clinical observation later reused in a genetic series
assessment: The primary abstract describes a juvenile-onset parkinsonism case with motor phenomena and psychotic behavior. The later family series expressly reuses this case and its video, then reports an FBXO7 finding. Neither abstract reports a count of visual experiences. The exposure is not a dried-fig comparison, and the case is shared across the two publications.

fit: Prospectively assessed dementia with imaging and autopsy
assessment: The 20 autopsy cases include eight Lewy body dementia cases. Visual hallucinations were once only in 2/8 vs 1/12 and persistent in 4/8 vs 5/12. The authors report no significant group difference. The study does not compare food exposure or count repeated episodes.

fit: Measured ochratoxin A in Rabat–Salé dried figs acquired in 2005
assessment: Thirteen of twenty dried fig samples were positive. Purchases in July–August 2005 distinguish this series from both the 2004 thesis and the 2006 Juan samples. The analyzed food supplies no observed consumer exposure or visual episode frequency.

fit: Separate conference member observations in alternate clinical contexts
assessment: The case reports on pages 243, 252 and 279 describe biochemical disturbance with visual symptoms, diagnosis revised to progressive supranuclear palsy, and visual impairment with Charles Bonnet syndrome, respectively. Figures are illustrations. No member supplies a dried-fig contrast for Parkinson visual frequency.

fit: Postmortem plaque and Lewy body association
assessment: The authors compared 40 Parkinson autopsies with 20 age-matched controls. The cortical association was stronger in the subgroup with moderate or greater amyloid plaque burden. The [2011 Compta report] identifies 23 of its 56 Parkinson cases as partly assessed previously in this study. The abstract has no visual-episode recurrence or assigned dried-fig exposure.

fit: Review of six-person unilateral pilot and separate sham trial design
assessment: Page 255 reports three new visual cases in the six-person unilateral pilot. The 2005 paper describes one case resolving with medication reduction and two spontaneously. This is the same pilot, without a dried-fig or visual episode-frequency comparison.

fit: authenticated ripe dried fig extract, isolated rabbit gut and human platelets
assessment: Complete methods identify ripe dried fig fruit and voucher FC-F-0905. The aqueous-ethanolic extract was assayed in isolated rabbit gut and ex vivo human platelets. The original prints a platelet concentration discrepancy between abstract and body. Extract bioactivity in these preparations supplies neither an oral exposure nor a Parkinson visual outcome.

fit: subcutaneous apomorphine case series and medication-linked visual symptoms
assessment: Table 1 records visual hallucinations before treatment in eight of twelve Parkinson patients. One later entry describes reduced but persistent visual hallucinations. The remaining entries do not describe persistent visual symptoms, and one patient with baseline complex hallucinations stopped because of falls. The mixed regimen and uncontrolled follow-up cannot isolate the drug or a fig effect.

fit: Prospectively diagnosed dementia autopsy cohort; formed visual history and onset
assessment: Table 1A records visual history in 35/43 probable DLB, 6/9 possible DLB and 0/24 probable Alzheimer cases. In Table 3, visual onset within three years differs across pathology groups while overall occurrence does not differ significantly. No dietary contrast or episode frequency.

fit: Side-of-onset clinical sleep comparison
assessment: The 14 left-onset and 17 right-onset Parkinson participants and 17 chronic-condition controls completed the Parkinson Disease Sleep Scale. Nocturnal hallucinations differed in the unadjusted comparison (overall p=.005). With mood adjustment, the left-onset group differed from controls (p=.007) and the right-onset group (p=.02). The measure represents reported nighttime frequency, without separate visual event counts or an assigned food exposure. The 2010 disconnection review reused this sample.

fit: Primary Parkinson GBA clinical history; no culinary contrast
assessment: Two neurologists reviewed the carrier records. Fourteen of 31 had visual hallucinations after motor onset. This is retrospective occurrence and onset timing, without measured episode frequency or dried-fig exposure.

fit: open-label apomorphine and visual hallucination severity
assessment: Available primary previews describe favorable severity and caregiver distress changes. The numerical results, follow-up and medicine changes remain unevaluated at original-body depth. The drug infusion provides no dried fig or visual episode rate comparison.

fit: Four Parkinson patients, open apomorphine challenge, proxy outcomes
assessment: Contrast sensitivity improved and attention performance worsened during the challenge. The authors explicitly did not score the infrequent visual events in the short observation. No dried-fig exposure.

fit: Primary autopsy from an active-treatment STEPS participant
assessment: This is a tissue and case-course report nested in the distinct randomized trial. It reports no patient motor benefit and no separately coded visual event or fig comparison.

fit: Primary visual task fMRI comparison at primary abstract depth
assessment: The reported groups were nine nondemented Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations, 14 without them and 13 controls. Before recognition of gradually revealed images, patients with hallucinations showed reduced activation in lateral occipital and extrastriate temporal areas. The report did not find the hypothesized increase in frontal activation. Hallucination status defined a group, and the main response was task-related imaging rather than the frequency of spontaneous visual events.

fit: Differential diagnosis review; cited case observations
assessment: Visual experiences may accompany fixed infestation belief or skin sensations. The article cites cases across diagnoses and supplies no dried-fig or separate Parkinson visual-frequency contrast.

fit: Longitudinal MRI and cognitive comparison at primary abstract depth
assessment: Twelve initially nondemented Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations, 14 without them and 12 controls were assessed again at roughly 30 months. Three quarters of the visual hallucination group were diagnosed with dementia, compared with none in the other Parkinson group. The first group also had more widespread gray matter loss. These results describe disease progression within baseline visual symptom groups rather than an effect of changing dried fig intake.

fit: Primary clinical event-related potential comparison at primary abstract depth
assessment: The study compared 11 Parkinson dementia patients with visual hallucinations and six without them, 24 DLB patients and 21 Alzheimer patients. The visual P3 response was slower in the hallucinatory Parkinson dementia and DLB groups than in the Alzheimer group. Auditory P3 latencies were comparable across the patient groups. Visual and auditory task latencies are separate from spontaneous visual event frequency or a food response.

fit: Review with re-presented sleep and perception studies
assessment: The review reuses the sleep comparison of 14 left-onset and 17 right-onset Parkinson participants with 17 chronically ill controls from PMID 18797256. The studies of spatial perception and sleep use different tests. In Figure 12 the review reverses the sleep-item scale for frequency display. Nocturnal hallucination ratings are not a separately counted visual-episode outcome for dried figs.

fit: Parkinson formed visual hallucination groups, NPI and receptor PET
assessment: Seven Parkinson patients with formed visual hallucinations and seven without them differed in serotonin 2A PET binding. The groups also differed in motor severity and treatment duration. The study makes no dietary exposure comparison.

fit: one-month Parkinson interviews by hallucination modality
assessment: Structured interviews of 116 consecutive Parkinson outpatients covered the preceding month. The authors report 42% with hallucinations in any modality, including 16% visual and 35% nonvisual with overlap. These are proportions of patients, and neither dried fig intake nor a food-linked change in episode frequency was measured.

fit: delirium hallucinations of unreported modality during magnesium and calcium disturbance
assessment: Page 168 lists delirium with hallucinations during a period of neurologic deterioration, with no modality or episode rate. Clinical signs and electrolyte abnormalities improved overall during intravenous magnesium treatment. Table 1 on page 169 reports serum magnesium of 0.42 mEq/L before and 1.48 mEq/L after infusion. The later clinical follow-up records changes in serum electrolytes and drug exposure. It does not separately track visual episodes. The NLM electronic date is May 20, 2010, and the printed note says May 21. There is no Parkinson or dried fig exposure in the case.

fit: Neuropathology review with tissue assay findings
assessment: The paper summarizes cortical Lewy body clinicopathology and describes work distinguishing presynaptic aggregates from conspicuous Lewy bodies. It reports mostly null correlations of broad body counts with clinical findings and cites regional temporal associations for formed visual hallucinations. Regional pathology, disease classification and episode frequency are distinct. No food intervention is described.

fit: Inherited neuroaxonal dystrophy case and tissue series
assessment: The study describes seven PLA2G6-associated cases with differing ages of onset. One adult case had transient visual hallucinations early in a progressive dystonia-parkinsonism syndrome and later had a cortical biopsy. The case description gives timing but no recurrence estimate. Its diagnosis, tissue findings and treatment history do not supply an idiopathic Parkinson food comparison.

fit: Complex early-onset parkinsonism family series
assessment: The case series examines five families with complex early-onset parkinsonism and reuses previously reported clinical descriptions. Visual hallucinations appear in the background on earlier ATP13A2 follow-up. One FBXO7-family case developed psychosis during levodopa treatment, prompting clinicians to withdraw it. The authors give no visual episode count for this case or a dietary comparison.

fit: 2011 ethnography of an attributed ojé spirit encounter
assessment: One account describes the spirit of ojé presenting itself during a dieta. The common name includes F. insipida and F. schultesii. Waking visual modality, species for that account, Parkinson diagnosis and episode frequency remain unspecified.

fit: Randomized transdermal-drug comparison
assessment: RECOVER randomized 287 participants with Parkinson disease to the rotigotine patch or placebo. The distressing-hallucinations sleep item did not improve within the active group in the reported post hoc summary. A broader perception and hallucinations score and one serious visual-hallucination withdrawal are separate observations. The trial studied a patch and did not count visual episodes after dried-fig intake.

fit: Narrative review
assessment: The review separates psychotic symptoms by dementia diagnosis and discusses formed visual experiences, other hallucinations and delusions. The Parkinson and DLB sections describe published clinical and imaging cohorts and cholinergic and serotonergic hypotheses. Its cited comparisons include perceptual tasks and presence or absence of symptoms. The review supplies no additional participant sample or dietary contrast.

fit: Primary neurochemical PET and clinical classification comparison
assessment: Seventy-five people with mild dementia received clinical and PET-based classifications. About 35% differed between approaches, with agreement kappa 0.39. The 14 people clinically classified with Lewy body dementia included 29% with a discordant PET classification. Spontaneous visual hallucinations were a diagnostic feature considered with other signs. The measured contrast is between classification methods, and there is no dried fig or episode-frequency comparison.

fit: Laboratory pharmacology and primate movement-disorder experiment
assessment: The experiment compared isolated drug enantiomers in a primate model and rated movement outcomes and observed psychosis-like behaviors during levodopa testing. The R enantiomer affected the disabling subset of the behavior measure without a significant change in the duration of any such behavior. These observer ratings do not establish what the animals saw or how often people with Parkinson disease hallucinate. Dried fig intake was not studied.

fit: Primary randomized STEPS abstract with sham comparison
assessment: The 35 vs 36 participant comparison shows similar mean 12-month motor changes. The abstract summarizes neurologic and psychiatric adverse events without visual modality coding or episode frequency. No dried-fig contrast.

fit: Primary longitudinal clinical PET cohort
assessment: Twenty-three people with Parkinson disease and 27 controls had baseline PET. Six Parkinson participants were later diagnosed with dementia. Lower glucose metabolism in visual association and posterior cingulate regions was associated with subsequent dementia. The discussion cites hallucination work, while the measured longitudinal event was dementia diagnosis. The dataset does not test a food exposure or separate visual hallucination recurrence.

fit: Primary retrospective clinicopathological cohort
assessment: The brain-bank analysis included 56 pathology-confirmed Parkinson cases. Dementia classification drew on recorded clinical courses, with visual hallucinations and fluctuating confusion noted as clinical context. The reported associations concern combined Lewy and Alzheimer-type pathology and dementia. Twenty-three cases had been partially assessed in a prior cohort analysis. The study provides no food-linked symptom change or matched event-count endpoint.

fit: Clinical literature review
assessment: The review discusses visual, auditory, tactile and olfactory experiences separately, contrasts early untreated observations with longitudinal treated cohorts, and surveys pharmacologic and disease-related risk factors. Reported prevalence estimates come from earlier studies with different designs. The review adds no independent participant series or ingredient comparison.

fit: retrospective Parkinson hallucination groups and regional structure
assessment: The retrospective structural MRI included 13 non-demented Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations and 16 without, plus 13 Parkinson dementia cases with hallucinations and 11 dementia with Lewy bodies cases. The non-demented Parkinson contrast found a pedunculopontine-region gray matter difference. The thalamic difference appeared in the combined comparison with dementia included. The exposure was clinical group status and the result was structural imaging.

fit: Exploratory analysis of the original RECOVER randomization
assessment: The paper reuses the RECOVER trial and describes post hoc subsets based on baseline symptom burden. The abstract gives sleep and quality-of-life items that favored rotigotine, mainly pain and mobility-related items. It supplies no separate hallucination-item estimate and notes the trial did not have statistical power for subgroup analyses. This is a reanalysis of the same randomization and not a dried-fig comparison.

fit: Primary longitudinal autonomic and clinical case
assessment: A person initially evaluated for pure autonomic failure reported visual hallucinations by the second follow-up year and worsening by the fourth year, as cognitive and motor findings evolved. The authors subsequently considered probable DLB. Imaging and autonomic measurements track different components of the course. The visual account records timing and perceived worsening with no comparable episode-count windows or food intervention.

fit: actual dried fig ingestion before elevated potassium, with no hallucination outcome
assessment: Pavletic described raised potassium during screening of an otherwise healthy 36-year-old volunteer. After normalization on follow-up, potassium rose again when the participant reported unusually large dried fig intake the preceding evening. The case was uncontrolled and contains no documented visual hallucination or Parkinson diagnosis.

fit: stimulus-evoked images and a separate Lewy body patient score
assessment: Cortical stimulation in 21 dementia with Lewy bodies patients and 19 controls found no overall group difference in phosphene threshold or response rate. Within patients both measures correlated with the past-month hallucination frequency-by-severity score. Six patients and no controls reported transient complex images during stimulation. This study does not measure a dried fig effect or spontaneous Parkinson episode rates.

fit: Adult Dravet syndrome phenotype series
assessment: In five adults with a history of Dravet syndrome, motor slowness, hypomimia and perseveration resembled features seen in other disorders. One narrative describes recurring hallucinatory symptoms in adulthood and no indication of hallucinations during a later examination. The article does not classify those experiences by sensory modality or compare diagnosed Parkinson participants receiving dried figs.

fit: Retrospective clinical onset and perfusion comparison
assessment: The investigators analyzed 41 people with probable or possible DLB. They compared 21 acute with 20 chronic presentations and separately grouped the initial complaints by cognitive features. Table 3 summarizes the distribution of symptoms within initial and subsequent symptom categories. The method describes onset and symptom mix rather than the number of recurring visual episodes per person. No dietary intervention was studied.

fit: fig paste in a drug-induced rat model of bowel dysfunction
assessment: The original abstract reports greater fecal output and intestinal transit length in fig paste groups. It addresses a different species, exposure form and outcome. Complete methods and numerical tables remain open.

fit: dementia group connectivity with visual diagnostic criteria
assessment: Resting-state imaging compared dementia with Lewy bodies, Alzheimer dementia and healthy controls. Visual hallucinations were among the core features used to classify the Lewy body cases. The analysis mapped connectivity between selected brain regions and did not assign or measure a fig exposure or its association with repeated visual episodes.

fit: canine fig paste phase and measured marker transit
assessment: Fifteen dogs passed through fixed successive periods. Fecal wet weight and transit improved during the fig-paste period relative to induced constipation. The sequential design leaves time and exposure inseparable. The diet and restriction remained during the paste period, and the right and rectosigmoid segment comparisons were unclear.

fit: Review with an original illustrative clinical course
assessment: An aging-study participant developed formed visual hallucinations before observed parkinsonism. Dream enactment and fluctuating cognition were recorded separately, and visual experiences recurred later in the Lewy body dementia course. Medication changes and disease progression occurred during follow-up. The illustrative history gives no dietary comparison or count of episodes over a common window.

fit: Primary DLB case-control imaging and symptom correlation
assessment: The comparison included 17 people with DLB and 19 controls, with perfusion available for 15 and 19. Caregivers provided a past-month visual hallucination rating combining frequency and severity. In DLB the combined score correlated inversely with V4 perfusion (rho −0.52, p = 0.04). The visual-task BOLD responses did not show a significant association with that score. The contrast concerns imaging and a composite rating without an assigned food exposure.

fit: Primary genetic cohort with clinical descriptions
assessment: The sample included 106 patients from 98 families across several dementia diagnoses, including four DLB and three Parkinson dementia cases. Descriptions of variant carriers include hallucinations amid broader cognitive and behavioral courses. The comparisons concern gene variants and diagnostic phenotypes. The report supplies no repeated visual event measurement tied to fig ingestion.

fit: Parkinson hallucination history and sleep related falling
assessment: Thirteen of 50 Parkinson patients reported sleep-related falling out of bed. The original reports more people with a history of visual hallucinations among those who fell. Five fallers with hallucinations had used quetiapine, and the groups differed in some medication use. This is a patient-history association with sleep-related falling, with no dried fig exposure or episode-rate comparison.

fit: Primary clinical diagnostic case series
assessment: The report describes three people initially assessed for an Alzheimer-type presentation with abnormal dopamine transporter imaging. One case had uncontrolled visual hallucinations without evident motor parkinsonism at examination. Another described brief experiences closer to misperceptions. The paper illustrates uncertainty in clinical classification. It does not follow visual episode rates under dried fig exposure.

fit: Primary neuropathology and sequencing series
assessment: One patient initially diagnosed clinically with Parkinson dementia experienced visual hallucination during a rapidly worsening course that included fluctuating consciousness and myoclonus. The paper places the clinical description in an atypical tauopathy series and includes a separate screen of pathologically confirmed idiopathic Parkinson cases. Neither the individual course nor the genetic screen estimates visual recurrence under a culinary exposure.

fit: timing of visual hallucinations and combined electrolyte abnormalities
assessment: The original case describes a sudden, hours-long episode of visual hallucinations with severe hypomagnesemia and hypocalcemia. The case presentation says the hallucinations had already resolved when blood tests were ordered the following day. Later overall symptoms resolved during magnesium and active vitamin D treatment. Distinguish the first visual episode from general improvement during the admission. The patient had no reported Parkinson diagnosis and no documented dried fig exposure.

fit: Randomized phase II DLB trial
assessment: The 140-person phase II trial randomized participants with probable DLB to placebo or three donepezil doses. Table 2 combined hallucinations with cognitive fluctuation in NPI-2. Baseline table 1 counted participants with visual hallucinations separately from other modalities. Figure 3 compared changes in the broader hallucination item. These are different measures. No arm varied dried fig exposure.

fit: Primary familial clinicopathology and genetic series
assessment: Records and neuropathology compare carriers of EIF4G1 variants. Selected case courses describe later delusions and hallucinations after motor or cognitive changes. Some narratives combine perceived presence, speech and visual material. They do not provide matched episode windows, an ingredient contrast or an estimate that separates the symptom modalities.

fit: Parkinson medication series, visual adverse and motor off-period observations
assessment: Reports both emergence of visual symptoms during infusion and improvement in off-period hallucinations in one person during intermittent treatment. Events lack a standardized rate. The 2001 review reuses these participants. No dried-fig exposure.

fit: Primary clinical case with postmortem diagnosis
assessment: The recorded course includes visual hallucinations, cognitive decline and motor decline. The postmortem investigation established a different disease context, isolated central nervous system Whipple disease. The symptom narrative gives neither an episode rate nor a comparison with dried figs, and it cannot be treated as idiopathic Parkinson evidence.

fit: symptom measurement review and cited network findings
assessment: The complete review discusses visual symptom classification, limitations of general hallucination rating instruments, visual processing, REM intrusion and the proposed interaction of resting-state and attention networks. Its network discussion revisits cited group findings. It supplies no oral fig comparison or estimate of visual episode frequency after dietary exposure.

fit: case observations in wet macular degeneration and a separate retinal experiment
assessment: Five people with advanced wet macular degeneration reported newly apparent or enhanced light-dependent patterned hallucinations during prescribed proton pump inhibitor exposure. The clinical cases had no Parkinson history. A separate retinal experiment addressed a possible mechanism for those drugs, with no dried fig exposure.

fit: diagnostic cohort with visual presence by visit
assessment: Visual symptoms were present in 49 of 67 DLB cases at baseline and 62 at follow-up. In Parkinson disease the counts were 0 and 31 of 111. The comparison counts people. Orange juice was shared in the separate rum challenge on tremor.

fit: Primary long-term clinical case
assessment: The case traces early-onset parkinsonism before recognition of Gaucher disease and describes multiple treatment changes over follow-up. Benign visual hallucinations are reported in the discussion of levodopa withdrawal, along with loss of response. The text does not identify an independent visual event rate, isolate a drug effect from disease course or measure dried fig intake.

fit: drug-induced parkinsonism case after traumatic brain injury
assessment: No auditory or visual hallucinations were observed at rehospitalization. Medication withdrawal relates to the motor syndrome. No repeated visual endpoint or food intervention.

fit: Dried fig crop sampling across orchards and processing stages
assessment: The 1991 author abstract reports aflatoxins in 29 percent and ochratoxin A in 3 percent of 103 fig samples pooled across stages. Stage-specific counts and finished-food scope remain open. The study has no patient exposure or Parkinson visual endpoint.

fit: experimental visual effects in healthy volunteers
assessment: Fifteen healthy volunteers were analyzed in a randomized double-blind within-person comparison of pharmacologically induced visual experiences and electrophysiologic measures. Receptor antagonism altered the induced effects in that setting. The study does not test dried fig, typical Parkinson symptoms, or clinical visual episode rates.

fit: Parkinson dementia phenotype review
assessment: Summarizes visual symptoms as a differentiating feature and links earlier cohorts. No independent episode-frequency measurement or fig exposure.

fit: Lewy body and Parkinson fluctuation comparisons
assessment: Repeated testing distinguishes within-day cognitive variation from objective alertness. These measures do not count formed visual events and were not examined after fig intake.

fit: secondary comparison of EXPRESS, IDEAL and ADENA
assessment: NPI-10 totals and change in the available trials summarize broad behavioral outcomes. Prior trial datasets are reused. No independent food comparison or visual episode rate.

fit: Dried fig material in nonclinical enzyme assays
assessment: The Dottato dried fig material gave the strongest cholinesterase inhibition among the reported cultivars. The original abstract reports acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase assay IC50 values of 26.9 and 31.8 micrograms per milliliter. Eating whole fruit, clinical exposure, Parkinson disease and visual episode frequency were outside the assay.

fit: clinical review of Parkinson dementia and psychosis
assessment: Discusses formed events and illusions and reviews medication studies. It supplies no dietary comparison or episode treatment effect of its own.

fit: visual hallucination status matched for cognition and age
assessment: A structural MRI study compares 25 people with Parkinson disease and current chronic visual hallucinations with 25 without hallucinations, matched for age and cognitive status. The authors assess visuoperceptive regions and separate cognition from hallucination group status. This comparison does not quantify a change in visual episode frequency after a documented food intake.

fit: LRRK2 fly visual gain model
assessment: Fly electrophysiology measures stimulus-evoked response and contrast. It cannot measure spontaneous or subjective clinical events.

fit: electrically elicited visual scenes in a person evaluated for epilepsy surgery
assessment: Different stimulation sites elicited formed visual scenes or distorted face perception. These provoked responses do not measure spontaneous clinical Parkinson episode frequency.

fit: resting functional connectivity in fluctuating Lewy body dementia
assessment: The sixteen-person Lewy body comparison assessed cognitive fluctuations and connectivity. Associated visual symptoms do not provide a food exposure or clinical episode rate.

fit: persistent thought disorder item in genotyped Parkinson comparison
