assessment: Sustained hallucinations by a composite thought-disorder threshold differed between genetic subgroups. Time to the threshold is distinct from a count of visual events.

fit: Dravet syndrome cohort and repeated AES member
assessment: Eleven of 12 adults had parkinsonian features and selected patients improved after levodopa. The same findings appear at AES 2014. No food or visual episode frequency was evaluated.

fit: autoimmune encephalitis and GABA-A receptor antibodies
assessment: A separate clinical syndrome includes a visual event amid seizures and delirium. It supplies no transfer to dried figs or usual Parkinson visual episodes.

fit: abstract of fig-supplemented chow and behavior in a transgenic Alzheimer model
assessment: The published abstract reports behavioral task results for fig-supplemented mice, with full preparation and animal lineage unresolved. Maze, movement and anxiety-like scores do not convey visual hallucination frequency. The related biomarker report cannot establish this study's preparation.

fit: Parkinson clinical visual groups and default-mode activity
assessment: Resting-state imaging compared 12 Parkinson participants with complex visual hallucinations, 12 without and 14 controls. Parkinson groups showed altered default-mode connectivity, with higher connectivity in the hallucination group than the nonhallucination group in the reported contrast. Grouping by established symptoms does not measure an exposure response.

fit: Alzheimer-model mouse chow with fig material
assessment: Maze escape latency favored the supplemented transgenic group. Preparation mentions dried flesh and an unclear possible extraction step. Neither the tested outcome nor the population measures clinical visual hallucinations.

fit: five botanical exposures and negative geotaxis in Parkinson-model flies
assessment: The source distinguishes opposing Bacopa climbing outcomes across genotypes, and reduced control climbing with Centella. Its preparation list and endpoint do not match.

fit: EEG prediction and clinical feature presence in an MCI cohort
assessment: Visual hallucination status appears in the clinical table, while EEG and diagnostic conversion are the measured prognostic assessments. No culinary contrast is present.

fit: commentary on an evoked visual hallucination case
assessment: The commentary repeats the primary stimulation case and compares possible networks. It supplies no independent clinical exposure or diet result.

fit: Parkinson visual outcomes and hippocampal MRI
assessment: Multimodal hippocampal MRI compared 12 Parkinson participants with visual hallucinations, 15 without and 14 controls. The hallucination group showed microstructural and connectivity differences, with no overall hippocampal volume or shape difference. It includes visual symptom characterization and visuospatial testing, with no dried fig-related outcome.

fit: metabolic parkinsonism case with a diet and medication timeline
assessment: Suspected visual hallucinations improved after pramipexole withdrawal. Earlier phenylalanine restriction and later motor levodopa testing are distinct observations.

fit: separate confirmatory DLB trial with composite efficacy and visual adverse events
assessment: The 12-week placebo-adjusted NPI-2 comparison was inconclusive. Visual hallucination was among severe psychiatric adverse-event terms in two patients with five events in total. The active exposure was donepezil. The composite does not establish a visual event-frequency effect.

fit: open-label extension of the NCT01278407 randomized cohort
assessment: Within-arm NPI-2 improvement persisted during the extension. Three severe visual hallucination events were reported among ten severe psychiatric events in the continuous-treatment group. These records share the phase III family and cannot supply a separate placebo-controlled visual frequency estimate.

fit: Parkinson visual-cue experiment with older and younger controls
assessment: The Necker cube experiment measures dominance and switching of interpretations of a present image. Spontaneous hallucination frequency is a different endpoint.

fit: frozen ground fig fruit added to chow and inflammatory measurements in Alzheimer-model mice
assessment: The study prepared fresh fruit by freezing and grinding it, and used separate fig, date and pomegranate diets. The authors measure inflammatory and other biomarkers. This is neither a clinical Parkinson comparison nor a visual episode measure. Related animal reports may share animal or formulation lineage.

fit: OPA1 family phenotype and clinical visual hallucination presence
assessment: A syndromic case reported visual hallucinations. Genetic and optic findings and clinical presence constrain inference to the documented phenotype.

fit: frontotemporal lobar degeneration genetic case
assessment: A variant carrier developed visual hallucinations and later bradykinesia. The order of findings is useful for phenotype comparison and has no dietary comparison.

fit: preceding-month NPI in Lewy body and Alzheimer dementias
assessment: The Lewy body group scored higher on the NPI hallucinations domain. The composite and group comparison cannot supply a Parkinson visual episode rate.

fit: diagnostic imaging with hallucination presence by group
assessment: Baseline clinical feature counts contextualize the DAT SPECT and cardiac MIBG comparison. The report has no clinical food intervention.

fit: SNCA carrier phenotype and visual symptom history
assessment: SNCA duplication case histories, genetic results and a literature comparison describe motor and nonmotor presentations. Some duplication carriers had hallucinations, along with sleep and cognitive symptoms. The clinical feature is reported with genetic disease and does not measure a culinary effect.

fit: two prospective medication conversion cohorts
assessment: Two of 450 participants converting from immediate-release carbidopa-levodopa discontinued for visual hallucinations. The count covers clinical withdrawals prior to randomization, not the randomized or overall event rate.

fit: secondary Lewy body stimulation and imaging with overlapping study lineage
assessment: The secondary comparison selected 16 dementia with Lewy bodies participants and 19 controls with both imaging and stimulation measurements. Average early visual responses to checkerboards and resting perfusion were similar, while the relationship between stimulation threshold and visual response differed. The authors cite the earlier stimulation dataset. No oral fig comparison was made.

fit: visual review distinguishing function from experienced hallucinations
assessment: The clinical review examines Parkinson visual function from acuity and eye movements to perceptions and hallucinations. It discusses overlapping diagnoses and medication context. None of these narrative observations compares dried fig intake with a Parkinson hallucination endpoint.

fit: visual symptom presence before conversion to Lewy body or Alzheimer dementia
assessment: Nine of 25 Lewy body converters and one Alzheimer converter had reported visual hallucinations at the mild cognitive impairment stage. Person counts do not establish episode frequency.

fit: 125-person apomorphine cohort and visual symptom trajectories
assessment: Of 38 with active visual hallucinations at treatment start, fourteen improved markedly, nine improved to some extent, three worsened and twelve lacked a follow-up outcome. Other dopaminergic, antipsychotic and cholinesterase inhibitor therapy changed. The assessment is qualitative and not paired to food intake.

fit: radiological differential and visual symptom phenotype
assessment: The completed AJNR review organizes causes of visual hallucinations by clinical presentation and characteristic imaging. Parkinson and Lewy body disease are part of a broader clinical differential. It summarizes imaging across conditions and does not present a fig study.

fit: NPI hallucination scale in dementia imaging groups
assessment: The 21-person dementia with Lewy bodies group had greater NPI hallucination scores than the Alzheimer group. That comparison differs in outcome, population and exposure from the dried fig claim.

fit: past-month general neuropsychiatric inventory across dementia groups
assessment: A retrospective matched dementia comparison includes 125 Parkinson dementia, 250 dementia with Lewy bodies and 500 Alzheimer dementia cases. The past-month caregiver inventory uses a general hallucination item. Participant-level symptom comparisons across diagnoses do not supply a visual-only food effect.

fit: Parkinson genetic case with visual symptoms during long-term care
assessment: The case describes visual hallucinations and brief antipsychotic treatment among other clinical changes. It does not compare dried fig consumption or count episodes.

fit: hallucination frequency as survival-model covariate
assessment: The clinical DLB paper adjusts the hippocampal volume survival comparison for hallucination frequency. The adjusted statistic concerns survival. It provides no food-associated visual event estimate.

fit: Parkinson drug withdrawal and case-level visual history
assessment: The clinical cohort follows dopamine agonist discontinuation and tabulates visual hallucinations in individual drug-related histories. The comparison concerns medication withdrawal. It does not identify dried fig intake or compare episode rates after meals.

fit: Dried fig in an ethanol liver model
assessment: The abstract reports lower damage markers in liver after rats fed dried fig plus ethanol were compared with animals exposed to ethanol alone. The complete methods are open. The tissue observations describe an animal injury model and not visual hallucinations.

fit: Parkinson visual phenotype and perception review
assessment: The review discusses distinct Parkinson visual measures, including acuity, visuoperceptual changes, illusions and formed visual hallucinations. Its clinical prevalence, genetic and pathophysiological summaries do not evaluate a dietary exposure.

fit: two randomized active doses in an open-label Parkinson dementia or Lewy body dementia trial
assessment: One and two hallucination adverse events were reported in the respective active arms. Other Parkinson drugs changed. The trial gives neither a visual episode rate nor a dried fig comparison.

fit: human fig preparation trial with different population and bowel endpoints
assessment: Controlled oral Ficus carica paste in 80 young adults with functional constipation compared with placebo for eight weeks. The paper excludes neurological disorders. Colon transit, stool form and abdominal discomfort favored the paste. Between-group weekly bowel movement frequency and pain remained inconclusive. The paste and gastrointestinal outcomes leave the intact dried fig and Parkinson visual outcome untested. PMID27440682 and NCT02138851 identify the same result family. NCT01185431 lacks posted results.

fit: scan-time symptoms and case histories in Parkinson dementia
assessment: Four of five PET and autopsy cases had the hallucination item at scan time. Several clinical timelines describe visual features alongside sleep symptoms. These observations do not measure dried fig intake.

fit: healthy adult dried banana feeding and urinary forms of salsolinol
assessment: Six healthy participants had the urinary S form in both post-intake collection windows. The 24-hour total urinary recovery was reported as 0.75% of the administered amount. Dried banana is a different fruit, and this feeding study does not include Parkinson patients or visual outcome measurements.

fit: companion correspondence without an independent result cohort
assessment: This complete AJNR correspondence comments on the separate imaging review PMID26744445 and emphasizes molecular imaging in the visual hallucination differential. It supplies interpretive context without a new patient sample or fig comparison.

fit: postmortem histamine binding and prior visual symptom ratings
assessment: Postmortem receptor binding was compared with prior symptoms in Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia. The authors report a stronger psychotic-symptom association for delusions. The visual-specific group comparisons did not reach statistical significance. There is no dried fig exposure or episode rate.

fit: antipsychotic trial synthesis using varied psychosis measures
assessment: Clozapine and pimavanserin results differ from inconclusive quetiapine and olanzapine trials. The review aggregates original evidence families and has no food comparison.

fit: dementia clinical visual history and pulvinar visualization
assessment: The memory clinic series relates pulvinar visibility across MRI sequences to the presence of prior visual hallucinations in people with dementia. Time after a food exposure and Parkinson-specific episode counts were not measured.

fit: Korean Parkinson K-NMSS composite and stage differences
assessment: The 323-person Parkinson sample reports higher perception problems and hallucination domain scores in advanced disease. The composite cannot identify a separate visual episode rate and has no dried fig exposure.

fit: cognitive phenotypes and ordinal hallucination item in Parkinson
assessment: The imaging paper uses item 1.2 of the MDS-UPDRS for presence and severity. Much of the positive item represents illusions or formed experiences with retained insight. No count of visual episodes by food exposure is supplied.

fit: Parkinson GBA variant phenotype and time to first symptom
assessment: The Parkinson clinical and genetic study observes greater prevalence of visual hallucinations in mutation carriers than noncarriers (47% versus 22%) in the cited comparison. Time-to-event models estimate first progression to a feature. Neither measure isolates food intake or episode frequency.

fit: Dried fruit as input to a solvent extract and animal pressure tests
assessment: The body identifies dried ripe figs as the feedstock for the tested extract. The higher tested concentration lowered rat blood pressure. The subjects consumed a processed extract and the results concern vascular measures. There is no observed Parkinson visual episode outcome.

fit: dried fig in a pooled supplement and nonspecific adverse outcomes
assessment: The controlled arthritis trial IRCT2013122015876N1 mixed dried fig with olive fruit and olive oil. The recovered register lists different intended enrollment and dosing from the published report. One severe-hiccup withdrawal was recorded. No separate fig arm or hallucination-frequency measure was reported. The authors link the earlier report to the same cohort.

fit: attention networks and neuropsychiatric group descriptors
assessment: The functional imaging comparison uses an attentional task in Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer dementia and controls. The hallucination subscale characterizes the groups. Task-linked network connectivity is the primary comparison, without a fig exposure.

fit: visual physiology in Parkinson without reported hallucinations
assessment: Ten Parkinson participants reported no hallucinations. The group comparison records evoked magnetic responses to visual stimuli and provides no edible exposure or clinical visual event rate.

fit: open-label Parkinson drug safety and people with visual adverse events
assessment: The open-label amantadine extension records visual hallucinations in 43 participants (19.3%). These are participants with a reported adverse event during follow-up, with no concurrent food comparison. Prior trial exposure and age are relevant to interpretation.

fit: imaging by visual hallucination status in dementia with Lewy bodies
assessment: Printed OP-367 is a member-level PET comparison. Symptom status and metabolic differences are reported in a different clinical population. No culinary exposure or separate visual episode count was assessed.

fit: dried fig mineral presence and separate postmortem Parkinson tissue fractions
assessment: USDA measured the four metals in dried figs. The primary postmortem report distinguishes soluble substantia nigra iron and copper from other fractions without measuring oral intake, uptake, or visual episodes.

fit: apomorphine cognitive cohort and post-discharge worsening
assessment: The original reports 32 of 45 with active visual hallucinations at baseline and no new or worsened symptoms during inpatient titration. Nine worsened after discharge, including five whose hallucinations later resolved after treatment of intercurrent infection. Recruitment site and periods overlap the 125-person cohort, and shared patients are unverified.

fit: psychological distress and a separate fluid-swallowing evidence family
assessment: The nonpharmacologic Lewy body dementia review includes psychological approaches addressing distress from visual hallucinations. The separate dietary fluid and postural trial addresses swallowing and aspiration. The distinct members provide no joint fig and visual outcome.

fit: sham-controlled basal forebrain stimulation and individual clinical visual observations
assessment: Six Parkinson disease dementia participants complete a double-blind crossover of active versus sham stimulation. The primary cognitive measures did not consistently improve. The exploratory total Neuropsychiatric Inventory contrast favored active treatment by a median five points versus sham (95% CI 2.5–8.5). Two participants reported near-cessation of visual hallucinations while stimulation was active and resurgence after it was turned off. This is the registered NCT01701544 intervention and the parent cohort of the 36-month report PMC9346244. The trial does not test food intake.

fit: hallucination presence across Parkinson motor subtypes
assessment: The final-visit motor-subtype comparison records hallucinations without a verified visual modality or episode rate. M255 has the same cohort features. No dried fig exposure is measured.

fit: first visual hallucination in a Parkinson cohort without food exposure
assessment: Thirty-one of 63 followed patients reported incident visual hallucinations. Table 2 estimates an adjusted odds ratio of 1.027 per Brief Fatigue Inventory point. The outcome is onset rather than episodes per patient, without eating dried fig data.

fit: observer-rated clinical signs and psychotropic dispensing in nursing homes
assessment: The nursing-home cohort uses caregiver or staff observation of visual hallucinations within a set of Lewy body features. It relates clinical signs to medications and diagnosis, without a timed meal or fig comparison.

fit: temporally observed changes in alertness and blood pressure
assessment: The case records regained alertness after change in body position and blood pressure. Visual hallucinations appear in the history as a separate manifestation. There is no dried fig timing or event rate.

fit: assigned medication and visual hallucination adverse event counts
assessment: Across two pooled Parkinson trials, 18/100 on extended-release amantadine and 3/98 on placebo reported visual hallucinations. These counts are incidence and time to first event under a medication comparison and do not estimate episodes per patient or fig effects.

fit: clinical status subgroup and sensory evidence accumulation
assessment: The peer-reviewed analysis includes 20 Parkinson patients with visual hallucinations, 25 without and 12 controls. Five Parkinson exclusions are documented. This is a linked analysis of the BNA work and offers no fig or episode-frequency comparison.

fit: postmortem pulvinar markers in dementia with Lewy bodies
assessment: The postmortem pulvinar comparison reports differences in transcripts and selected synaptic proteins in dementia with Lewy bodies. Clinical visual hallucinations frame the rationale. Tissue findings cannot supply the exposure or episode rate in the frozen claim.

fit: prospective older spinal-surgery cohort and postoperative delirium
assessment: The analysis includes 104 older people undergoing spinal surgery. It measures postoperative delirium and baseline Parkinson-related nonmotor features. Visual hallucinations are discussed in differentiating syndromes and are not counted against an edible exposure.

fit: mild cognitive impairment diagnostic groups and dopamine-transporter imaging
assessment: Clinical features and imaging characterize 75 participants with mild cognitive impairment across Lewy body and Alzheimer categories. The visual features are part of clinical classification. The original provides no study of visual episode frequency after dried fig ingestion.

fit: longitudinal clinical psychosis onset and remission in Parkinson
assessment: The diagnosis can include hallucinations or delusions. Follow-up visits and medication comparisons address clinical diagnoses, without a visual event count or dietary intake comparison.

fit: recurrent formed visual symptom definition and cortical perfusion
assessment: The study defines clinical presence using formed recurrent images and compares perfusion, metabolism and tau imaging. Meeting an occurrence criterion is distinct from counting visual episodes over time after an ingredient.

fit: TOLEDO medication trial, visual adverse-event reports and ascertainment
assessment: Of 107 randomized participants, 106 entered the efficacy analysis, 53 in each group. TOLEDO's main endpoint was daily off time, not recurrent visual hallucinations. The report lists two hallucination adverse-event cases in each arm in the neuropsychiatric summary and separately lists a visual hallucination withdrawal during apomorphine treatment. These counts should not be added without an event-level linkage. Moderate psychosis was excluded, while very mild visual phenomena with insight were allowed. The trial is NCT02006121, distinct from the registered refractory visual hallucination study NCT02702076.

fit: clinical psychosis measures and quantitative brain susceptibility imaging
assessment: The recruited groups include Parkinson with and without dementia and healthy comparison subjects. Psychosis rating and iron imaging are clinical context. No independent dried fig exposure and visual episode response are observed.

fit: Fig fruit and gastrointestinal outcomes in a randomized IBS trial
assessment: The publisher excerpt verifies 142 completers of 150 and four withdrawals from the fig group. Fig and flixweed groups had favorable bowel symptom frequency compared with usual diet. Pain severity and C-reactive protein did not clearly differ. The registry gives 90 g fig fruit daily and the December 2018 secondary summary specifies two dried-fruit servings. The original Methods still need verification. NCT02559245 describes the same trial, with no Parkinson visual event measure.

fit: cause-specific patient proportions in very mild dementia
assessment: The retrospective very mild dementia series reports visual hallucinations in 31.6% of dementia with Lewy bodies, 11.4% of Parkinson dementia and 4.0% of Alzheimer dementia participants. These are proportions by diagnosis. Dried fig exposure and rates of episodes per patient were not measured.

fit: changes in visual and other hallucinations in secondary vascular parkinsonism
assessment: The two case timelines describe secondary rather than idiopathic parkinsonism. Symptoms recurred during unresolved fistula disease and improved after treatment in Case 1. Food intake and visual episode rates were not measured.

fit: Parkinson visual hallucination history across morning motor groups
assessment: Table 2 gives 8 of 20 versus 26 of 72 participants with a visual hallucination history by motor benefit group. This largely overlapping prevalence comparison did not quantify subsequent episodes or test diet.

fit: feeling of presence and first visual hallucinations in a Parkinson follow-up
assessment: The 78-person follow-up records 17 new feelings of presence and 26 people with newly reported visual hallucinations. First onset and preceding presence are distinct from episode frequency under a food exposure.

fit: sleep-attack review with co-occurring hallucination terms
assessment: The source table separates visual and auditory experiences in cited dopamine agonist cases. Its primary outcome is sudden sleep onset, and case modality is secondary reporting.

fit: pooled clinical proportions with modality and ascertainment differences
assessment: The systematic review pools auditory and visual prevalence separately. Its visual prevalence estimate is 28.2% in Parkinson and 61.8% in dementia with Lewy bodies, with wide intervals and variation by ascertainment. The outcome is proportion of patients, with no exposure-stratified dried fig rate.

fit: visual symptom prevalence in tau PET diagnostic syndromes
assessment: Clinical presence was reported for 13 of 33 with dementia with Lewy bodies and two of 18 with posterior cortical atrophy. The study compares clinical syndromes and tracer uptake without a culinary exposure or timed visual episode rate.

fit: historical synthesis of medicinal alkaloids and single-vine extract
assessment: This secondary viewpoint describes the single adverse event in the 2001 trial as visual, while the primary paper leaves modality unspecified. One attributed event cannot estimate dried fig effects.

fit: Lewy body dementia viewpoint and published caregiver accounts
assessment: The authors cite literature and caregiver experiences. The excerpts describe general safety and psychosis during care, with unclear visual modality and no food exposure or independent efficacy comparison.

fit: Five selected Parkinson cases; visual and tactile symptoms
assessment: The case table records visual and tactile experiences in all five selected Parkinson cases. Duration refers to the infestation syndrome. Varying medication changes and absent food measurement preclude a dried-fig comparison.

fit: clinician concerns about levodopa and visual hallucinations
assessment: The survey compares 100 neurologists with 100 psychiatrists. Possible visual symptom worsening influenced reported prescribing decisions for dementia with Lewy bodies. The questionnaire does not count clinical visual episodes after assigned food or medication.

fit: follow-up diagnosis and visual symptom presence in an FDG-PET cohort
assessment: Seventy-two patients ultimately met dementia-with-Lewy-bodies criteria. Visual symptom presence was part of clinical ascertainment, with family observations and uncertainty in some entry records. It provides no dried fig timing or episode count.

fit: larger consortium imaging and visual hallucination status
assessment: The original abstract describes cross-sectional PET comparisons in 171 people with dementia with Lewy bodies. The imaging cohort may overlap with OP-367. No food comparison is described and the full tables are still open.

fit: ATP13A2 juvenile parkinsonism case contrasted with earlier phenotypes
assessment: The reported patient had no hallucinations, although visual hallucinations are described in earlier cases. This concerns genetic parkinsonism and lacks a food exposure.

fit: pimavanserin and chart-recorded global psychosis improvement
assessment: Clinical improvement was documented for 69 of 91 treated patients in an uncontrolled retrospective review. The outcome spans forms of Parkinson-related psychosis. It does not estimate a separate visual episode rate or food effect.

fit: functional imaging dynamics and visual symptom severity
assessment: The original reports no clear association of selected dynamic imaging measures with visual hallucination severity in the clinical dementia-with-Lewy-bodies group. This concerns imaging correlation and does not address dried fig intake.

fit: stem-bark extract and its fraction in nonclinical convulsion experiments
assessment: The original body confirms stem bark. Outcomes concern provoked convulsions and righting reflex, while a separate central assay examines glycine-related effects. No culinary fruit or human Parkinson outcomes are tested.

fit: Parkinson hallucination neuroimaging synthesis
assessment: The neuroimaging synthesis includes nine studies of Parkinson hallucination groups alongside separate dementia and cognitive analyses. Coordinate convergence and anatomical network projections address spatial localization. No underlying dried fig comparison or exposure-specific episode rate is reported.

fit: Parkinson binary visual history and substantia nigra sonography
assessment: Of 111 Parkinson patients with usable sonography, 18 reported visual hallucinations. The authors use presence as a binary outcome to model association with substantia nigra echogenicity and covariates. It is not an episode count or dietary comparison.

fit: family history and clinical phenotype in Lewy body dementia
assessment: The retrospective comparison uses family history, first symptom and longitudinal cognition in 154 familial and 137 sporadic participants. It provides diagnostic and biomarker context without a separately assigned dried fig exposure.

fit: independent placebo-controlled Georgetown nilotinib study
assessment: The 75-person trial reported a nonserious hallucination in placebo and a serious hallucination in the higher nilotinib arm. Adverse-event categories do not provide a dedicated visual episode rate or food comparison.

fit: experimental visual perception by established hallucination group
assessment: A laboratory visual learning task compares 17 Lewy body participants with hallucinations, 20 without and 20 controls. Prior visual templates improved disambiguation more in the hallucinator group. The task measures an effect of prior information on perception, without oral fig or clinical episode rates.

fit: open-label amantadine and ever-reported adverse events
assessment: EASE LID 2 follows 223 participants receiving open-label extended-release amantadine for Parkinson dyskinesia. Hallucination adverse events and time to onset were tracked; the common named event was reported in 24.2% of participants. The extension re-enrolled participants from earlier trials and also enrolled a deep-brain-stimulation cohort. NCT02202551 is a medication safety study without a dried fig exposure or controlled food comparison.

fit: nighttime hallucinations during a recurrent severe magnesium depletion case
assessment: Initial ataxia and vertigo improved during intravenous magnesium replacement. Three months later, nighttime hallucinations of unspecified modality were reported with recurrent motor symptoms and a measured serum magnesium concentration of 0.9 mg/dL. Overall symptoms improved during repeat replacement and proton pump inhibitor cessation. The original does not separately quantify hallucination resolution, frequency, or a Parkinson or dietary fig exposure.

fit: visual hallucination presence and future dementia in a prodromal cohort
assessment: Visual hallucinations were present in 37 of 73 participants with MCI and Lewy body features. The clinical features informed selection. Follow-up analyzed conversion to dementia. Presence and time to dementia are distinct from food-linked visual episode frequency.

fit: subthalamic stimulation and a nighttime distress item
assessment: A Parkinson cohort was followed after bilateral subthalamic stimulation. The sleep scale includes an item for distressing nighttime hallucinations, which differs from all-day visual episode counts. Stimulation follow-up and medication context provide no comparison by dried fig intake.

fit: specific hallucination subscale in a registered Lewy body stimulation crossover
assessment: The six-person crossover was reported first in the 2019 congress. Table 2 covers five analyzable NPI records. The median hallucination subscale difference is zero for active versus sham, p = 0.655, while the total score contrast is -13, p = 0.066. The prespecified visual interview is distinct. No fig exposure is present.

fit: open-label opicapone and serious adverse-event context
assessment: OPTIPARK is an open-label opicapone safety and effectiveness study for motor fluctuations. Visual hallucination appears among serious events considered possibly treatment related. Seven of 495 participants had one or more of the listed related serious events, a grouped figure that cannot be assigned to visual hallucination alone. The study intervention was opicapone and there is no dried fig exposure.

fit: cross-sectional retinal measurements by visual symptom group
assessment: Ocular imaging compares 26 people with illusions, 28 with hallucinations and 28 with neither. Parafoveal thinning was associated with the hallucination group. The comparison measures symptom presence and retina structure, without food timing. The nested manuscript and follow-up reuse this cohort.

fit: Dried fig in a four-fruit human crossover
assessment: The four-fruit mix containing dried Black Mission figs gave no clear LDL difference against the matched snack. Mean fasting glucose was 0.08 mmol/L higher. The trial does not isolate fig effects and measures no Parkinson visual episodes. NCT03020758 describes the same trial.

fit: firsthand interview priorities in Lewy body dementia
assessment: Telephone interviews of 20 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and 25 caregivers elicited research priorities. The reported experiences and priorities do not estimate a response to dried fig or establish visual episode timing after meals.

fit: separate French Lewy body stimulation pilot and free recall
assessment: The French six-person NCT01340001 trial compared three-month active and sham conditions with free recall as the primary outcome. It supplies no separate visual episode-frequency contrast after food and is a separate study from the UK NCT02263937 trial.

fit: open-label extension of the 75-person Georgetown parent trial
assessment: Sixty-three parent-study completers were rerandomized to active dose groups. Hallucinations appear in event records. The extension is not an independent cohort and did not count food-timed visual episodes.

fit: food frequency categories and fecal microbiome comparison
assessment: The dietary table lists seventeen food and beverage categories without figs or a fruit intake item. The analysis compares fecal taxa with diagnosis and sleep phenotype. Visual hallucinations appear in disease background, with no exposure-timed episode outcome.

fit: multicenter randomized NILO-PD trial with placebo and active groups
assessment: The 76-person trial measured tolerability, central exposure and motor scales. It found little CSF exposure and no treatment-related dopamine metabolite difference. No ingredient comparison or prespecified visual episode rate applies.

fit: dried fig intervention with perceived stress outcome in students
assessment: Amanak randomized 107 and analyzed 99 after exclusions, as reconciled by the publisher erratum. Whole dried fig was associated with lower perceived stress during menstrual cycles. Visual hallucinations and Parkinson disease were outside the study.

fit: Parkinson visual contrast and object identification experiment
assessment: The psychophysical experiment adjusts the contrast of visual stimuli in Parkinson participants with and without hallucinations. Discrimination under the task improves with higher contrast. The outcome is object identification, and it supplies no change in clinical hallucination frequency or fig exposure.

fit: autopsy-confirmed clinical hallucination and delusion profiles
assessment: The retrospective 372-case autopsy cohort compares hallucination and delusion characteristics across confirmed neuropathologies. Presence, content and distress are distinct charted features. The cohort does not relate an identified food exposure to episodes.

fit: Primary Parkinson case; visual and tactile symptom narrative
assessment: The patient reported seeing and feeling ants after addition of ropinirole. The report describes resolution after withdrawal without controlled rechallenge, episode counts or measured dried-fig exposure.

fit: care partner interviews about hallucination modality and experience
assessment: The qualitative study interviewed care partners about lived experience of Parkinson psychosis and reports multiple hallucination modalities. The interview data provide symptom and caregiving context. They supply neither a dried fig comparison nor a prospective count of visual episodes by diet.

fit: fig leaf-derived cell-culture extract applied to skin
assessment: Forty healthy exam-period students ages 20–27 used active cream or vehicle in two groups of 20 in a reported double-blind comparison. The article reports lower transepidermal water loss at recovery with active cream and separate cultured skin-cell measurements. The exposure is topical leaf-derived cell-culture extract, with no whole fruit ingestion or visual episode outcome.

fit: patient, caregiver and clinician measures and future dementia
assessment: The baseline Parkinson cohort included 328 participants. Of 202 followed without baseline dementia, 51 developed dementia. The instruments observe neuropsychiatric symptoms, and the study analyzes future dementia rather than post-ingestion visual episode frequency.

fit: randomized amantadine and pooled hallucinations and psychosis item
assessment: The pooled post hoc analysis uses EASE LID and EASE LID 3 data, NCT02136914 and NCT02274766. At week 12 the MDS-UPDRS hallucinations and psychosis item was 0.2 points higher after Gocovri than after placebo in the adjusted analysis (P < 0.001). The scored item combines experiences and cannot be treated as an independent food effect or a count of visual episodes. This analysis overlaps the parent randomized trial populations, which also contributed extension participants.

fit: cardiac scintigraphy diagnostic classification and visual hallucination features
assessment: The prospective study compares cardiac MIBG in 95 people with mild cognitive impairment. Scans are abnormal in 22 of 37 probable and two of 15 possible Lewy body cases, and normal in 38 of 43 Alzheimer-type cases. The group sizes and probable-Lewy and Alzheimer-type scan counts match EANM 2020 abstract OP-592, marking a single diagnostic cohort. Visual hallucinations are a diagnostic feature. Food intake and episode-rate change are not measured.

fit: Parkinson delusional jealousy and symptom co-occurrence
assessment: The systematic review and small case series describe Parkinson delusional jealousy with medication histories and other symptoms, including visual hallucinations in some records. The primary phenomenon is a delusion, and neither source arm examines dried fig intake.

fit: frequency and duration in a nested Parkinson visual symptom comparison
assessment: The accepted manuscript compares 54 people from the parent 82-person cohort. Hallucinations were reported more often and lasted longer than illusions on the Psycho-Sensory Hallucinations Scale, p = 0.02 for each. The analysis separates symptom groups and supplies no ingestion-timed exposure comparison.

fit: underrecruited placebo comparison for minor Parkinson visual hallucinations
assessment: The CHEVAL trial randomized 91 participants, 46 to rivastigmine and 45 to placebo. It ended recruitment early. The reported time-to-treated-psychosis and dementia comparisons were inconclusive. Treatment initiation is distinct from visual episodes per time unit and is unrelated to a dried fig exposure.

fit: visual attention task across dementia groups
assessment: The study compares visual attention and modeled sensory evidence in a reused Lewy body cohort, including 13 people with Parkinson dementia. Task performance is distinct from hallucination frequency following fig ingestion.

fit: sensed presence phenotype in Lewy body dementia
assessment: Ten participants reported feeling a presence and 24 did not. The original distinguishes sensed presence without sight or sound from visual episodes. The comparison looks at imaging and symptoms without a culinary exposure.

fit: postmortem Parkinson disease dementia tissue marker and measured dried fig constituent
assessment: The study analyzes nine brain regions from nine neuropathologically confirmed Parkinson disease dementia donors and nine controls. Table 2 reports about 40% lower pantothenic acid in case cerebellum, substantia nigra and medulla. Primary visual cortex does not show a clear case–control difference. The comparison measures tissue concentration without dried fig intake or recurrent visual hallucination counts.

fit: differential symptom histories in autopsy-defined dementia
assessment: The autopsy study compares clinical and cognitive profiles of LATE neuropathologic change and FTLD-TDP. Visual hallucinations are retrospective symptoms distinguished by pathology. It does not follow a Parkinson culinary intervention.

fit: single Parkinson case after a seven-ingredient Kampo extract
assessment: The authors describe daytime visual hallucinations and dream enactment ceasing two days after treatment began. The six-month statement addresses parasomnia only. The oral extract included jujube, cinnamon bark and ginger among seven ingredients, without figs. The uncontrolled timeline supplies no attribution to a constituent or dried fig effect.

fit: Parkinson fluctuating pain and visual symptom history
assessment: Records from 331 Parkinson patients are grouped by no pain, nonfluctuating pain and fluctuating pain. The fluctuating-pain group had more people with a visual hallucination history than the no-pain group. This is symptom co-occurrence, without a fig exposure or a change in visual episodes.

fit: self-reported visual complaints in Parkinson disease
assessment: The systematic review compiles patient-reported visual complaints across studies and distinguishes them from functional visual tests. It documents heterogeneity in phenotyping and does not identify an intake comparison using dried figs or a defined change in visual episode frequency after food.

fit: 5-HT3 antagonist effects on sensory measures and psychosis
assessment: The human-study review compares sensory processing and pharmacologic evidence and cites earlier uncontrolled ondansetron reports in Parkinson hallucinosis. It identifies the ongoing TOP HAT trial as separate. Neither medicine nor the reviews establish a dried fig exposure or episode result after food.

fit: Parkinson structural imaging and receptor-map correlations
assessment: The structural imaging synthesis assesses Parkinson visual hallucination groups and compares patterns with independent receptor maps. Regional associations and receptor-map alignment do not provide an intervention, named food exposure or visual episode-rate comparison.

fit: Lewy body symptom-category frequency, duration and connectivity
assessment: The study combines symptom interviews and network imaging in 35 analyzable people with Lewy body disease. It codes hallucination content, duration and frequency separately. Imaging correlations are linked to characteristics of reported phenomena, without a dietary exposure.

fit: clinical hallucination ratings and Lewy body network imaging
assessment: The original compares functional and structural networks across Lewy body dementia hallucination groups. Clinical ratings distinguish degrees of frequency and severity. Imaging and clinical associations do not test eating dried figs.

fit: fasting blood biomarkers by minor Parkinson hallucination status
assessment: The cross-sectional study compares 34 Parkinson participants with minor hallucinations with 65 without them. Mean fasting plasma homocysteine was higher in the minor-hallucination group. Folate, B12, drug dose and disease duration are separate measures. The study does not measure dried fig intake or rates of episodes after a specific food.

fit: telephone follow-up of the baseline ocular cohort
assessment: The two-year interviews reclassified visual symptom states and checked concurrent eye and medication treatment. The same cohort and transition results appear in conference member 1436. The original abstract gives presence categories rather than counted episodes after fig consumption.

fit: longitudinal plasma pTau181 and clinical visual symptom ratings
assessment: The cohort compares biomarker trajectories across mild cognitive impairment with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer categories and applies the North-East Visual Hallucinations Inventory. Ratings are higher in probable Lewy body cases than in the Alzheimer-type group. The later plasma paper reuses pTau181 measurements. Neither gives a dried fig intervention or food-timed visual episodes.

fit: first Parkinson symptom milestone and survival
assessment: The ParkWest cohort uses predefined clinical thresholds for onset of hallucinations and other disease milestones, then analyzes mortality. Reaching a clinical threshold is distinct from changes in repeated visual episodes. The cohort does not compare dried fig intake.

fit: common fig fruit used as an assay reagent
assessment: The study uses fig fruit to make a fluorescent probe and applies it to aged cheese, cured meat, sausage, pickled olives and canned fish. The authors report a calibration range of 5–400 ng/mL and a quantitation limit of 1.68 ng/mL. Those values describe the method. The abstract gives no fig tyramine concentration or clinical outcome.

fit: resting-state network evidence and mixed hallucination definitions
assessment: The review synthesizes resting-state connectivity studies in neurodegenerative conditions with hallucinations. Eleven eligible articles contribute imaging comparisons with heterogeneous symptoms. It does not identify a fig exposure or causal dietary outcome.

fit: visual phenomenology in different psychiatric diagnoses
assessment: This 56-person exploratory study compares visual experience descriptions in schizophrenia, post-traumatic stress disorder and the combination. The measures concern psychiatric groups and trauma-related contexts. No Parkinson fig intake or comparable clinical episode rate is measured.

fit: Parkinson carrier clinical history and cell findings
assessment: The paper combines a Parkinson case associated with an LRRK2 variant and patient-derived cellular comparisons. The original exposure contrast concerns genotype and laboratory function. It does not test dried fig or clinical visual episodes.

fit: 36-month follow-up of a small Parkinson dementia stimulation trial
assessment: Five of six participants from the earlier basal forebrain stimulation trial enter long-term follow-up. Individual NPI hallucination scores include improvement, no change and worsening. This open longitudinal phase reuses the 2017 crossover cohort and has no dried fig exposure.

fit: postmortem measures and binary Parkinson visual history
assessment: In a small postmortem Parkinson series, six of eight patients had a visual hallucination history. The inspected tissue measures did not show a clear correlation with hallucination presence in the reported regions. The finding is about pathology and a binary history, without dietary exposure.

fit: functional network dynamics by Parkinson hallucination group
assessment: The MRI cohort compares 16 Parkinson visual hallucinators, 75 Parkinson nonhallucinators and 32 controls. Dynamic network states are the outcomes. Classification by clinical report does not establish a dietary cause or measured change in visual episodes.

fit: retrospective exposure to identified Annonaceae plants and composite parkinsonism severity
assessment: Visual hallucination presence is 18.00% in the milder profile and 46.75% in the severe profile. Adjusted dietary results give odds of composite-profile membership by fruit, juice or herbal tea exposure. The study does not estimate visual episode frequency given an exposure, and the plant family differs from common fig.

fit: Dutch three-day dietary diary and microbiome outcomes
assessment: The Dutch DUPARC cohort records nutrients with a three-day diary for microbiome covariate adjustment. Public sequences are linked. Original meals and visual hallucination events are not linked in the publication.

fit: self-reported visual features and diagnostic limits in an MSA registry
assessment: The Global Multiple System Atrophy Registry survey records patient-reported symptoms, including a proportion who answered that they saw things that were absent. It examines association with levodopa history and discusses diagnostic uncertainty. It does not track fig consumption or episode counts.

fit: optic radiation anatomy by Lewy body visual history
assessment: The MRI comparison evaluates optic radiation features in Lewy body disease grouped by visual hallucination status. Imaging and a clinical history indicator are the relevant measurements. It does not compare dietary exposures.

fit: fig peel cultivar extracts in a nematode amyloid model
assessment: Original abstract reports less paralysis and amyloid aggregation with Peggy Red peel extract. Full outcome tables remain restricted. The model does not measure human hallucination frequency.

fit: visual frequency and severity at baseline and later cognition
assessment: A prospective Parkinson analysis evaluates baseline visual hallucinations and subjective cognitive complaints as predictors of later cognition. The NMSS perception domain records frequency and severity over the prior four weeks. The modeled outcome is cognitive impairment during follow-up and the study does not compare dried fig intake.

fit: Parkinson psychosis diagnosis and treatment outcome risks
assessment: The clinical record analysis compares treatment and outcome risks among Parkinson patients with and without psychosis and across medication choices. Hallucinations contribute to the clinical syndrome. Neither the treatment groups nor the measurements identify a fig exposure.

fit: caregiver-rated NPI profiles across clinical diagnoses
assessment: The clinical comparison includes Parkinson disease with cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia. It relates Neuropsychiatric Inventory outcomes to caregiver distress and other clinical variables. Those domain ratings are separate from counted visual episodes after eating dried figs.

fit: donepezil challenge, withdrawal and re-exposure in two dementia cases
assessment: Two original cases report complex hallucinations around donepezil exposure. One describes cessation after withdrawal, and the other recurrence after re-exposure. These are medication time courses in dementia with no dried fig contrast or Parkinson visual episode assessment.

fit: Parkinson pareidolia task and threshold-dependent discrimination
assessment: The 20-item noise task tests whether perceiving nonexistent targets in ambiguous images distinguishes Parkinson participants with a complex hallucination history. Its sensitivity and specificity depend on the task-error threshold. This is a diagnostic task response rather than a dietary effect.

fit: robot-induced sense of presence in Parkinson disease
assessment: Conflicting sensorimotor stimulation examines sensed presence among different Parkinson symptom groups. In the four phantom-boarder cases, three reported complex visual hallucinations, separately from phantom-boarder episodes. The experiment neither changes food intake nor records visual episodes after dried figs.

fit: Parkinson imaging review with clinical outcome heterogeneity
assessment: The review systematically compares structural, task-based and resting-state neuroimaging in Parkinson complex and minor hallucinations. Differences in symptom definition and scales are noted. None of the reviewed contrasts measures a specified fig exposure.

fit: primary cholinergic PET case-control comparison and visual symptom presence
assessment: The imaging report compares 25 newly diagnosed dementia with Lewy bodies participants, 15 Parkinson participants and 15 healthy controls. The visual hallucination interview is used to record presence or absence. In the dementia with Lewy bodies group, voxel-wise analyses do not find a clear relationship between tracer uptake and hallucination presence. This is the same study discussed in the commentary at PMC10473551. It has no dried fig exposure or food-timed clinical episode-rate measure.

fit: nigrostriatal uptake and visual hallucination status
assessment: The DLB and mild cognitive impairment imaging analysis relates lower regional dopamine transporter uptake to recorded hallucination status and other clinical features. Association with occurrence is distinct from change in episode frequency after eating, and food exposure is not measured.

fit: measured dried fig constituent and severe deficiency treatment case
assessment: Case 2 had a low serum magnesium concentration, cerebellar edema and delirium with visual hallucinations. Overall symptoms improved after intravenous magnesium, withdrawal of antiviral medication and prior thiamine treatment. Later low magnesium recurred with ataxia and no reported cognitive symptoms. Dried figs contain measured magnesium, but the case has no Parkinson diagnosis, food exposure or separately timed episode frequency.

fit: plasma biomarkers and presence of core DLB features
assessment: The investigators assay 172 baseline plasma samples, with repeated samples in 55. The second recruitment cohort uses the previously reported cardiac MIBG method, and a prior p-tau181 result is reused. Visual hallucinations are rated as present or absent for clinical classification, without a dried fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson reasoning task and clinical psychosis association
assessment: A cross-sectional Parkinson comparison tests reasoning with a beads task and assesses psychosis and impulsivity. The reported task performance did not clearly associate with Parkinson psychosis. It does not test an exposure-linked change in visual hallucinations.

fit: Dried fig toxin detections in a wider Moroccan food surveillance study
assessment: The abstract gives fig detection percentages for two contaminant groups, while per-food sample counts and dates remain open. The intake calculations do not measure individual symptoms. Keep mixed-food co-occurrence separate from an unreported fig-specific value.

fit: selected severe hypomagnesemia case synthesis and visual outcome citation boundaries
assessment: The review identifies 60 patients with neurological symptoms during hypomagnesemia. Inclusion required movement or eye movement abnormalities and clinical reversal following correction. The resulting series cannot estimate the probability of improvement without that selection, or a visual hallucination treatment effect. References 41 and 42 describe hallucinations without specifying the sensory modality in the original cases. Reference 4 remains at publisher preview depth. Do not count this synthesis as additional independent case evidence. It contains no dried fig feeding or Parkinson episode-frequency comparison.

fit: early Parkinson psychosis scales, visual subtype and frequency limitations
assessment: The original reports any psychotic features in 27 of 70 early Parkinson participants and three of 74 controls. The 10PDQ identifies sensory type separately from frequency of the worst psychotic experience, and CAARMS scores combine frequency and duration. The study does not track dried fig intake or separately count visual episodes after meals.

fit: pareidolia, visual perception and clinical symptom distinction
assessment: The noise pareidolia task results are interpreted in relation to visuoperceptual performance and reported hallucinations. The findings do not justify treating a laboratory false perception as an equivalent measure of a spontaneous episode. There is no fig exposure.

fit: dried figs as a tested product in a calcium digestion study
assessment: The primary abstract places dried figs among products with calcium bioaccessibility below 10% under static in vitro digestion. Exact product data await the full report. The measured fraction has no direct Parkinson visual outcome.

fit: modeled biomarker and a separate urinary metabolite citation
assessment: Transcriptome-based modeling predicts candidate metabolic changes and cites an earlier urinary salsolinol comparison in levodopa-treated patients. Neither the modeled estimates nor the cited figure establishes fig content or any food-linked clinical visual effect.

fit: reported hallucinations and postmortem nigral loss by sex
assessment: The multicenter clinical-pathological analysis relates substantia nigra cell loss and clinical features by sex. Hallucinations are self- or caregiver-reported clinical features. Tissue loss and symptom history cannot identify a fig-related episode effect.

fit: separately enrolled randomized postmarketing DLB comparison
assessment: Global change and NPI-2 differences were inconclusive. The NPI-2 contrast was −0.2 points with a 95% CI from −1.48 to 1.01. A favorable secondary cognitive result addresses a different outcome. This was a drug comparison.

fit: drug-trial NPI-2 composite combines hallucinations and fluctuation
assessment: The meta-analysis uses data from three double-blind randomized donepezil comparisons in dementia with Lewy bodies. The NPI-2 combines hallucinations and cognitive fluctuations. This drug outcome is broader than visual episode frequency and contains no dried fig comparison.

fit: Primary Parkinson case; medication-associated infestation delusion
assessment: Crawling sensations and infestation belief followed piribedil escalation, with resolution after withdrawal. The narrative does not separately ascertain a visual event and contains no fig comparison.

fit: virtual human estimates and sensed presence rather than visual clinical frequency
assessment: The virtual reality and patient analyses report estimation bias and induced sensed presence. Clinical groups and exclusions distinguish sensed presence from formed visual hallucinations. The test does not identify an oral food exposure or assess episode rate after ingestion.

fit: diet-history questionnaire and Parkinson microbiome composition
assessment: The published predictors are aggregate diet quality, fiber and added sugar and the outcomes concern microbial profiles. A specific dried fig intake and clinical visual episode rate remain unreported.

fit: prodromal diagnostic differential for visual hallucinations
assessment: The pragmatic review distinguishes prodromal Lewy body dementia from prodromal Alzheimer presentations. It emphasizes clinical features including early visual hallucinations and fluctuations. These are diagnostic observations without a fig efficacy comparison.

fit: frontotemporal attention and working-memory profiles
assessment: The frontotemporal dementia study compares attentional, memory and imaging profiles by reported hallucination status and relevant genotype. It distinguishes a visual subgroup. Its disorder, measurements and exposure differ from the frozen Parkinson food premise.

fit: fig leaf extract and behavior after acute or chronic stress in rats
assessment: The original figures distinguish lower anxiety-like behavior during chronic stress, better acute recognition task performance, and inconclusive acute immobility. They do not measure a visual episode or dried fruit effect.

fit: 2024 DLB tissue comparison and a measured nutrient in dried figs
assessment: The original measures pantothenic acid in 20 dementia with Lewy bodies and 19 control donors, with lower concentrations in six of ten regions, including primary visual cortex. It mentions visual hallucinations as a possible interpretation of the anatomy. Food composition separately confirms that dried figs contain this nutrient. The tissue comparison has no individual food intake, supplementation, or clinical episode counts.

fit: Lewy body visual phenomenology and MRI regional associations
assessment: The MRI comparison includes 28 people with Lewy body disease and visual experiences, separating minor and complex phenomena in ratings. It associates regional structure with symptom characteristics. It contains no food exposure or time-linked change after dried fig.

fit: visual features in atypical parkinsonism diagnostic reassessment
assessment: The retrospective case series describes progressive supranuclear palsy phenotypes in people of South Asian descent. Visual hallucinations prompted consideration of alternative diagnoses in some cases. It supplies no reported fig exposure or diet-linked Parkinson episode rate.

fit: self-reported and measured visual impairment within a dementia cohort
assessment: The analysis covers 624 participants with dementia and distinguishes reported visual impairment from measured near acuity. Neuropsychiatric outcomes are questionnaire measures and not meal-linked observations. There is no dried fig exposure or Parkinson-specific treatment effect in this analysis.

fit: genetic proxy for generic dried fruit and diagnosis risk
assessment: The analysis reports a positive relation with diagnosis risk for a broad UK Biobank dried-fruit exposure. A diagnosis endpoint, broad exposure instrument and genetic proxy do not measure visual symptom frequency after dried fig intake.

fit: review of cholinergic and visual mechanisms in Parkinson disease
assessment: This review synthesizes visual hallucination studies involving cholinergic dysfunction, Lewy pathology, visual attention and distributed brain circuits. It describes reports in medication-naive patients and an earlier levodopa challenge with no elicited episodes. The underlying observations are medication and mechanism leads, with no dried fig comparison.

fit: visual hallucination onset after initial correction in severe magnesium depletion case
assessment: The patient entered hospital with very low serum magnesium and coexisting electrolyte abnormalities. Visual hallucinations first appeared after extubation, when measured serum magnesium had risen to 2.2 mg/dL. They persisted during further correction and oral supplementation, then were absent the day after quetiapine and melatonin were added. Multiple therapies and the changing critical-care state preclude attributing the visual course to magnesium alone. There is no Parkinson or dried fig comparison.

fit: late-life psychosis, visual features and subsequent dementia
assessment: Records of 2,204 people diagnosed with very late-onset psychosis are followed for dementia outcomes. Visual hallucinations and other Lewy body features at onset are predictors. The follow-up outcome is dementia, without a dietary exposure or Parkinson episode-rate contrast.

fit: Parkinson dementia patient and care partner agreement on psychosis ratings
assessment: The study compares Parkinson dementia patient and caregiver ratings in 21 dyads. Agreement for the SAPS-PD summary score is ICC 0.464, with poor agreement on six of nine items. The source is directly relevant to whose report a symptom scale captures, but neither reporter supplies a food-timed dried fig comparison.

fit: reported dietary magnesium and prevalence of Parkinson disease
assessment: This NHANES analysis includes 20,010 adults over 40, 240 with Parkinson disease. The adjusted magnesium depletion score association is an odds ratio of 1.47 per unit (95% CI 1.16–1.86). The authors report insufficient evidence for a clear association between dietary magnesium intake and Parkinson disease in the main intake analysis, and describe a nonlinear model separately. The study compares recorded disease status, with no visual hallucination outcome or isolated dried fig exposure. The first online date precedes the July 2025 issue.

fit: Parkinson psychosis imaging synthesis across broad symptom definitions
assessment: The published review reports 29 articles and 1,367 participants, of whom 514 had psychosis and 853 did not. It shares PROSPERO CRD42020221904 with the 2022 preprint. Imaging comparisons include heterogeneous hallucination and delusion definitions and no dried fig ingestion outcome.

fit: autopsy tissue and diagnostic group comparison
assessment: Autopsy groups with Alzheimer disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, mixed disease, Parkinson disease dementia and controls were compared on regional tau, amyloid and synuclein burden. The design measures neuropathology by diagnostic group; dietary fig consumption and episode timing are absent.

fit: drug-naïve Parkinson structural MRI comparing visual phenomena
assessment: The study of drug-naïve Parkinson participants compares MRI associations with pareidolia task performance and separately reported visual hallucinations. Distinct imaging patterns are reported. The study contains no dried fig intake or changes in spontaneous episodes after eating.

fit: Parkinson questionnaire with separate visual and nonvisual experiences
assessment: The 369-person survey measures unusual sensory experience over the preceding month. It reports item frequency and pooled experience and distress measures without a documented dried fig or dietary trigger analysis.

fit: longitudinal Parkinson hallucination scale and probable REM sleep behavior symptoms
assessment: The reported early probable REM sleep behavior disorder group had a higher prevalence and greater later severity of hallucinations on clinical assessment. The report compares phenotype and severity over disease-time intervals. It does not count visual-only episodes after a food exposure.

fit: documented ICU episode timing and modality outside Parkinson food exposure
assessment: In 7,525 critically ill adults, clinical note screening identified 625 with hallucinations. Among those 625, 281 had more than one documented episode of any modality. Median time until the first episode resolved was 15 hours. Medication associations use a nested cohort. The design does not measure dried figs, Parkinson-specific episodes or a food-timed effect.

fit: binary antemortem hallucination phenotype and postmortem tissue
assessment: The original labels hallucination presence or absence from antemortem clinical notes and examines methylation networks in postmortem Parkinson brain tissue. It relates biology to recorded symptom occurrence without dried fig exposure or counts of recurrent visual episodes.

fit: observational dopaminergic infusion and adverse-event reports
assessment: ELEGANCE interim safety analysis covers 167 treated Parkinson patients. The narrative counts seven patients with any hallucination report and notes resolution in six. The adverse-event table separately codes visual hallucination and its serious subset. These are drug-treatment reports, not episode rates following dried fig.

fit: actigraphy and clinical features across Lewy body diagnoses
assessment: Eleven participants with dementia with Lewy bodies, 12 with Parkinson disease and 11 age-matched controls completed clinical and rest-activity measurements. The study compares motor activity and circadian patterns across clinical groups. Core symptom information is clinical context and was not tied to dried fig or meal timing.

fit: psychosis scales across Parkinson and atypical diagnosis groups
assessment: The Parkinson comparison group contributes MDS-UPDRS psychosis scores. The Cambridge Behavioural Inventory in other diagnostic groups separately asks about visual and auditory hallucinations and beliefs. Scale and group differences provide no food-attributed visual episode comparison.

fit: cerebral microbleeds and presence of visual hallucinations
assessment: Among 929 mixed Lewy body and Parkinson cognitive syndrome patients, the crude odds ratio linking microbleeds with visual hallucination presence was 1.264 with a confidence interval crossing one. The fully adjusted OR was 1.597 with 95% CI 1.014–2.517. This is diagnostic-cohort symptom presence, with no dietary exposure or recurrence measure.

fit: incident psychosis after minor phenomena in a selected Parkinson cohort
assessment: The prospective cohort followed people with baseline minor phenomena, including illusions, feelings of presence and passage hallucinations. Of 38 recruited, 34 entered the primary analysis and 24 developed psychosis during follow-up. Time to onset on the MDS-UPDRS and enhanced SAPS-PD is a composite incident outcome, with no dried fig intake measurement or food-specific visual episode rate.

fit: secondary clinical sample and PPMI visual status with fMRI
assessment: PPMI classified 25 Parkinson participants with a broad hallucination or psychosis item and compared them with 56 Parkinson participants without symptoms and 24 controls. The separate ICICLE-PD sample used a dedicated visual interview and a severity score combining frequency, duration and type. Resting connectivity and subsequent clinical measures were compared without dried fig or other food-timed episode counts.

fit: visual episodes after neurosurgical conditions with vision loss
assessment: Two institutional cases and 17 patients from 13 papers document visual phenomena in a neurosurgical Charles Bonnet context. Some episodes were restricted to visual field loss. These are different underlying conditions and there is no oral food comparison.

fit: genetic disease and psychiatric presentation in a case series
assessment: Three of 958 patients in a psychiatry-based dementia cohort had pathological NOTCH2NLC expansions. Their case histories and diagnostic work-up describe different disorders and do not measure a response to dried fig consumption.

fit: sleep-transition hallucinations and other psychiatric symptoms in narcolepsy
assessment: The literature review distinguishes sleep-transition hallucinations and psychiatric comorbidities in narcolepsy cohorts. It describes a separate sleep disorder and does not measure Parkinson visual episode frequency after fig consumption.

fit: atypical parkinsonism protocol with planned diet and clinical phenotyping
assessment: ATPARK plans collection of food habits and environmental risk factors, along with longitudinal clinical phenotyping across atypical parkinsonism syndromes. Visual hallucinations appear in the literature discussion of phenotypes. The protocol does not identify a dried fig item or an outcome estimate linked to food intake.

fit: Parkinson visual hallucination status and paracingulate MRI
assessment: The comparison uses MRI in 32 Parkinson participants with visual hallucinations and 33 without them. The regression explicitly uses presence versus absence. The anatomic findings address group status without an ingredient exposure or a counted change in frequency.

fit: separate visual, medication and nutritional cases in the general medicine congress
assessment: The complete meeting publication includes separate cases of recurrent Charles Bonnet phenomena, severe malnutrition after sleeve gastrectomy, medication-associated perceptual symptoms and vision loss in a person with Parkinson. The original members do not connect measured dried fig intake to Parkinson visual episode frequency.

fit: stimulation-elicited visual sensations in an epilepsy cohort
assessment: The original study records intracranial EEG and elicited visual sensations in 69 people with medically refractory epilepsy selected for reporting an induced percept. The experimental comparison is stimulation-related physiology. It does not measure clinical Parkinson visual episodes or food exposure.

fit: validation of Parkinson perceptual and behavioral rating items
assessment: The Canadian study assesses the Mild Behavioral Impairment Checklist in Parkinson and compares model structures and agreement with other clinical ratings. Visual and auditory items are separable. The authors report instability in the psychosis domain, and the design does not test any food.

fit: visual symptoms as prognostic evidence in longitudinal cohorts
assessment: The systematic review includes people without dementia at enrollment and studies subsequent diagnoses of dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease dementia or broader Lewy body dementia. It evaluates prior visual symptoms as possible predictors, without a dried fig comparison or post-meal episode outcome.

fit: neuroimaging and Parkinson visual hallucination group status
assessment: Groups of people with Parkinson disease with and without hallucinations were compared on imaging measures of networks involving the amygdala and nucleus basalis of Meynert. The association is based on clinical group status. The food exposure, temporal attribution and episode frequency required for the frozen claim were absent.

fit: cross-sectional prevalence of minor and formed Parkinson hallucinations
assessment: The study included 372 people with Parkinson disease. It recorded 114 with one or more minor phenomena and 55 with visual hallucinations, with overlap. These counts describe people and clinical phenotypes, rather than the number of episodes after food consumption.

fit: cognitive fluctuation instrument in Parkinson disease without dementia
assessment: The article assesses the Dementia Cognitive Fluctuation Scale in people with Parkinson disease without dementia. The investigators distinguish fluctuations of attention or arousal and discuss visual hallucinations as part of the clinical background. Scale performance and correlates are separate from the effect of eating dried figs on visual hallucinations.

fit: Parkinson reading and contrast vision tested during drug and stimulation states
assessment: The original uses within-person levodopa or stimulation comparisons for reading speed and color contrast acuity. Immediate comparisons were generally inconclusive, with exploratory changes in selected conditions after surgery. The visual tasks do not count spontaneous hallucinations after eating.

fit: retrospective Capgras delusion and co-occurring visual reports
assessment: The retrospective study extracts Capgras misidentification and other clinical features from Lewy body disease records, with matched imaging subsets. Co-reported visual hallucinations and the delusional misidentification phenotype are distinct observations. There is no fruit exposure or post-intake episode rate.

fit: clinical scale scope and psychosis outcome distinctions
assessment: The Movement Disorder Society scoping review surveys outcome assessment instruments across 19 Parkinson constructs and 504 included studies. It discusses measurement and validation context, with no primary exposure or food-attributed episode-frequency measurement.

fit: Parkinson variant groups and clinical nonmotor phenotype
assessment: The original genotypes 3,058 Malaysian Parkinson participants, with detailed phenotyping in 185. The reported nonmotor comparison shows no group differences for visual hallucinations. This is a genetic subgroup comparison, with no tested dried fig consumption or timed clinical episode rates.

fit: sex and gender in phenotypes across Lewy body disorders
assessment: The narrative review synthesizes published differences in diagnosis, symptom profiles, progression and treatment in Lewy body disorders. Reported visual symptom differences are secondary clinical context without ingredient intake or measured food-timed recurrence.

fit: withdrawal drug study with composite relapse and shared HARMONY registration
assessment: A post hoc HARMONY subgroup analysis evaluates continued pimavanserin versus randomized withdrawal in selected responders with Parkinson disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies. Relapse occurred in 1 of 19 continuing drug and 11 of 20 on placebo in the interim efficacy set. The endpoint combines hallucinations and delusions with other relapse criteria, and there is no food exposure. The subgroup is part of NCT03325556.

fit: clinical minor hallucination status and visual-to-semantic performance
assessment: The clinical sample has 93 Parkinson outpatients, 55 without hallucinations and 38 with minor phenomena. The group comparison uses visual-to-semantic assessments. Those task measures and a history of minor phenomena do not provide repeated visual event counts after a meal.

fit: initial clinical phenotype and time to dementia in a Peruvian cohort
assessment: The retrospective cohort stratifies dementia with Lewy bodies by initial cognitive, motor or behavioral symptoms. Cognitive-onset patients progressed to dementia sooner in the observed cohort. Onset phenotype and later clinical domain observations provide no food-timed changes in visual episode count.

fit: expert and trial context on subcutaneous levodopa adverse effects
assessment: This expert and trial synthesis covers initiation and maintenance of a subcutaneous medication and discusses prior hallucinations or psychosis as clinical context. The reviewed exposures concern drug administration, without a fig intervention or an original food-timed episode estimate.

fit: Parkinson psychosis review and clinically distinct triggers
assessment: The European perspective summarizes hallucinations, delusions and management of potential clinical and medication triggers. Its underlying evidence involves disease progression and drug or concurrent illness contexts. It offers no measured dried fig or dietary timing comparison.

fit: hydrocephalus meeting member with a visual presentation
assessment: The full published proceedings contain independent hydrocephalus reports. One diagnostic member notes visual hallucinations and falls in a case with imaging-supported possible normal-pressure hydrocephalus. A separate shunt member tracks neuropsychiatric and functional measures. Neither measures a dried fig exposure, and the clinical cases are distinct.

fit: two Parkinson colitis cases and changes in medication route
assessment: Two case reports and a literature review track microscopic colitis during oral dopaminergic therapy and resolution following treatment changes. The observations concern bowel symptoms and drug routes. Dietary fig and visual episode frequency are outside the comparison.

fit: timed diagnostic chart features with linked neuropathology
assessment: The autopsy-linked study uses onset data for clinical features from 949 patients who developed parkinsonism within three years of disease onset. The model predicts later neuropathological classification using clinical history. Occurrence or onset of symptoms provides no culinary exposure or episode-rate comparison.

fit: blood pressure variability and cross-sectional Parkinson hallucinations or psychosis
assessment: The combined item or treated psychosis definition classified 46 of 121 Parkinson participants. An association between that group and blood pressure variability does not identify the frequency of visual episodes or any food exposure.

fit: meal timing in a blood pressure case series with cognitive outcomes
assessment: The series links caregiver-recorded cognitive fluctuations in four people with Parkinson disease dementia to immediately preceding low blood pressure on ambulatory monitoring. Meal timing appears in the plots and the authors propose more detailed food documentation in future studies. Visual hallucinations are recorded in case histories, rather than as the events associated with meals. No fig is identified and the study gives no comparable visual episode frequency.

fit: visually elicited event counts and clinical-history groups
assessment: In eleven participants, the controlled VR procedure records 17 misperceptions and six visual hallucinations. The counts come from the laboratory setting. No dried fig comparison or naturalistic duration measurement follows a dietary exposure.

fit: patient-specific metabolic predictions and dietary inference limits
