assessment: The study applies genome-scale models to infer patient-specific metabolite secretion patterns and summarize candidate Parkinson biomarkers. Predicted metabolites, including vitamin-related compounds, are distinct from a measured dietary source. It records no dried fig intake or visual episode frequency after food.

fit: mouse behavior used as a proxy for visual hallucinations
assessment: The experiments distinguish locomotion, staring, eye-tracking and responses in a pharmacological mouse model. Observable behaviors are proxies for an inferred state and carry no patient account of spontaneous visual episodes. The original does not administer dried fig.

fit: tissue findings and clinical hallucinations reported in prior studies
assessment: The review compares proximity ligation approaches to characterize alpha-synuclein oligomers. It cites a tissue association with visual hallucination presence in dementia with Lewy bodies. This is a cited neuropathological association without a culinary exposure or clinical recurrence measure.

fit: clinical sleep and psychiatric onset in dementia with Lewy bodies
assessment: The 359-person clinical series groups dementia with Lewy bodies participants by sleep profiles and relates them to disease onset characteristics. A psychiatric-onset group and sleep symptom prevalence do not supply a dried fig exposure or a rate of recurrent visual episodes.

fit: abstract-depth comparison for grouped dried fruit and diagnosis risk
assessment: The publisher abstract reports a generic dried-fruit risk association for Parkinson diagnosis. It does not distinguish figs, individual clinical symptoms or independence from earlier genetic exposure inputs. Main tables remain open.

fit: congress members on separate diet and Parkinson psychosis questions
assessment: The complete published congress supplement contains separate whole-diet protocols, a nutrition education pilot, dietary risk associations and medication or surgery psychosis analyses. No inspected member exposed a Parkinson cohort to dried figs and tracked visual episode frequency. The whole-diet, constipation and psychosis findings belong to distinct sets of participants.

fit: nonmotor features across PSP and Parkinson diagnostic groups
assessment: The cross-sectional comparison tracks synuclein-related and nonmotor features in Parkinson disease and two progressive supranuclear palsy phenotypes. The comparison of symptom patterns and biomarker status does not measure timing after dried fig or Parkinson visual event rates.

fit: resting EEG and visual symptom status in dementia with Lewy bodies
assessment: Resting high-density EEG compares 33 early dementia with Lewy bodies participants with 21 controls. Visual hallucination and REM sleep behavior status are examined separately in relation to alpha-band connectivity. There is no monitored fig exposure or change in the number of visual episodes.

fit: structural MRI comparison with matching medRxiv cohort
assessment: The journal results analyze 83 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and 86 controls after quality control, as in the May preprint. Cortical shape and thickness, regional transcriptomic maps and connectivity are measured or compared. The design contains no food exposure or within-person visual episode-rate outcome.

fit: task-evoked visual processing with Parkinson visual symptoms
assessment: The clinical sample from NCT03661125 comprised 18 people with Parkinson disease without hallucinations and 20 meeting Parkinson psychosis criteria. A dedicated interview characterizes visual phenomena. The experiment compares visual mismatch EEG and model-based connectivity, with no food intervention or food-timed clinical episode rate.

fit: observational Parkinson infusion outcomes and adverse reports
assessment: Ten observational studies of continuous subcutaneous levodopa strategies contributed to the review. Motor effects and reported neuropsychiatric adverse events concern medication exposure and heterogeneous follow-up, without a dietary ingredient comparison.

fit: pure autonomic failure with visual misidentification and glucose-associated hypotension
assessment: The original distinguishes a reported visual misidentification from a recorded glucose challenge and blood pressure drop. The clinical diagnosis and endpoints do not substantiate a relation between dried figs and Parkinson visual episodes.

fit: genetic Parkinson case with subcutaneous and oral drug changes
assessment: A case of PINK1-related Parkinson disease describes timed plasma drug measurements and neuropsychiatric observations while infusion, oral levodopa and a COMT inhibitor were adjusted. Several medication changes preclude a single-exposure comparison. Dried fig was not an exposure.

fit: visual hallucinations and real-world infusion discontinuation
assessment: Of 50 consecutive advanced Parkinson patients who initiated subcutaneous treatment, two discontinued after visual hallucinations and both had prior psychosis. This implementation report counts discontinuations, without a controlled dietary exposure or recurrent visual episode frequencies.

fit: practice observations separate medication, meals and adverse reports
assessment: The article draws on German clinicians' practical experience with subcutaneous levodopa and discusses protein and motor OFF timing as a possible clinical consideration. The clinical guidance and adverse-event discussion are separate. No individual dried fruit or food-timed visual outcome is tracked.

fit: distinguishing delusions from clinical visual hallucinations
assessment: The review includes seven eligible studies. It treats delusions, delusional misidentification and visual hallucinations as related but distinct outcomes. The source includes no dried fig intervention and supplies no fig-attributed recurrent visual episode counts.

fit: clinical observational adverse events after Parkinson infusion
assessment: The 77-person advanced Parkinson chart review records seven new hallucination cases during subcutaneous levodopa prodrug infusion, usually distressing and at night. The table separately counts other psychiatric events and reports median time to first hallucination of 14 days. This is onset during a drug exposure with treatment adjustments, with no dried fig intake or counts of repeated episodes.

fit: PPMI early hallucination-related status and brainstem MRI
assessment: The study uses PPMI structural scans and item 1.2 during screening or early follow-up as a proxy for hallucination-related status. The item does not separate all visual subtypes and modalities. MRI-derived volume and presence or absence of the broad proxy do not provide food-timed episode frequency.

fit: Parkinson minor phenomenon interviews and resting fMRI
assessment: The journal article uses 18 Parkinson participants with minor visual phenomena, 14 without hallucinations and 31 controls. Clinician assessments distinguish presence and passage phenomena, illusions or pareidolias, with overlap across categories. The paper describes cross-sectional functional connectivity and concurrent cognitive scores. The 2025 preprint describes the same Parkinson cohort.

fit: visual hallucinations after levodopa in juvenile monogenic parkinsonism
assessment: The original case records visual hallucinations with dopaminergic side effects during treatment. Neither episode frequency nor dried fig exposure is recorded. Dried blood spot and figure labels account for the lexical overlap.

fit: printed case proportion at presentation versus later subacute course
assessment: The 1984 retrospective series identifies 121 confirmed and 31 probable Creutzfeldt–Jakob cases, with possible diagnoses handled separately. In printed tables 4 and 5, visual hallucinations are recorded at presentation in 1% and during the subacute course in 17%. These are proportions of patients with the sign in a different disease and time window. The series supplies no dried fig exposure or Parkinson episode-rate estimate.

fit: 1984 interviews on distinct Ficus identities
assessment: Ojé is identified as Ficus insipida and renaco only as Ficus sp. Some plant teachers are described in contexts of dreams, dizziness or visions. No isolated exposure or clinical episode count is reported for dried edible fig.

fit: Clinical differential review, prior comparison of visual histories
assessment: Quinn describes visual hallucination history in diffuse Lewy body disease. The review also cites a comparison in which visual hallucinations and fluctuations were as common in pure Alzheimer disease, qualifying how specifically those symptoms distinguished diagnoses in the cited evidence. The source supplies diagnostic history without a new patient sample, a visual episode-frequency measure or dried-fig exposure.

fit: Parkinson treatment review, separate visual phenotypes and motor effects
assessment: Quinn distinguishes visual illusions, perceived presence, experiences with retained insight, and visual hallucinations. The review discusses psychotic symptoms during motor off periods and dietary protein in the context of levodopa response and motor fluctuations. The dietary discussion supplies no evidence for dried figs or a visual episode-rate comparison.

fit: Acute delirium and Parkinson medication differential review
assessment: Lloyd describes visual hallucinations in severe delirium and distinguishes symptoms arising during Parkinson therapy from symptoms attributable to disease. This is clinical diagnostic context. No separate visual episode rate or dried-fig comparison is reported.

fit: Vascular and Lewy body dementia differential review
assessment: Amar and Wilcock contrast vascular dementia with other dementias, including dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson disease dementia. The diagnostic box uses early prominent visual hallucinations as one contextual feature. The review reports no new symptom-frequency or dried-fig comparison.

fit: Author abstract of diagnostic tracer and perfusion comparison
assessment: The 7 versus 6 clinical dementia groups showed different imaging patterns. The abstract mentions hallucinations in background and does not measure episodes after food exposure.

fit: visual components among pooled hallucinosis and illusion reports
assessment: Of 129 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, 32 reported hallucinosis or illusions and 30 of those reported a visual component. Episode rate and dried fig exposure were not measured.

fit: historical allergy symptoms after dried culinary fig
assessment: A case describes itching, angioedema and dizziness after fresh fig, then similar allergic symptoms with kiwi and dried fig. The narrated history and sensitization testing give no hallucination frequency or Parkinson diagnosis.

fit: Parkinson apomorphine motor comparison, adverse-event texts pending
assessment: Colzi and colleagues followed 19 people with Parkinson disease and severe motor fluctuations. The abstract reports changes in dyskinesia and time spent off. Its frequency result refers to dyskinesia. Visual hallucination reporting in the complete follow-up remains unresolved.

fit: Parkinson visual hallucination history and urinary biomarker in levodopa users
assessment: The original abstract reports a nearly threefold group difference in mean urinary salsolinol. It compares treated patients with and without visual hallucinations and cites the dried-banana feeding study. The group association identifies a biomarker lead. It supplies no measured fig intake or repeated visual episode rate.

fit: Visual hallucination case, final diagnosis and main body pending
assessment: The case conference concerns an older patient with behavioral changes and visual hallucinations. The accessible primary opening and bibliographic data identify the case, with final diagnosis and timing details still open. The record supplies no verified dietary comparison.

fit: Primary outpatient sleep and hallucination/illusion overlap
assessment: Altered dreams overlapped with the combined hallucination or illusion category. Sleep fragmentation was not associated directly with this category in the model. A combined category is not a separate visual event rate.

fit: Cultured fungal isolates from Skoura dried figs
assessment: The 68 percent denotes 30 of 44 isolates from ten fig samples. The study describes fungi and processing. Toxin concentrations come from separate cited studies, and no Parkinson visual event was measured.

fit: randomized single-vine extract versus manzanilla in early Parkinson disease
assessment: The extract arm improved on the motor total with worse resting tremor. The original records one transient hallucination labeled without modality in the event table. This is a different plant and preparation.

fit: Complete issue and independent clinical vignettes
assessment: Pages 209 and 251 describe an insulinoma evaluation with visual history and a suspected grapefruit–medication interaction with acute visual and auditory hallucinations. They are separate members and neither compares dried-fig intake in Parkinson disease.

fit: oral fruit extract and rat drug-challenge task timings
assessment: The larger fruit-extract group shows shorter reward-chamber and transfer latencies than scopolamine alone. The smaller group contrasts are inconclusive. The test uses a fruit extract and maze proxies, with no clinical visual episodes.

fit: Dried fig and oxidative measures in rat lung and muscle

fit: healthy participants chewing celery

fit: cooked mixed-vegetable ratatouille containing celery

fit: celery stalk in the airway after a meal

fit: raw carrot identified in Parkinson case-control questionnaire
assessment: Raw carrot was a questionnaire item. No hallucination-frequency comparison was reported.

fit: curcumin phytosome combination and oral regimen tolerability

fit: turmeric in the original-source scope for swallowing difficulty severity

The original reports do not isolate culinary turmeric or a Parkinson swallowing or pain result.

fit: curcumin extract alongside a weight-loss diet in PCOS
assessment: No separate Parkinson symptom or culinary turmeric result was recorded. Within-group metabolic changes do not establish a between-group clinical response.

fit: turmeric-colored bread and child sensory preference

fit: thyme sniffing in multi-odor postinfectious smell rehabilitation

fit: thyme-containing multi-ingredient product and measured olfaction in acute rhinosinusitis

fit: inhaled thyme extract in a fixed four-odor post-traumatic regimen

fit: confirmed thyme odor in multi-odor post-traumatic training
assessment: The 2024 original Methods confirm thyme in fixed training and in the first rotating month. They explicitly identify the same cohort as the 2021 report. The whole sniffing program does not estimate an isolated or oral thyme effect in Parkinson disease.

fit: thyme odor within a 12-scent post-COVID protocol
assessment: The nonrandomized comparison favored the odor program on total smell function. The study does not isolate thyme or test fresh thyme by mouth.

fit: uncontrolled piperine blend and digestive symptom reports

fit: isolated piperine with no constipation outcome in the abstract

fit: crude pepper extract and mixed gut model responses

fit: defined MCT and measured Parkinson fatigue, without virgin oil isolation
assessment: The likely ISRCTN13221188 companion has 16 completers, fixed phase order and a C8/C10 supplement by participant product choice. No virgin coconut oil was identified as an assigned exposure.

fit: virgin versus refined coconut oil and acute perceived exertion

Acute exertion is distinct from Parkinson fatigue severity.

fit: two soluble mango leaf extract doses and a transient mood-depression subscale

fit: dried mango offered among optional snacks and aggregate affect

fit: soluble mango leaf extract and exploratory POMS depression in healthy students

fit: isolated eugenol and gait-related tasks in MPTP mice

fit: injected allspice leaf extract and gross motor depression in rats

fit: lentinan and behavioral assays in Parkinson model mice
assessment: Behavioral improvement with isolated lentinan does not specify cooked food or rest tremor.

fit: lentinan carrier and Parkinson model behaviors

fit: lovage in a shared Parkinson vegetarian menu and composite motor outcome

fit: filtered dried-marjoram tea and aggregate motor examination

fit: marjoram in a honey mixture evaluated in people with Parkinson disease
assessment: The Methods give a named marjoram exposure and follow-up in 35 patients. Leaf preparation and walking speed were unreported.

fit: reported marjoram use and broad motor symptom frequencies

fit: oral corn oil comparator and sustained-attention task

fit: oral Parkinson trial vehicle and aggregate cognition

fit: reported pediatric exposure to product coded allspice oil

fit: Adults without diagnosed PD; multicomponent diet score with legume component; binary probable dream-enactment screen

fit: 101 people with isolated polysomnography-confirmed RBD; general legumes and estimated prodromal Parkinson probability
assessment: Observed legume associations concern estimated prodromal Parkinson probability and marker count rather than dream-enactment episode frequency; no canned chickpea intake or diagnosed Parkinson cohort is established.

fit: whole sweet pepper in two Parkinson diet menus and overall Part III motor examination

fit: oral Capsicum fruit extract and rearing in a rat motor model

fit: purified nonpungent Capsicum and accelerometer-recorded activity

fit: paprika vegetable in a Parkinson diet with gait in the motor examination

fit: isolated capsiate and timed 10 km running

fit: bedside cough by solid and liquid bolus in early Parkinson disease
assessment: Cough followed liquid in 40% and solid in 5% of 65 participants. The boluses were unnamed and the bedside screen supplied no baked-potato or instrumental aspiration result.

fit: maximum water swallowing volume and esophageal transit in Warsaw
assessment: The 2003 report gives mean 6.23 mL versus over 20 mL in controls. An earlier related report used the same tests in a smaller group with unverified overlap. The available reports give no baked-potato result.

fit: contrast jelly versus sugar water and immediate aspiration
assessment: Among 25 participants with Parkinson disease and dysphagia, 13 aspirated cup-administered sugar-water contrast. None of those 13 aspirated spoon-administered jelly contrast during the test. Texture and delivery differed. Baked potato, clinical choking and longer-term severity were outside the comparison.

fit: reported potato intake in a Parkinson dietary survey
assessment: Table 1 gives 21.7 versus 20.9 g of unspecified potatoes in 80 Parkinson cases and 69 controls, with no significant difference. Preparation and swallowing outcome were unreported.

fit: fatal choking autopsies and unavailable Parkinson food attribution
assessment: The publisher preview identifies the grape case as an infant. The food in the Parkinson case remains unverified.

fit: solid-food intake and swallowing in a Parkinson cohort
assessment: Potato is a food coding example and no patient-level potato preparation or swallowing estimate was recovered.

fit: applesauce, cracker, water and milk used in Parkinson swallowing assessments
assessment: Among 57 with Parkinson disease, 33 underwent FEES. The assessment pooled across foods and examinations, reporting 41/57 abnormal. It provides no result for baked potato or ingredient-specific choking.

fit: thickened and unthickened contrast liquids, outcomes pooled across diagnoses
assessment: Two of 85 dysphagia patients had Parkinson disease. The primary report separates viscosity groups and does not identify Parkinson-specific or named solid food outcomes.

fit: instrumental comparison of liquid and solid texture classes in Parkinson disease
assessment: The abstract reports tracheal aspiration in 46 percent of 24 patients and worse abnormalities with liquid boluses. The solid food ingredients and item-specific results remain unavailable.

fit: aspiration pneumonia in two geriatric units
assessment: The abstract reports grouped pneumonia and clinical context. Patient-level food identity and the full report are unresolved.

fit: baked or boiled potato options in a whole-diet comparison
assessment: The menu permits either preparation. No actual portion or comparison on the individual swallowing item was published.

fit: food examples in a large Parkinson dysphagia questionnaire
assessment: The questionnaire includes example foods and pooled responses from 470 people with Parkinson disease, without a baked potato comparison.

fit: human Parkinson endoscopy with named solid and liquid boluses
assessment: Biscuit increased swallow-trigger difficulty and residue, and thin milk was associated with aspiration. No potato exposure was tested.

fit: autopsy-confirmed asphyxia in a Parkinson case series
assessment: Five aspiration pneumonia deaths and three asphyxia deaths were identified among 16 autopsies. The accessible primary abstract supplies no individual bolus or potato preparation.

fit: video-recorded eating and swallowing observations
assessment: The related dissertation and report describe 24 Parkinson participants and distinguish swallowing from food handling. The accessible abstracts do not report menus or food-specific estimates.

fit: named liquid and biscuit in serial Parkinson swallowing assessments
assessment: The protocol names lemon juice and cornstarch biscuit. The 2014 report gives ten improved, five unchanged, and nine worsened after combined management. The likely overlapping 2013 report has conflicting figure and summary values. The reports supply no ingredient-level effect.

fit: biscuit mastication and pharyngeal residue during Parkinson videofluoroscopy
assessment: Fifty-six participants took a biscuit and two liquid textures. Biscuit images were used for mastication and residue. Airway outcomes were assessed with the thin liquid and do not establish baked potato choking.

fit: clinical volume-viscosity test
assessment: The study assessed water and thickener among 19 screen-positive patients. There was no potato preparation.

fit: cold water swallowing and dilute barium aspiration in a French cohort
assessment: The paper gives slower cold-water swallowing in early Parkinson and reports three aspiration events during barium imaging. The reported 5% overall uses a different denominator from the 31-person imaging subset. No baked potato or other solid was tested.

fit: reported potato intake by swallowing symptom status
assessment: The 72 participants with swallowing disturbances reported 67 versus 50 g/day of potatoes among the 528 without disturbances. Fried potato intake was similar. The potato preparation and whether intake preceded the symptoms are unresolved.

fit: bolus-specific endoscopic aspiration with water buttered wheat bread and wheat biscuit
assessment: The journal and dissertation describe one cohort. Dissertation tables identify PAS 6–8 in 30/119 on water, 3/119 on buttered bread and 3/117 on biscuit. All six solid-bolus ratings were silent aspiration and may overlap within participants. No potato was tested.

fit: fixed contrast jelly and aspiration-pneumonia prediction
assessment: The 2018 and 2022 reports represent one cohort of 184 and assess swallowing a common contrast jelly. Neither reports a baked-potato comparison.

fit: water, pudding, buttered bread and biscuit in a stimulation crossover
assessment: Table 3 has water aspiration in 1, 2 and 2 of 11 across three stimulation conditions and one biscuit aspiration with stimulation off. The fixed protocol used no potato.

fit: standardized potato-salad lunch and dysphagia
assessment: Existing eating difficulties were associated with intake. The study did not test dysphagia change after baked potato.

fit: named snacks and concurrent swallowing rehabilitation
assessment: Ice cream, cream puffs and sweet red-bean soup were examples of calorie additions during multimodal recovery. The study gives no baked potato exposure or isolated food result.

fit: boiled potato as a diagnostic solid bolus
assessment: Swallow studies excluded neurological disease. Baked potato and Parkinson symptom change were outside the design.

fit: roast potato obstruction with Parkinson status unreported
assessment: The case records an acute roast potato obstruction. The report does not identify Parkinson disease or compare swallowing difficulty by food.

fit: potato starch in soup and acceptability
assessment: The intervention evaluated taste, texture and other acceptability measures. Baked potato and swallowing difficulty efficacy were not tested.

fit: endoscopic swallowing outcomes during respiratory muscle training
assessment: The protocol used white bread, unnamed puree and dyed liquid. The primary comparisons are summed across bolus trials and do not isolate a potato effect.

fit: aggregate potato and Parkinson counts in a choking series
assessment: Table 1 lists three Parkinson cases, three potato obstructions and one french-fry obstruction in separate totals. It gives no patient-level linkage or preparation for potato.

fit: hospital incident narratives with named foods
assessment: The narratives include food identities, without a paired Parkinson and baked potato case or a comparative outcome.

fit: potato obstruction in a clinical dysphagia interview
assessment: The narrative names potato and a participant with traumatic brain injury. The preparation and an effect among Parkinson participants are unverified.

fit: named foods in a Parkinson videofluoroscopy protocol
assessment: Of 82 participants, supplementary Table S2 classifies the worst airway-entry outcome across the five bolus types as 49 subglottic aspirations, 16 supraglottic penetrations and 17 with no airway entry. It gives no bolus-specific counts or comparisons.

fit: Japanese hospital food-obstruction study
assessment: The report describes 300 food obstructions. Case-level linkage between Parkinson diagnosis and a potato preparation could not be confirmed.

fit: named rice and yogurt boluses in videofluoroscopy
assessment: The Parkinson cohort swallowed yogurt, rice porridge and boiled rice during testing. Airway invasion categories pool results across boluses, with no potato test or per-food estimate.

fit: oven-baked potato served during observed Parkinson meal
assessment: One participant with Parkinson disease was served boiled potatoes at one meal and oven-baked wedges at another. The observer reported no potato-specific swallowing response, confirmed portion consumed or isolated contrast.

fit: named fixed boluses in endoscopic swallowing tests
assessment: Applesauce and biscuit residue fell after mask training in 11 completers. The same boluses were used before and after, with no potato comparison.

fit: named shortbread bolus and texture ratings
assessment: Two analyses of the same 31-person sample document the contrast-coated cookie bolus. Separate ratings show more difficulty with hard and dry foods than soft foods. The reports do not test baked potato.

fit: named dry biscuit and vanilla pudding boluses
assessment: Penetration or aspiration occurred in 20 of 28 water tests, 15 of 33 vanilla pudding tests, and six of 27 dry biscuit tests. Rates are descriptive and exclusions differ by bolus. Baked potato was outside the study.

fit: named pineapple and pudding boluses with swallow-level outcomes
assessment: The author data reproduce the pooled trial scores. Two of 11 concordantly coded pineapple-and-juice baseline swallows and two of 32 pudding swallows reached the aspiration score range. These are protocol observations with different food volumes and trial schedules. No potato was tested.

fit: within-person swallowing test with named liquids
assessment: At 90 mL, 27 of 80 paired tests showed shallower airway invasion with carbonated mineral water, six worsened and 47 were unchanged. The comparison does not involve potato.

fit: shortbread and pudding in a respiratory coordination experiment
assessment: Cued bolus holding changed some respiration-swallow timing outcomes. The 20-person study gave no instrumental airway invasion or baked-potato result.

fit: airway-obstructing choking series including two Parkinson patients
assessment: The report describes 31 choking episodes among 18 psychiatric patients, two with Parkinson disease. It gives no case-linked food, preparation, or Parkinson-specific fatal outcome.

fit: videofluoroscopy of dry barium-coated toast before and after medication
assessment: In 15 people with Parkinson disease, toast oral-phase and initial swallow durations increased after levodopa. The article defines aspiration as persistent entry into the laryngeal vestibule. It includes no potato or baked-potato-specific endpoint.

fit: reported potato intake and clinical dysphagia assessment
assessment: Potato intake was reported weekly or monthly among 25 Parkinson participants. Preparation and a potato-by-swallowing-severity analysis are absent.

fit: barium-coated cracker in a clinical swallowing series
assessment: Aspiration was reported in 10 of 25 Parkinson participants and 21 of 82 symptomatic controls across four contrast preparations. Choking counts differ between tables and discussion. The solid preparation was cracker, with no potato test.

fit: IDDSI level 7 solid as an unnamed texture after combination therapy
assessment: The university abstract reports one DOSS-level improvement in three Parkinson participants with dysphagia. The exact solid and choking outcomes remain unverified. No baked-potato comparison.

fit: bread and water in a clinical assessment with observed choking
assessment: Observed choking was reported in 13% of 47 Parkinson participants and 0% of 47 matched controls across the protocol. The result is pooled across bread and water and supplies no potato effect.

fit: mashed and boiled potato in a mixed-diagnosis protocol
assessment: The protocol names mashed potato as a bedside test bolus and boiled potato on a modified tray. The results do not identify a Parkinson participant's potato exposure or response.

fit: named solid and liquid boluses in a Parkinson cohort
assessment: The protocol names Maria biscuit and juice–barium mixtures. Results are pooled by dysphagia status.

fit: dysphagia screening and grouped food intake in a Parkinson clinic
assessment: Sixteen of 55 participants screened positive for dysphagia. The reported diet measures give no individual baked potato comparison.

fit: indirect
assessment: One man with Parkinson and dementia progressed from a chopped diet to bite-sized foods without reported aspiration during repeated nutrition visits and adjusted textures. No baked potato was documented or compared.

fit: curry leaves listed in a multicomponent Parkinson diet with motor composite
assessment: The ingredient table does not confirm species, cooking or individual consumption, and the report gives no handwriting change or isolated curry leaf comparison.

fit: methanolic basil leaf extract and rodent motor tests
assessment: Rotarod times were 31.0 and 32.7 seconds versus 12.7 seconds with haloperidol alone, and catalepsy scores were lower. Taxonomic naming and group sizes are internally unclear. No fresh culinary leaf or clinical Parkinson outcome was tested.

fit: holy basil leaf extract and animal catalepsy
assessment: The higher-dose oral ethanolic holy basil extract was associated with lower catalepsy scores in mice under a reported comparison whose labels are unclear. Species, preparation, model and outcome differ from fresh culinary basil and human muscle rigidity.

fit: injected sweet basil extract and rotarod/stair tasks
assessment: High-dose injected extract increased rotarod time from 57.3 to 144.6 seconds and shortened stair task time from 35.8 to 29.3 seconds. The text conflicts with tables at the lower level. There was no isolated clinical symptom measure.

fit: separately numbered conference member with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-05.2-64 is a material comparison using processed basil seed mucilage. Its swelling and microscopy measures supply no fresh leaf exposure or Parkinson rigidity outcome.

fit: fresh basil in both Parkinson trial diet menus
assessment: Both diets list fresh basil in different dishes. Motor outcomes cannot isolate the ingredient or give a rigidity estimate by individual basil intake.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes rigidity, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: intranasal peanut-oil comparator in postviral olfactory loss
assessment: The oil group improved 3.88 TDI points on average. The adjusted difference between vitamin A and the oil comparator was inconclusive, and no untreated arm or oral preparation was used.

fit: Parkinson baseline turkey and general speech symptom
assessment: Very small positive correlation in duplicated plots reports no sound-level or intelligibility-specific measure and no baking or roasting preparation.

fit: pooled poultry item and total Parkinson symptom score
assessment: The combined poultry comparison gives no identifiable roasted turkey exposure or speech intelligibility estimate.

fit: levodopa challenge and Parkinson acoustic speech measures
assessment: A limited acoustic effect and poorer on-state voice measures associated with axial dyskinesia inform medication-state confounding. The study did not use a turkey meal or test its effect on intelligibility.

fit: diet-pattern association and probable REM sleep behavior disorder
assessment: Questionnaire-defined probable RBD was measured in participants without Parkinson disease. A separate chard estimate and prospective dream-enactment counts were unavailable.

fit: injected corn oil and motor behavior
assessment: The corn oil arm did not clearly improve motor proxy outcomes over saline. It gives no estimate for refined oral corn oil and human bradykinesia.

fit: oral corn oil with injected toxin and time to combined motor signs
assessment: Combined phenotype appeared in 14.00 versus 20.21 days (p<.0001) in the two toxin groups. Oil-only animals did not exhibit the composite during observation. Animal replacement, oil grade, composite timing and species limit transfer to clinical bradykinesia severity.

fit: corn oil in the original-source scope for bradykinesia severity
assessment: Page 3 mentions shared corn oil vehicle in a cited mouse skin photoaging experiment. No separately attributable corn oil or Parkinson symptom effect is reported.

fit: corn oil changed in oral feed with stepping and locomotion measures
assessment: Corn oil went from 10 to 4 g/kg as safflower and soybean oil and DHA also changed. Four motor assays showed no clear diet effect. The mice and formulation do not estimate refined corn oil and human bradykinesia.

fit: corn oil in mixed oral diets with timed motor measures
assessment: Corn oil was 30, 25 and 10 g/kg across three formulas. High-DHA mice did worse on the pole test and retained late open-field activity. The formula changed several ingredients and no oil grade was reported.

fit: corn oil changed in a diet with a forelimb endpoint
assessment: The study did not isolate corn oil or its refining grade. The forelimb stepping result followed simultaneous changes to feed and exercise in mice.

fit: corn oil gavage vehicle and pole timing in a lycopene mouse study
assessment: Pole turn and descent times measure model motor performance. Control groups are described inconsistently, and oil-only bradykinesia contrasts and refining grade are unverified.

fit: cold-pressed pumpkin seed oil and broad neurobehavior after colchicine in rats
assessment: The primary preview verifies cold-pressed oil and lists open-field and elevated-plus-maze outcomes. The precise challenge route and an attention-specific result remain unverified.

fit: oral nutmeg extract and sucrose intake in rotenone-exposed rats
assessment: Sucrose intake increased, a reward-related surrogate. The study does not measure Parkinson apathy or culinary nutmeg.

fit: acute drooling after concentrated oral laurel decoction
assessment: One infant presented with drooling together with other acute symptoms after repeated concentrated decoction. No ground exposure or graded Parkinson drooling outcome.

fit: blinded oral bay leaf extract trial in healthy adults
assessment: The records identify a controlled bay-leaf extract study. Its original outcomes, endpoint scope and patent overlap remain open.

fit: ground bay leaf capsules in a type 2 diabetes trial
assessment: The metabolic trial tested ground bay leaf and excluded neurologic disease. Drooling was unmeasured.

fit: acute drooling during a bay leaf foreign-body episode
assessment: The primary excerpt describes gagging, drooling and cough after lodging during a meal. A fragment was identified in contemporary reporting. No ground preparation, Parkinson diagnosis or drooling scale was reported.

fit: human leaf extract tablet and salivary weight
assessment: Single intake increased salivary weight in the extract arm relative to baseline. Saliva output is a different outcome from drooling severity.

fit: blueberry powder in juice and composite motor outcomes
assessment: An institutional announcement reports preliminary walking-variability observations without a trial ID or quantitative results. Facial expressiveness remains unreported.

fit: mixed dietary patterns include optional raw or frozen blueberries; aggregate motor score
assessment: Menus allow blueberries but selection and consumption are unverified; UPDRS Part III total includes facial expression and no facial item or isolated blueberry estimate is reported.

fit: clinical facial palsy with earlier combined herbal use
assessment: The case timeline records no facial improvement during prior Nigella and rosemary use. The formulation and separate response are unreported, and the diagnosis was a structural peripheral lesion.

fit: isolated thymoquinone and peripheral facial nerve electrophysiology
assessment: An isolated constituent improved measured facial nerve conduction outcomes after traumatic injury in rabbits. No ground seed or Parkinson facial expressiveness was tested.

fit: caraway seed extract and essential oil in mouse motor coordination testing
assessment: Neither injected preparation clearly changed rotarod retention compared with vehicle. The coordination task did not measure stride length or ground caraway ingestion.

fit: isolated S-(+)-carvone and mouse locomotor activity
assessment: Injected carvone reduced spontaneous movement at early time points. Locomotor activity, plant constituent and study population differ from the ground-caraway stride claim.

fit: aqueous curry leaf extract and toxin-model motor tests
assessment: Table 2 reports rotarod falls under a rigidity label. Bar-test immobility was shorter with the extract. Neither test quantifies clinical muscle rigidity.

fit: curry leaf fractions and drug-induced catalepsy
assessment: The fractions prolonged haloperidol-related bar-test immobility. No muscle tone or cooked curry leaf comparison was measured.

fit: methanol curry leaf extract and haloperidol bar-test immobility
assessment: The acute mouse experiment reported shorter bar-test immobility. Muscle tone and cooked leaf were untested.

fit: curry leaves in a Parkinson diet menu with composite motor score
assessment: The menu lists curry leaves and UPDRS III includes rigidity. Leaf preparation and the individual rigidity score are unreported.

fit: rye bread named in a Parkinson food questionnaire
assessment: Rye bread was separately listed in a 26-Parkinson and 26-control questionnaire. The study measured blood mycotoxins and intake associations, with no assigned bread or voice measurement.

fit: rye kernel bread and mood and cognitive measures
assessment: A crossover assigned rye and white wheat breads and measured cognition and mood. No vocal loudness outcome or Parkinson cohort.

fit: self-reported voice handicap in a Parkinson whole-diet comparison
assessment: Self-reported handicap scores favored the ketogenic arm in the reported changes. No rye bread intake or objective acoustic voice volume was identified.

fit: original source context with different preparation, outcome, attribution or population
assessment: Four participants had baseline end-dose dystonia. The comparative outcomes are broader fluctuations and dyskinesia under different levodopa formulations. No fresh-sage exposure.

fit: Parkinson medication crossover and composite motor outcomes without fresh sage
assessment: The matched parent DIVE-I trial measured dyskinesia and bradykinesia combined. Secondary measures combine dystonia with dyskinesia or other motor indicators. No separate dystonia effect or fresh sage. Overlap with the later case remains unverified.

fit: traditional sage and broad antispasmodic wording
assessment: Common sage's reported antispasmodic reputation is not an observed dystonia response after fresh leaves.

fit: symptom measurement, clinical outcome or comparison without the frozen culinary exposure
assessment: A Parkinson case describes less dystonia during a change to dopaminergic treatment. It provides a clinical symptom observation without fresh-sage exposure or an independent control.

fit: symptom measurement, clinical outcome or comparison without the frozen culinary exposure
assessment: The Parkinson diary cohort records off-dose dystonia at baseline in 17 of 28 participants. Rater agreement concerns motor states and supplies no fresh-sage or dystonia-severity response.

fit: oral sage extract and peripheral motor function
assessment: Footprint recovery after nerve injury gives no measure of dystonia.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes facial expression, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: Capsicum annuum extract and rat rearing activity
assessment: The original Figure 1 describes rearing and the other results describe biochemistry from a different preparation. It gives no culinary paprika or rest-tremor measurement.

fit: acute dermal capsaicinoid gel and nonspecific rat tremor
assessment: The full Table 2 lists transient tremor at higher dermal exposure with other signs. There is no Parkinson population, resting-state measure or oral ground paprika exposure.

fit: isolated oral capsaicin and acute rodent tremor observations
assessment: Tremor was reported among severe acute signs in some mice. The study did not isolate rest tremor severity or use a Parkinson population or culinary ground spice.

fit: corn oil capsule placebo and planned Epworth scores in soldiers
assessment: The official protocol names corn oil and a planned daytime sleepiness scale. Results and linkage to the 2014 report remain open.

fit: corn oil as an active treatment comparator with planned ESS; linked results retracted
assessment: The registry supplies protocol context. The linked journal outcomes are ineligible after retraction.

fit: corn oil ethyl ester comparator and daytime sleepiness correlation in deployed soldiers
assessment: Opening original Methods says 106 agreed to participate. The abstract allocates 44 and 34 to treatment and the corn-oil ethyl-ester comparator. The original Epworth timepoint and outcome denominator remain unverified. Neither the active comparison nor the population fits refined culinary corn oil in Parkinson disease.

fit: corn oil in the original-source scope for daytime sleepiness severity
assessment: PDF p. 12 contrasts custom linoleic- and oleic-acid-rich diets in rats and reports thermal nociception and autonomic measures. The researchers replaced standard corn oil in both arms. This constituent context supplies no direct refined corn oil effect for the frozen outcome.

fit: corn oil as capsule placebo with a daytime sleepiness scale
assessment: The investigator's thesis gives arm-level Epworth scores with no clear difference at 4, 8 or 12 weeks. The comparison evaluated cannabidiol against the oil capsule and does not estimate refined corn oil's independent effect.

fit: banana-flavored grain reward in a macaque drug comparison
assessment: Four rhesus monkeys received a banana-flavored reinforcer. The later papers confirm flavored grain pellets. Drug assignment, uncertain fruit content and reinforcement outcomes leave eating raw banana for the named Parkinson symptom open.

fit: Listed banana in mixed options and anxiety items within composite distress
assessment: Bananas were among listed ingredients in optional commercial fruit smoothies. SCL-10 included fear and tension items, but the trial published only overall distress change and did not assign or quantify banana separately. No uncooked banana or Parkinson cohort result was reported.

fit: open randomized Cavendish banana trial with tension–anxiety rating
assessment: No significant between-group change in tension–anxiety in 20 healthy adults. The comparison was small and fruit processing was not specified.

fit: whole bananas and HARS outside Parkinson disease
assessment: Banana-only arm regression coefficient −7.84 (p < .001). Original conference abstract describes random allocation in a four-arm adolescent study. Preparation and full methods remain unavailable.

fit: whole bananas and HARS in schizophrenia inpatients
assessment: Four high-intake groups had lower post-treatment anxiety than controls. Nonrandomized or unclear allocation, different medication histories, and baseline imbalance limit transfer to raw banana in Parkinson disease.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-31-019 evaluates banana lectin as an experimental immunomodulatory input in work on allergic responses. This is a constituent, not a culinary banana anxiety intervention.

fit: banana in the original-source scope for anxiety severity
assessment: Clinical member 173526 on PDF p. 218 describes a banana with a mocha drink before syncope in a post-bypass hypoglycemia case. The mixed meal and metabolic outcome do not isolate raw banana or measure anxiety in Parkinson disease.

fit: source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits
assessment: P-728 records topical banana peel use on a finger lesion later diagnosed as carcinoma, without oral use or Parkinson outcomes.

fit: measured comparison or exposure context with a different preparation, outcome or population
assessment: A banana-like amyl acetate odor was tested under different treatment states. It is a sensory stimulus rather than raw fruit, and the study does not measure anxiety after ingestion.

fit: banana exposure and circulating versus rat tissue markers
assessment: The original reports increased circulating salsolinol after banana intake in six healthy adults. In a separate rat experiment, increases in plasma did not correspond to clear changes in striatum or nucleus accumbens. Anxiety and Parkinson symptom severity were not measured.

fit: verified original exposure, population or endpoint context
assessment: The clinical advice article lists a banana portion among several snack options in a discussion of levodopa-associated nausea. Separate sections discuss anxiety, treatment timing, and dyskinesia. Banana is a genuine suggested exposure. Preparation and measured response to that snack remain unspecified. The article reports no banana comparison for anxiety or dyskinesia.

fit: banana named as a prebiotic source in mental health review
assessment: No raw-banana anxiety contrast, banana subgroup or Parkinson-specific estimate accompanies the food list.

fit: fruit extracts and unrelated cell or animal endpoint
assessment: The source records true fruit and extract identities with antioxidative and other laboratory comparisons. It gives no outcome for the frozen culinary anxiety comparison.

fit: banana in the original-source scope for anxiety severity
assessment: A cited crop study concerns banana plant material and disease resistance. It supplies agricultural context for the named fruit without any food consumption or anxiety comparison.

fit: authenticated original with distinct ingredient preparation or endpoint limits
assessment: This review names bananas, lentils and oats as sources of different dietary fiber classes. Anxiety outcomes arise in separate microbiota or probiotic research. A food-list association is relevant exposure context without a comparison isolating any of those ingredients or a Parkinson postural-instability outcome. Any frozen ingredient effect requires a separately assigned or traceable culinary exposure and a matched symptom estimate.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: The clinical study compares Sniffin' Sticks, including banana as an odor stimulus, in Parkinson disease and REM behavior disorder groups and controls. The stimulus measures identification and classification, without banana ingestion or an anxiety outcome attributable to banana. Best-before dates are product logistics and provide no date-fruit and apathy comparison.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: The review describes salsolinol as a compound measured in some foods including banana and cites plasma and other model findings. Parkinson anxiety appears in disease background. A dietary biomarker and experiments with the isolated compound do not estimate raw banana's effect on clinical Parkinson anxiety. The review supplies no raw fig and rest tremor comparison.

fit: reported food categories and overeating
assessment: LBP2.005 records banana in a food-addiction grouping. The report measures food or overeating responses without testing raw banana and anxiety.

fit: fresh banana juice and levodopa exposure in rats
assessment: Lower drug exposure in three rats receiving fresh juice. Anxiety was not measured.

fit: combined nutrition support, banana-flavored formula option and anxiety
assessment: HADS anxiety declined from 14.88 to 9.07 with six weeks of uncontrolled individualized care. A liquid supplement was available in banana flavor. The study did not verify raw banana exposure or report an outcome by formulation or flavor.

fit: suspected interaction and other outcome
assessment: One case suggests reduced levodopa benefit. No anxiety result was available.

fit: postoperative randomized whole banana and SAS with arithmetic inconsistency
assessment: Reported anxiety means favor banana. The reported t statistic conflicts with means, SDs and group sizes. The postoperative comparison remains a low-weight lead.

fit: low
assessment: The Parkinson diet appendix lists pumpkin seed oil among several alternatives. Figure S2 reports total UPDRS III, not separate dyskinesia or Part IV effects. Oil grade, intake and ingredient contrast were not published.

fit: low
assessment: Haloperidol model work used methanolic pumpkin seed extract and reports improvements in broad motor functions. It supplies no cold-pressed oil arm or separately verified levodopa-induced or other dyskinesia measure.

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking
assessment: Vegetables were offered in conjunction with a reward. The sample was children, and neither adult symptoms nor the matched preparation were assessed. The registration gives n = 82, while the two arm counts in the poster add to 84.

fit: tomato in the original-source scope for executive function impairment
assessment: PDF pp. 58–59 compare tomato and other flavors in amino-acid and glycomacropeptide samples tasted by 67 people with phenylketonuria. The endpoint is liking, and the ingredient formulation gives no whole-tomato intervention or frozen symptom result.

fit: cooked tomato sauce intervention with oxidative biomarkers
assessment: A prepared tomato meal increased lycopene in men with prostate cancer. Executive and rigidity outcomes are unavailable.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: PO1.137 serves tomato sauce with both pasta conditions and measures appetite and breath hydrogen. The pasta contrast cannot estimate cooked tomato or the frozen neurological outcome.

fit: shared collection original source context
assessment: Whole-food tomato meals, including cooked sauce, are cited for oxidation and lycopene outcomes. No separate executive function result in diagnosed Parkinson disease.

fit: isolated lycopene in a rotenone rat model
assessment: Oral lycopene had favorable neurobehavioral results in toxin-exposed rats. The abstract lacks an executive outcome estimate and the exposure differs from cooked tomato.

fit: isolated lycopene and water-maze performance in a rotenone mouse model
assessment: The authors report favorable water-maze and tissue outcomes with isolated lycopene. The outcome and exposure differ from the frozen executive-function claim.

fit: Parkinson executive MoCA subsection after a whole-diet intervention
assessment: The ten-week Mediterranean diet comparison was favorable on the executive subsection in diagnosed Parkinson disease. It supplies no isolated cooked tomato treatment estimate.

fit: multicomponent fruit and vegetable capsules and TESEN in healthy adults
assessment: Capsules including tomato gave favorable within-period TESEN results. The report supplies neither a direct crossover contrast with uncertainty nor an isolated cooked tomato or Parkinson-specific estimate.

fit: boiled tomato powder in congee and cognitive processing in healthy older adults
assessment: Four-week auditory Cz P300 latency differed from control but eight-week comparisons did not. The study measured processing, memory and serum biomarkers in participants without Parkinson disease.

fit: pooled tomato paste and executive test in healthy adults
assessment: The randomized crossover executive index contrast was +0.7 (95% CI −1.9 to 3.4, q = 0.669). The first-period and all seven Table S4 and S5 executive-index sensitivity intervals also crossed zero. Both serving methods were pooled and the trial did not enroll a defined Parkinson cohort.

fit: three-extract formula and knee osteoarthritis pain versus naproxen
assessment: The original Persian Table 2 gives week-four VAS 4.53 versus 4.37 and inconclusive group p=.747. Both arms changed over time. Likely companion cohort to the separate English PGE2 report. No cracked pepper or Parkinson sample.

fit: inhaled black pepper essential oil and immediate NRS pain
assessment: n=54. Immediate median pain 3 versus 6 after 15 minutes of pepper oil or sesame oil inhalation, p<.001. Route, timeframe and population differ from the claim.

fit: oral isolated piperine and tail-flick response in rats
assessment: Longer withdraw latency versus vehicle under experimental dosing. This is a rodent reflex and isolated compound, with no cracked black pepper or clinical Parkinson pain.

fit: registered curcumin and piperine blend with stent-symptom outcome
assessment: Official record lists nine actual enrollees and a secondary stent-symptom questionnaire. No results posted. Single arm, multiple ingredients, no Parkinson group.

fit: verified original context with an exposure, population or endpoint mismatch
assessment: The overview summarizes curcumin in Alzheimer research, reports a traditional turmeric pain use, and cites purified piperine as a curcumin absorption modifier. Its mention of ginger names a botanical family. Retain turmeric pain tradition and black pepper constituent pharmacokinetics as different contexts. Neither reports a Parkinson pain comparison. The botanical family name is not grated ginger exposure.

fit: isolated piperine and animal nociception endpoint boundary
assessment: The abstract lists a nociceptive response assay, with grouped behavioral conclusions and no separately attributable pain estimate.

fit: piperine in a swallowing review without pain severity assessment

fit: ALA-varied developmental diets and olfactory behavior in mice

fit: EPA and DHA with olfactory training and postviral odor threshold

fit: nanomicelle curcumin and composite Parkinson scale

fit: reported use of turmeric products for voice care

fit: oral mustard rice and short-term whole-saliva collection in healthy volunteers

fit: unstimulated salivary flow in Parkinson disease without a food intervention

fit: rat salivary secretion after perfusion of a mustard constituent

fit: injected thyme extract in a rat brain ischemia balance test

fit: isolated carvacrol and coordination tasks in lesioned rats

fit: isolated thymol injection and rat motor tasks

fit: thyme extract and coordination tests in paraquat mice

fit: oatmeal and total Parkinson symptom burden

fit: diet-pattern scores and measured Parkinson apathy

fit: meal timing and Parkinson levodopa concentration variability

fit: sumac extract applied to Parkinson donor skin cells
assessment: No oral exposure, levodopa coadministration or medication-state outcome was included.

fit: marjoram infusion and composite nonmotor symptom score

fit: grapeseed oil enema and colon tissue injury in rats

fit: oral combined grapeseed oil carrier and colitis stool composite
assessment: The carbon-60 and grapeseed oil combination lowered a disease activity composite containing loose-stool and bleeding scores (p < .05). The study had no oil-only arm or constipation outcome.

fit: Leaf-enriched rice bran oil and rodent immobility outcomes

fit: Rice bran oil placebo and clinical Parkinson motor complications
assessment: Part IV was prespecified. The sources give no item 4.6 painful OFF-state dystonia estimate or isolated dystonia severity, and do not specify oil grade.

fit: chives on a Parkinson pilot diet menu and composite motor score
assessment: The Appendix A menu names chives and the pilot reports changes in UPDRS III. It gives neither chive preparation nor an ingredient-specific stride measure.

fit: chemical measurements in culinary oil pressed from roasted pumpkin seeds

fit: isolated p-coumaric acid and measured stride length in a haloperidol mouse model
assessment: Two higher purified-compound groups showed longer stride versus disease control. Oil concentrations are much lower than the tested isolated doses, with no established transferable effect.

fit: pumpkin seed extract and narrow-beam traversal in rotenone mice
assessment: Day-28 crossing time was 8.0 or 4.85 seconds with extract versus 29.25 seconds with rotenone alone. Traversal time differs from stride length, and the two publications describe one seed-extract experiment.

fit: methanolic Cucurbita pepo seed extract and measured stride length in a haloperidol rat model
assessment: Publisher Figure 4 shows longer stride at ascending extract levels than disease control. This applies to the extracted seed and animal model, with no toasted-oil or patient contrast.

fit: Cucurbita maxima seed ethanol extract and differing rod-task results

fit: pumpkin seed oil in a Parkinson diet and a composite motor score

fit: fermented red cabbage blend and DASS depression in healthy adults

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking

fit: oral red cabbage anthocyanin extract in aging mice

fit: sumac extract in Parkinson-derived fibroblasts

fit: Self-reported urinary volume symptom after brewed leaf tea

fit: sweet potato test bolus in a primate model
assessment: Sweet potato served as a shared chewing stimulus. Dyskinesia was outside the experiment.

fit: Curry leaf extract and coordination in a rat model

assessment: The iron product is a botanical extract rather than cooked curry leaves. The primary publication reports no adverse events but does not separately measure rest tremor and does not enroll Parkinson participants.

fit: curry leaves in a Parkinson diet menu with composite motor score
assessment: The menu lists curry leaves and UPDRS III includes resting tremor. Cooked preparation and the individual tremor score are unreported.

fit: PD pooled bean category and whole-diet drool association; no pinto exposure estimate
assessment: The drool association concerns total MIND score, not canned pinto beans or an ingredient-specific effect.

fit: reported fish intake and aggregated psychotic-like experiences among Swedish women
assessment: The published fatty-fish category shows associations in both directions across intake levels, with a broader psychotic-like symptom outcome.

fit: Parkinson diet plans list canned and pan-cooked salmon; a visual hallucination event occurred in ketogenic assignment

assessment: Water extract inhibited AChE and BChE, with a null dichloromethane result. There was no attention task.

fit: injected sumac fruit extract and avoidance learning in adult male rats
assessment: The abstract identifies longer dark-compartment entry latency with the lower extract dose. The task did not measure attention after eating ground sumac.

fit: injected sumac extract and avoidance learning in gonadectomized rats
assessment: Injected sumac extract lengthened avoidance-related latency in a gonadectomy model. Learning was measured in a shuttle box.

fit: olive oil grades and older adult gait speed

fit: extra-virgin olive oil in a factorial diet study with planned stride measures

fit: topical ozonized extra-virgin olive oil and pressure wound resolution

fit: topical extra-virgin oil comparator and rat wound microbiology

fit: topical extra-virgin olive oil comparator and rat tail withdrawal

fit: olive oil comparison arm and measured stride length

fit: olive oil diet and mouse footprint outcomes after focal stroke
assessment: Oil alone gave no clear improvement in reported footprint measures. The model was ischemic stroke and processing was unspecified.

fit: topical capsaicin and localized neuropathic pain

fit: independent myocardial infarction report after cayenne pill exposure
assessment: The author abstract reports a separate adult case. The conference item appears to describe the same report, with no separate culinary or Parkinson pain evidence.

fit: pepper and clove constituents in cardiac experiments

fit: oral red pepper powder and epigastric pain in functional dyspepsia

fit: oral ground red chili and urgency thresholds in healthy adults
assessment: Three days of 5 g/day ground Capsicum frutescens in capsules lowered first, moderate and severe rectal urgency thresholds relative to placebo. The pressure range elicited no pain threshold, and there was no Parkinson population.

fit: meal with ground red chili and acute abdominal pain in IBS-D

fit: colon-release whole ground red pepper and daily abdominal pain in IBS

fit: repeated red chili powder capsules and separate abdominal pain, burning and first rectal sensation endpoints in IBS-D

fit: topical capsaicin and experimentally provoked localized hand pain
assessment: Study participants in the pain group averaged 3.5/10 before the training task. No participants in the NoPain group reported pain. Skin provocation cannot estimate Parkinson pain after consuming ground cayenne.

fit: commercial ground red chili and separate acute pain and burning outcomes
assessment: In a double-blind randomized crossover, 15 healthy adults and 15 people with nonerosive reflux disease consumed commercial ground Capsicum frutescens or placebo in capsules. The reflux group’s postprandial abdominal burning scores were 2.2 ± 2.5 versus 0.3 ± 0.8 (p < .05). Abdominal pain was collected separately and was inconclusive, as were both pain and burning comparisons in the healthy volunteers. The red chili cultivar and clinical context differ from ground cayenne and Parkinson pain in 0448.
