fit: Fibromyalgia stigma extract versus duloxetine and Global Fatigue Index
assessment: Change difference +0.68 (95% CI −6.52 to +7.87). Active comparator, non-Parkinson cohort and extracted stigma.

fit: saffron water extract syrup and fatigue in multiple sclerosis
assessment: One-arm Table 2 showed lower reported fatigue. Its baseline mean exceeds the described untransformed scale range. No comparator or Parkinson outcome.

fit: saffron in the original-source scope for fatigue severity
assessment: Abstract P976 on PDF pp. 356–357 compares saffron pills and placebo in 66 people with knee osteoarthritis. Both groups changed on WOMAC and the abstract does not give an interpretable separate between-group result for the frozen symptom.

fit: saffron suspended in fly feed and separate climbing and survival outcomes
assessment: The in vivo feed and distinct crocetin arms are verified. Climbing and life span do not measure fatigue severity.

fit: original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint
assessment: The SF-36 energy/fatigue score improved within the saffron extract arm (p=.001). Change versus placebo was inconclusive. This perimenopause trial tests a standardized extract.

fit: clinical saffron comparisons with other endpoints in a cognition review
assessment: Table 1 saffron rows concern Alzheimer disease or mild cognitive impairment. Separate rosemary trial describes mental fatigue. No measured saffron fatigue contrast.

fit: preparation, endpoint or population context from an authenticated source
assessment: The fatigue mention points to a prior pooled mood review across preparations and populations. There is no independent dried-saffron Parkinson fatigue estimate.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: Caffeine is discussed as a DLB risk variable. Coffee and olive-oil constituents, saffron stigma and spearmint extract occur in distinct laboratory or mechanistic examples. No matched culinary intervention and symptom comparison appears for the assigned coffee, saffron, spearmint and olive oil scopes. Disease risk and protein behavior are separate outcomes from clinical symptom change.

fit: original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint
assessment: The review discusses fatigue in exercise, energy and quality-of-life context. No independent clinical Parkinson fatigue estimate for dried saffron is given.

fit: reviewed fatigue adverse-event counts in several non-Parkinson trials
assessment: The review traces the original Alzheimer comparisons and contains their same denominators. The source records are related separately and the review adds no independent efficacy comparison.

fit: verified original context with an exposure, population or endpoint mismatch
assessment: The review includes a saffron hydroalcoholic extract and endurance-training experiment in rats. It separately discusses an oligonol mixture from lychee and green tea and isolated EGCG in disease or mechanistic models. Mitochondrial outcomes and training synergy do not supply clinical insomnia or fatigue estimates for saffron. The extracts and blends give no brewed-green-tea fatigue effect.

fit: dried stigma powder in tablets and matching fatigue outcome
assessment: Fatigue scores favored saffron in the randomized Parkinson trial. The original registration omitted the standalone fatigue scale, and the first archived revision listing the scale follows manuscript receipt. The tablet regimen and outcome chronology limit transfer and confidence.

fit: isolated piperine plus levodopa and rat movement composite
assessment: The axial dystonia assessment was included in a total abnormal involuntary movement score, without a separate dystonia estimate. The model intervention used isolated piperine with levodopa.

fit: topical grapeseed comparator and sleep duration
assessment: Two-week wrist application showed no clear lavender-versus-grapeseed differences in tracker-derived total, light or deep sleep. There was no oral or untreated comparison, and insomnia severity was unreported.

fit: oral grapeseed oil cookie and registered sleep questionnaire
assessment: The oral cookie comparison registered correlations of blood linoleic acid with questionnaire sleep. The published reports do not provide those estimates. No Parkinson participants or insomnia endpoint were identified.

fit: nonoral grapeseed comparison and registered hospital sleep outcomes
assessment: Grapeseed oil on gauze was compared with lavender and usual care for planned hospital sleep quality and duration. The terminated study has no posted outcome estimates.

fit: oral grapeseed oil cookie and registered sleep quality
assessment: The healthy-adult pilot plans a correlation involving global sleep quality after an oral grapeseed oil cookie. No results are posted, and the study does not measure Parkinson insomnia severity.

fit: high-linoleic cookie and registered insomnia severity
assessment: The single-arm study plans an Insomnia Severity Index, actigraphy and EEG in adults with insomnia symptoms. The oil is unnamed. It is not yet recruiting and no results are posted.

fit: oral essential oil and measured whole stomach emptying
assessment: Nonsignificant gastric results across baseline and both drug contexts differ from the detected intestinal inhibition. The tested oil had no levodopa or clinical fluctuations arm.

fit: oral fruit tea and clinical postoperative bowel recovery
assessment: An earlier return of flatus and bowel movements cannot distinguish gastric emptying or levodopa wearing-off.

fit: fennel oil and anethole in drug delayed emptying
assessment: The oil and compound improved experimentally delayed emptying in mice. A normal-baseline anethole comparison did not indicate acceleration. No oral toasted seed or levodopa arm.

fit: oral extract and loperamide delayed stomach emptying
assessment: Reduced retention in drug-challenged mice is a relevant mechanistic lead. Whole seeds, levodopa and clinical daily OFF time remain unmeasured.

fit: fennel seed infusion on excised stomach muscle
assessment: Proximal relaxation and increased antral amplitude establish distinct regional muscle effects. The protocol cannot estimate whole-stomach emptying or clinical OFF time.

fit: registered external fennel and postoperative ileus
assessment: Topical heated fennel and planned ileus outcomes do not estimate oral exposure or Parkinson OFF time. Registry results are absent.

fit: peanut oil as injected carrier in a primate parkinsonism model
assessment: Freezing contributes to the composite motor scale. The paper gives no separate freezing frequency or isolated oil comparison.

fit: isolated oral thymol and endurance, grip and coordination in accelerated-aging mice
assessment: Treated mouse treadmill distance roughly doubled from baseline and the control average stayed near baseline. Grip strength was near baseline after thymol versus a 36% decline in control. Coordination favored thymol. Single-compound exposure, survivor analyses and no length-of-stride measure. Earlier GSA abstract and mouse work overlap in source lineage.

fit: dried oregano infusion and mouse coordination
assessment: Higher-dose infusion reduced rotarod retention and slowed chimney climbing. This leaves stride length following fresh oregano unresolved.

fit: oregano essential oil and rotarod in healthy rats
assessment: Rotating-rod retention was inconclusive and high-dose males showed more exploration. Neither result measures stride length after fresh oregano in Parkinson’s.

fit: Randomized pharmaceutical butylphthalide adjunct in Alzheimer patients with a composite that includes hallucinations
assessment: The BEHAVE-AD score is reported only as a composite; no visual-hallucination item or frequency, Parkinson sample, or dried celery-leaf exposure is reported.

fit: methanolic celery seed extract and behavioral outcomes in alcohol-exposed mice
assessment: Groups have contradictory dose labels in the protocol and Results. Locomotion, stereotypy and social measures supply no visual hallucination counts. Seed preparation and model do not match the culinary Parkinson claim.

fit: celery seed hypertension crossover safety and psychological outcomes
assessment: The safety and mental-health reports belong to one trial family and use different analysis counts. The authors reported BAI and BDI from the seed-extract study. The specific adverse-event table and a visual hallucination outcome remain unverified.

fit: standardized celery seed extract and diary safety in metabolic syndrome
assessment: The 14-per-arm trial reports mild adverse events with no clear group difference. The formulation was seed extract with substantial butylphthalide content. No hallucination-specific outcome or dried-leaf group.

fit: independent venlafaxine case with transient visual hallucinations
assessment: The symptoms began after drug initiation and resolved while the drug continued. Recent alcohol withdrawal and laboratory abnormalities were alternatives. No celery exposure or Parkinson cohort.

fit: dried celery leaf powder with thyroid case outcomes
assessment: The case involves 45 days of dried leaf powder and reports thyroid symptoms. Visual hallucination frequency and Parkinson outcomes were unmeasured. Powder cessation coincided with methimazole.

fit: pharmaceutical butylphthalide and a composite questionnaire with hallucinations
assessment: The PDQ-39 total includes a question grouping distressing dreams or hallucinations. No item-level or separate visual outcome is published. Itemized adverse-event counts and the reported total differ. The official registry remains inaccessible.

fit: celery extract of unspecified plant part and a thyroid case with blurred vision
assessment: The case separately reports blurred vision during a thyroid presentation. The product is an extract of unspecified plant part, and hallucination frequency was unmeasured. Extract cessation and methimazole began together.

fit: same Khalid celery-root case and secondary symptom report
assessment: The 2016 primary abstract confirms mania and elevated venlafaxine. The 2022 review attributes unspecified hallucinations to that same patient. Its nearby explicitly visual report concerns a different ginseng case. The primary full body, onset and modality remain unverified.

fit: historical mixed preparation and unquantified case impressions
assessment: Four-page original discusses celery stalks and a proposed fluid extract before a multi-ingredient product. Case reports provide no isolated celery, identified dried leaf or visual hallucination frequency.

fit: dried stem-and-leaf powder with official metabolic registry and general safety monitoring
assessment: Official IRCT20100223003408N8 lists metabolic outcomes. The article reports 50 randomized, 36 analyzed and no side effect attributed to celery during general calls. It gives no hallucination ascertainment, leaf-only contrast or Parkinson group.

fit: rice bran emulsion oral spray and TOMASS after head and neck radiotherapy
assessment: Swallowing test outcomes were inconclusive, while the separate subjective dry-mouth measure improved modestly.

fit: Authenticated rice oil odor control and measured swallowing in dysphagia
assessment: Control repetitive saliva swallowing and both water swallow tests had no clear pre-post changes. Six participants had unspecified neurodegenerative disease, with no subgroup estimate or oral oil exposure.

fit: rice bran oil placebo and composite Parkinson outcome
assessment: Registry and conference sources report composite outcomes and no chewing and swallowing item estimate. The placebo oil grade and active formulation carrier are unspecified.

fit: isolated raspberry ketone and behavioral outcomes in stressed mice
assessment: Forced swim, tail suspension, locomotion and sucrose preference measured depression-related and activity proxies after oral isolated ketone. No whole frozen Rubus fruit or separate anxiety endpoint. This is distinct from the retracted 2022 work.

fit: raspberry juice powder and raised maze behavior after nicotine cessation
assessment: Applicant reports lower closed-arm time with juice powder in mice. The exposure and behavior differ from frozen raspberries and clinical Parkinson anxiety.

fit: red raspberry powder and mood in older adults with overweight or obesity
assessment: The completed registry schedules Profile of Mood States at baseline, two and six hours and posts no results. The 2023 investigator report gives no separate tension or anxiety estimate. A possible related serum assay supplies no mood values or independently confirmed participant linkage. The tested exposure is freeze-dried raspberry powder in a non-Parkinson cohort.

fit: dried mixed berries and state anxiety in healthy older adults
assessment: After 12 weeks the state-anxiety change favored the dried berry mixture versus cocoa in an exploratory Dunn comparison (reported z = -1.88, p = .031, conventionally about .060 two-sided). Within the berry arm p = .185. Raspberry was 16.7% of the dried mixture. The comparison cannot isolate frozen raspberry, and the analyzed volunteers did not have Parkinson disease.

fit: raspberry in the original-source scope for anxiety severity
assessment: The cross-project Alaska Native coping analysis on PDF pp. 393–394 reports raspberry gathering among several practices and foods. The separate berry paper on pp. 798–804 measures antioxidant properties. These leave frozen raspberry intake and clinical anxiety unmeasured.

fit: fruit extracts and unrelated cell or animal endpoint
assessment: The source records true fruit and extract identities with antioxidative and other laboratory comparisons. It gives no outcome for the frozen culinary anxiety comparison.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: The review lists dried raspberry as one source of kaempferol and summarizes isolated-compound and derivative experiments across nervous system disorders. Food-source listing and isolated flavonol outcomes do not establish anxiety after consuming the frozen raspberry preparation.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: Food-science study evaluates a different Rubus species as fermented juice and measures food and laboratory properties. No frozen raspberry consumption, anxiety outcome or Parkinson comparison is reported.

fit: original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint
assessment: Raspberry polysaccharides altered gut metabolites in an animal comparison without a frozen raspberry and anxiety result.

fit: mixed thawed berry smoothie and negative affect
assessment: PANAS negative affect did not show a clear intervention effect. The drink contained four fruits including raspberry and the trial did not measure clinical anxiety.

fit: freeze-dried raspberry and mouse anxiety-related behavior
assessment: Twenty-four weeks of red or yellow raspberry did not change open-field grooming or defecation clearly. This was an Alzheimer model and the exposure was freeze-dried.

fit: clinical case or dietary history without a matched ingredient comparison
assessment: A severe arrhythmia case reports a dual-ingredient supplement containing raspberry ketones. It gives neither whole raspberries nor an isolated effect.

fit: raspberry juice powder and categorical anxiety in two smokers
assessment: Applicants report less anxiety during cessation counseling without concurrent matched control, arm-level numeric scores or Parkinson cohort. Later family publications reuse the same disclosure.

fit: mint-flavored gum and balance performance in Parkinson’s
assessment: Balance scores improved during chewing. Falls were not followed and the botanical flavor was unspecified.

fit: spearmint in the original-source scope for fall frequency
assessment: B-0162 presented spearmint as a pleasant odor in olfactory MRI in 10 patients with major depression. The post-treatment difference reported concerns the unpleasant comparison odor. Spearmint odor and BOLD response do not estimate the effect of eating fresh spearmint or a Parkinson symptom change.

fit: standardized spearmint extract and reactive agility
assessment: Some sensor task results improved and others were null. The study did not measure falls or fresh leaf ingestion in Parkinson’s.

fit: cruciferous vegetable recalls and estimated indole intake
assessment: The study includes broccoli, cauliflower and kale within a food inventory. Neither constituent exposure nor a symptom effect is established for a particular preparation.

fit: mixed garden produce distribution
assessment: The garden reported distribution of green beans, kale, chard and watermelon within a mixed harvest. The evaluation concerns program delivery without an ingredient-specific intake or clinical symptom measurement.

fit: cooked kale in a calcium questionnaire and falls in an education trial
assessment: The education arm had fewer reported falls by rank, with a median of zero in both arms. The study did not estimate roasted kale intake or effects.

fit: oral canola oil and a paced tapping imaging task
assessment: Motor BOLD decreased after canola oil during instructed tapping. No separate tapping-performance result, refined-oil confirmation or Parkinson sample.

fit: canola crossover and monitored paced finger-tapping rate
assessment: Tapping was 2.09 ± 0.27 Hz SEM across trials with no significant variation at the paced target. Speeded dexterity or accuracy and refining were unverified.

fit: canola oil in mixed oral diets with limb motor measures
assessment: Canola oil was 10 g/kg in control feed and absent from both alternate formulas. The motor results concern whole chow diets in mice and no oil grade was reported.

fit: Crisco canola hand-arthritis comparator with invalid grip measurements
assessment: Grip data were discarded because the instrument failed. Product composition was reported without confirmed processing or a dexterity result.

fit: other whole oily fish and manual dexterity
assessment: Herring and mackerel meals modestly improved nondominant-hand peg test time relative to meat in children. The dominant-hand comparison was inconclusive.

fit: Chives listed in multi-ingredient Parkinson diet, preparation and actual individual amount unclear; no drooling result
assessment: Baseline UPDRS II total is not a reported saliva item or intervention comparison; the published follow-up reports UPDRS III total and cannot determine the effect of dried common chives on drooling.

fit: pooled legume intake according to self-reported swallowing status
assessment: Reported intake was higher among people with existing swallowing disturbances. Neither drooling severity nor canned kidney beans was measured.

fit: pediatric kidney bean allergy and cross-reactivity
assessment: The children experienced immediate hives or facial swelling following ingestion. The observations do not measure Parkinson drooling or visual hallucinations.

fit: pooled legume or bean intake and whole-diet drooling scores
assessment: Table 2 reports drooling against whole diet scores. Table S4 evaluates pooled bean or legume intake against aggregate symptom burden and does not identify species or preparation.

fit: oral allergic symptoms after a mixed meal and laboratory reactivity to canned kidney bean extract
assessment: The mixed chili provoked oral and systemic allergic symptoms. Extract from canned kidney beans showed IgE reactivity, while preparation and drooling after kidney bean ingestion remained untested.

fit: mixed thyme tablet and patient urgency intensity
assessment: Urgency intensity changed from 1.357 to 1.26 with p=.705. The uncontrolled mix does not separate fresh thyme, urgency frequency or Parkinson outcomes.

fit: thyme essential oil and ex vivo bladder contractility
assessment: Thyme oil decreased evoked tension but showed a concentration-dependent reversal in spontaneous variability in longitudinal guinea pig bladder strips. No urgency counts or culinary intake.

fit: Thymus vulgaris oil in a multi-oil cystitis comparison
assessment: The original abstract records void frequency after eight oils, with no separate urgency outcome or fresh thyme comparison.

fit: oat milk-associated acute allergy and dysphonia
assessment: Case records acute dysphonia with laryngeal allergy after oat milk. Loudness, ordinary rolled oat consumption and Parkinson disease were not studied.

fit: distinct oat milk hypersensitivity case with acute dysphonia
assessment: A distinct adult presented with dysphonia during acute allergy to oat milk. Neither speech loudness nor an ordinary rolled-oat effect in Parkinson disease was measured.

fit: oatmeal and total Parkinson symptom burden
assessment: The survey did not specify rolled oats or report acoustic voice volume.

fit: objective voice measures during Parkinson medication challenge
assessment: Levodopa ON and OFF testing provides endpoint context but no oat exposure.

fit: regional ethnopharmacological survey of gastrointestinal plant use
assessment: The El-Bayadh plant table and interview scope were verified. Its 62 species include no date palm. The separate 2000 Béchar report remains necessary to verify the date-fruit attribution.

fit: four date fruit extracts, paw volume and arthritis score
assessment: The original abstract reports smaller paw volume and arthritis scores. Pain-specific outcomes and score components are unavailable at this access depth.

fit: date-palm flower-bud extract on Parkinson plasma; ex vivo marker only
assessment: The common date palm plant part was a male flower bud. No person consumed dried dates or had pain measured.

fit: aqueous date cultivar extracts, animal edema
assessment: The 48-rat paw comparison reports more edema suppression for Jihl than Bouskri at the reported timepoints. The methods and figure caption disagree on dosing. No pain outcome or whole-date exposure was measured.

fit: pitted Deglet Noor active comparator in an older-adult protocol
assessment: The preprint confirms the date cultivar and recruitment for NCT05358210. No comparator estimate or dedicated Parkinson pain scale is reported.

fit: same registration and separate published denominator
assessment: The Persian original reports 64 participants and lower acute labor-pain VAS at 60 minutes, with an inconclusive 30-minute contrast. It cites the same date-syrup registration as Taavoni. Later comparison counts and control data limit interpretation.

fit: Ajwa fruit-pulp extract and experimental lung injury
assessment: Lung histology and tissue markers concern induced injury. The article does not measure chronic pain severity following consumption of whole dried fruit.

fit: Ajwa pulp fraction and chemical liver injury
assessment: This is a mouse liver outcome rather than clinical pain. Groups differ in the printed model-agent schedule, and the exposure was extracted pulp.

fit: pollen capsules and muscle soreness markers outside Parkinson disease
assessment: The 36-athlete trial found no clear difference in its markers. The accessible abstract and linked registration give no direct pain intensity result.

fit: untreated or yeast-fermented date-waste fibre fed to rats
assessment: The original abstract verifies an eight-week comparison of nutrition and tissue measures. It supplies no pain, stool frequency, or Parkinson endpoint and the diets use processed fibre.

fit: date palm sap and labor pain
assessment: The blinded comparison reported no clear change in pain ratings. Acute obstetric pain and sap differ from the frozen claim.

fit: date fruit extract and inflammatory surrogate endpoints
assessment: The mouse study measured paw edema and blood markers under induced inflammation. Pain severity was unmeasured.

fit: date remedy label and menstrual pain in a cross-sectional survey
assessment: Mean WaLIDD was 6.67 among 24 date-remedy responses and 6.07 among 131 other or unrecorded responses. The data give no timing or dried preparation and cannot establish an effect or a Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: whole date fruit and premenstrual symptoms
assessment: The accessible primary results give symptom timing and hormone associations. A between-group cramp-severity estimate remains unverified.

fit: date syrup in a controlled labor-pain comparison
assessment: The full primary pain report confirms shared registration with the labor-progress article. The second-stage pain means were 7.25 for date syrup, 7.67 for honey-saffron syrup and 8.47 for placebo.

fit: dried Zahedi dates and evoked heat response in mice
assessment: The recovered full report describes shorter hot-plate latency at month two in the date group. The within-group change and fruit-versus-chow comparisons were statistically inconclusive.

fit: date-containing mixture and menstrual pain
assessment: Two reports describe one uncontrolled cohort and lower pain scores after a drink containing dates, lemongrass and coconut water.

fit: date and herb mixture and menstrual pain
assessment: An uncontrolled comparison reports less pain after a ginger, lemongrass and date drink.

fit: date-flesh extract jam and rat paw swelling
assessment: The date-extract jam arm showed less swelling than the arthritic control, and combined oil formulations were separate arms. The study measures swelling and biomarkers rather than pain and does not assign whole dried fruit.

fit: date fruit pulp extract in a paraquat rat model
assessment: The study reported motor coordination, biomarker and histology outcomes. Dried dates and pain were untested.

fit: fresh date extract and thermal nociception in diabetic rats
assessment: After gavage of fresh-fruit extract, hot-plate latency was 6.9 vs 3.7 seconds for vehicle. Results and Figure 1 use p<.05, while the abstract says p<.01. Tail-flick was inconclusive and its figure caption conflicts with the Methods on route. The model does not measure Parkinson pain.

fit: date syrup and labor pain
assessment: The study reported lower ratings at several times. The unsweetened control and acute obstetric population limit applicability.

fit: traditional pain uses and cautions by plant part
assessment: Pages 72–73 describe customary pain indications and a headache caution with unspecified drying state, and distinguish leaf and root accounts for toothache. No patient-level or Parkinson pain comparison is reported.

fit: Deglet Nour phenolic fractions and acute pain behaviour in mice
assessment: The groups had fewer abdominal writhes after the isolated fractions. Table 1 protection percentages differ from its means under the printed formula, and methods and results name different active controls. No whole dried date or chronic Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: attributed customary date fruit use for abdominal pain
assessment: The conference discussion attributes use to southern Algerian residents. The primary 2000 source is unverified and the journal pages describe a different plant. The account has no exact preparation, diagnosis or measured outcome.

fit: topical date-palm preparation and osteoarthritis pain
assessment: The official record specifies a planned unblinded topical comparison and visual analogue and WOMAC pain measures. The original dissertation and outcome values remain unverified.

fit: whole Mazafati dates and menstrual pain
assessment: The retrospective registration specifies whole dates and pain intensity. The fruit drying stage, the discrepant enrollment descriptions and numerical outcome values remain unresolved.

fit: oral date-palm distillate and migraine pain
assessment: The registry plans a distillate versus placebo for migraine. The pain outcome fields differ in product label, scale and timepoints, and the study reports no observed result.

fit: aqueous date-fruit preparation and evoked heat withdrawal
assessment: The higher extract group of the convenience-allocated experiment had longer tail-flick latency. Nociceptive response and ear swelling are distinct. Inconsistent omnibus statistics and the non-Parkinson population limit interpretation.

fit: oral date-flesh extracts and rat paw swelling
assessment: Date-flesh water and methanol extracts reduced rat paw swelling. A separate seed extract arm also reduced swelling. The outcome is swelling and gauged inflammation without a clinical pain result.

fit: masked controlled Parkinson medication trial with dedicated pain intensity outcome
assessment: At week 16 the posted full analysis set net change was -0.7 points (95% CI -1.75 to 0.32) on NRS-11. This compares a medication with placebo without any dried-date intervention.

fit: whole Ajwa dates and abdominal pain in children with autism
assessment: The three-group comparison of reported pain improvement was statistically inconclusive. The registry and report disagree about allocation. The population and pain measure differ from the frozen claim.

fit: assigned whole dried-date comparator without Parkinson pain severity outcome
assessment: A twelve-week randomized older-adult trial assigned dried dates against frozen blueberries. No standalone pain endpoint is registered and no group outcomes are posted.

fit: uncontrolled Parkinson bar pilot with unresolved date exposure
assessment: The primary congress abstract reports digestive and composite Parkinson outcomes in 18 participants. No pain estimate or complete ingredient list appears.

fit: date paste in a mixed fiber bar with pain included in a composite assessment
assessment: Both registered bar flavors contain date paste. The planned Part IB total includes a pain item, but the listed item comparison concerns constipation. No results or isolated date exposure are available.

fit: edible portion and seed extracts, rat paw thickness
assessment: The original Table 2 reports smaller paw thickness increases after two edible-part extracts and a seed extract. The study measures swelling and blood markers without a pain behavior endpoint.

fit: Parkinson medication state and standardized peanut chewing
assessment: The medication-state comparison uses peanut chewing in 12 patients in both states. Measured jaw velocity and occlusal measures do not provide a dried-date intervention or clinical pain response.

fit: whole-fruit comparative labor outcomes
assessment: Comparative late-pregnancy date fruit cohort reports labor progression and induction outcomes. The accessible author abstract does not give pain severity by group.

fit: date fruit or orange juice and pooled labor progress
assessment: The offered-carbohydrate arm could choose dates with water or tea, or orange juice. The comparison reports labor progression and analgesic use. It does not provide an ingredient-specific measured pain result.

fit: date palm pollen and treatment-related oral pain
assessment: Twenty participants were allocated sequentially. Day-29 oral pain means were 0 versus 3.0 during cancer treatment. Pollen suspension, unequal cancer regimens and treatment-related oral pain limit transfer to dried date fruit and Parkinson pain.

fit: Tamr Ajwa preparations in laboratory fermentation and cell assays
assessment: The experiment used human donor faecal cultures and an intestinal cell line. No participant received a treatment for pain. Preserve the later 2015 human dietary study as a separate design.

fit: wild date-palm extract and animal nociception
assessment: The highest tested extract arm had a longer hot-plate response at 120 minutes. The preparation, species and acute mouse endpoint differ. Separate reduced activity can complicate interpretation of response latency.

fit: pain attributed to perceived insects and gabapentin in a Parkinson case
assessment: Author abstract reports that pain and visual hallucinations subsided after gabapentin in one patient. This describes concurrent symptoms and a drug exposure, without a dried-date diet or separate pain severity estimate.

fit: date fruit and clinically investigated hereditary fructose intolerance
assessment: One of three relatives described abdominal pain with possible date intake. Clinical fructose testing involved two relatives and did not establish a dried-date pain contrast.

fit: Omani date-palm customary use
assessment: The date entry gives tonic, cooling and bronchitis use, without a dated fruit or pain response. Stomach ailments appear in a separate ginger entry.

fit: cultivar-specific ethanol extracts of identified dried ripe date fruit and evoked withdrawal in mice
assessment: Mean writhing counts were 21.0–25.0 across extract groups versus 33.0 with vehicle. Hot-plate delays were longer while movement and exploration were lower. No whole-fruit or Parkinson clinical comparison.

fit: Parkinson medication trial reanalysis and concomitant pain treatment
assessment: The pooled post hoc analysis found lower additional pain-treatment use and assessed a bodily discomfort domain. The intervention was a medicine, and this is not an independent study family or dried-date exposure.

fit: ethnobotanical date syrup and sore pain in an oasis survey
assessment: Table 3 records syrup as a customary remedy. It gives no route, counted symptom-specific reports or measured pain change. Distinct from chronic Parkinson pain and dried date consumption.

fit: date fruit at iftar in interviews of adults with diabetes
assessment: Two Riyadh groups describe the ceremonial practice and differences in amounts. There are no date-attributable pain measurements or Parkinson population.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy without the frozen food preparation
assessment: Parkinson pain scores and thermal pain thresholds were measured separately in the neuropathy study. The comparison involves nerve findings and disease status without date fruit.

fit: same protocol honey arm and potentially shared controls
assessment: Honey versus water provides registration and cohort provenance, without a date comparison. Five control VAS means and SDs match the date-syrup report exactly, while one row differs.

fit: fasting and medication adjustments in a Parkinson cohort
assessment: The authors analyzed 20 of 24 people and report an unchanged nonmotor total. The foods at iftar and pain items are unreported. Treat MDS abstract 1106 as a probable same-cohort report.

fit: fresh fruit with noncomparative pain categories
assessment: The trial compared fresh Rutab fruit with and without water against no fruit. Table 1 combines 76 pain categories across participants and supplies no arm-specific pain result.

fit: obstetric endpoints outside pain severity
assessment: The review synthesizes labor duration and cervical endpoints without a pain-severity result. Its cited cohorts are not independent new observations.

fit: secondary search for human trial families with date palm preparations
assessment: The primary abstract identifies 26 studies across different plant parts and indications. It does not give an exact pain comparison after dried fruit or a Parkinson cohort. Full tables remain open.

fit: date seed powder case with acute abdominal pain
assessment: Severe abdominal pain and portal-system thrombosis followed self-reported use of seed powder. The case provides no fruit-flesh exposure or demonstrated causality.

fit: uncontrolled Parkinson medication cohort with dedicated pain scale
assessment: The dedicated pain total improved over six months in a single-arm cohort. A separate controlled trial of the medication supplies an interval crossing zero. Neither compares dried dates.

fit: Parkinson prebiotic bar and abdominal symptom composite
assessment: Abdominal discomfort was included in the instrument. The full paper presents total GI score and selected other items, without a separate pain estimate or identified date exposure. The trial is distinct from the Stanford and Sorridi bars.

fit: date-seed exercise companion biomarker report in the measured pain family
assessment: Biomarker paper and 2022 pain paper share IRCT20150205020965N9, intervention and cohort. Pain results are from the 2022 paper. No independently assigned whole dried fruit.

fit: Zahidi fruit flesh and seed powder separately from pain
assessment: Ten-participant crossover with date flesh and seed powder measured blood markers and supplied no pain result.

fit: registered Parkinson feasibility protocol with diet and nonmotor measures
assessment: NL9438 schedules diet questionnaires and symptom data. Abdominal pain is in background discussion and the protocol neither assigns dried dates nor publishes pain results.

fit: primary context for the symptom or clinical comparison
assessment: Controlled comparison of mood and activation across mobile states. Pain exacerbation describes the arthritis comparison population. No dried or other date fruit intervention.

fit: labor pain citation and duplicate cohort review
assessment: Two distinct syrup trials provide favorable comparisons. Two papers share participants, and the fresh-fruit paper supplies no between-arm pain estimate. No pooled pain estimate or new cohort.

fit: qualitative iftar fruit routine and a separate meal-size and discomfort account
assessment: One participant mentions dates and water. Another attributed less hunger discomfort to smaller portions. The observations do not form an ingredient comparison and the cohort is not Parkinson-specific.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy without the frozen food preparation
assessment: The nonmotor diary captures pain presence per hour and relates it to motor-state agreement. There was no dried-date exposure.

fit: date use in an ethnobotanical survey and separately cited customary headache use
assessment: The 142-person questionnaire concerned immune-support practices. Headache is a prior literature attribution in Discussion and no measured fruit-specific clinical pain outcome was reported.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy without the frozen food preparation
assessment: Pain reporting in Parkinson was compared across population groups and did not show a clear group difference. The design did not measure dried-date intake.

fit: medication and aggregate nonmotor scores during Ramadan in Parkinson disease
assessment: Seventy-five fasting participants self-selected medication groups. Table 2 reports overall questionnaire totals but no pain item or fruit exposure.

fit: clinical symptom measurement or proxy outside the frozen dietary comparison
assessment: The medication cohort reports 53 versus 37 participants with a pooled pain, anxiety and distress fluctuation item. The measure is a count and provides no dried-date or pain intensity contrast.

fit: primary context for the symptom or clinical comparison

fit: arugula extract in a vascular crossover

fit: repeated kindergarten vegetable exposure, intake and liking

fit: raw arugula allergy context
assessment: An acute salad-associated reaction presents a different pathway and endpoint. It supplies no Parkinson fatigue outcome.

fit: rocket salad beverage and blood pressure in healthy adults

assessment: A first-person reply describes regularity with a multi-food smoothie and cereal as an alternative. Ginger's role, amount and diagnosis are uncertain.

assessment: The 82-person original reports poststroke urinary outcomes after a composite topical exposure and acupuncture. The later registered pilot uses a different design and has no linked results. Neither provides a bowel outcome.

fit: dried ginger suspension and esophageal motility

fit: rat small-intestinal stimulated contraction after prior oral exposure or direct application

fit: pediatric gastrointestinal literature screening without measured ginger treatment comparison

assessment: The accessible abstract gives an inconclusive nine-hole peg contrast with no signed estimate. NCT01951937 lists 200 participants and the paper reports 205 randomized. Full tables and cooking details remain open.

assessment: The open-label study reported shorter anosmia duration with oil. It did not measure smell-test performance, ground seed or Parkinson disease.

assessment: The higher groups had lower rigidity scores and fewer rotations. Rigidity and dystonia are distinct, and the exposure was injected extract.

assessment: Challenge reproduced a marked pressure and pulse decrease. The discussion calls the pepper cayenne without verifying the preparation. No measured falls or Parkinson cohort.

assessment: There was no preparation-specific estimate on postural instability.

fit: cocoa in rice beverage

fit: mixed vegetables and device adverse event

fit: pooled leek and spinach intake in a Parkinson cohort

fit: dried summer savory infusion and awake rat activity

fit: diet pattern and composite outcome

fit: pumpkin seed oil on a Parkinson diet menu and motor-scale speech item

fit: injected cilantro leaf extract and mouse anxiety behavior

fit: exact mushroom species fraction in a Parkinson model

fit: ginger and tea beverage against aerobic exercise with conflicting comparator reports

fit: ginger in a mixture and menstrual pain

fit: two distinct ginger species in cosmetic documentation

fit: traditional reported abdominal pain use

fit: Parkinson upper abdominal pain diary in a separate botanical drug trial

fit: traditional ginger preparation and reported joint or back pain use

fit: secondary traditional report of compound use for stomach pain

fit: ginger root powder and placebo-controlled menstrual pain

fit: ethanol ginger extract and acute exercise soreness

fit: constipation-associated pain in a whole formula add-on comparison

fit: eight-component formula and abdominal pain

fit: combined herbal extract and abdominal pain outside Parkinson disease

fit: ginger supercritical extract and adult joint pain during exercise

fit: pepper and clove constituents in cardiac experiments

assessment: The matched observational study includes cinnamon, coffee and cloves among 12 odor-identification sticks. Seven participants with mild illness identified 6 ± 3 odors versus 10 ± 1 in seven controls (p=.028). The measured contrast is a total correct odor score across health groups. Smell stimulation is distinct from ingestion and provides no odor-specific treatment effect, no Parkinson cohort, and no cinnamon, coffee or clove fatigue or pain result.

assessment: A SARS-CoV-2 smell identification comparison used standardized odor items, including clove and cherry. The reported proportions reflect correct recognition of odors in antibody-positive and antibody-negative participants. The odor cards are genuine ingredient-related sensory stimuli. The comparison does not assess clove consumption and pain, cherry consumption and fatigue, or date consumption and pain in Parkinson disease.

assessment: The review names clove, cinnamon, ginger, turmeric and nutmeg in its source discussion and cites distinct eugenol nociception and forced-swim studies. The oral and injected pain experiments use isolated eugenol and have different peripheral, thermal and motor results. The behavioral mood references do not assign grated nutmeg. The review supplies no ingredient-specific Parkinson pain or depression estimate.

fit: traditional clove decoction for toothache
assessment: The survey lists a decoction for intended symptom relief. Ground preparation and comparison data are absent.

assessment: This review gives clove and nutmeg odors as cues in a rodent discrimination and reversal-learning task. Changing the reward contingency measures learning and cognitive flexibility. assessment: The experimental study compares two Parkinson-like zebrafish model conditions using motor and anxiety-like readings. Clove oil serves as procedural anesthesia. A shared procedural use gives no comparison of ground culinary clove for Parkinson anxiety, rigidity or pain.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: The narrative review discusses exercise and inflammation and cites clove supplementation in an Alzheimer-like rat memory study. The source does not supply a ground culinary clove contrast for Parkinson pain, falls or anxiety.

fit: verified context with exposure or endpoint boundaries
assessment: The study compares material characteristics of particles with different botanical extract treatments, including clove. Turmeric extract appears in background on other materials studies. These material properties do not test culinary clove or turmeric for Parkinson pain. The article reports no dried date fruit pain comparison.

fit: topical ground clove and immediate dental pain
assessment: The ground-clove gel yielded lower needle-pain scores than placebo. A local dental procedure cannot establish the effect of eating clove on Parkinson’s pain.

fit: isolated oral eugenol and evoked thermal or mechanical rat responses
assessment: Day-five thermal latency 11.4 versus 6.1 seconds, p<.01. Mechanical tests were inconclusive and did not generate allodynia. The formulation differed from the saline comparator. Neither arm corresponds to ground clove or clinical Parkinson pain.

fit: topical clove oil cream and chronic anal fissure healing
assessment: The author abstract reports 60% versus 12% healing at three months and lower manometric pressures. The full paper is needed to verify a pain outcome separately.

fit: clove odorant among four scents and olfaction
assessment: Eugenol was one of four smelled odorants. The intervention measured olfaction and gives no pain estimate after ground clove.

fit: injected clove oil and mouse nociception
assessment: The oil group showed fewer writhes and longer hot-plate latency than saline. The article mentions sedation with higher doses. No ground clove or clinical Parkinson outcome.

fit: oral standardized clove extract and composite hangover symptoms
assessment: Mammen and colleagues reported a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover of standardized oral clove polyphenols in 16 men following a controlled alcohol challenge. The report gives an overall 55.34% reduction in composite hangover severity. No separate pain, ache, or headache contrast could be verified from the accessible report. The code printed with the study belongs to the ethics committee rather than an identified trial registry. Article access and the later reanalysis are documented separately.

fit: topical clove-papaya gel and pediatric dental injection pain
assessment: This pediatric active-comparator study tested a clove–papaya formulation, benzocaine and precooling. No separate clove effect or clinical Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: topical eugenol and needle pain in hemodialysis
assessment: The crossover enrolled 34 patients and reported mean pain of 3.29 with topical eugenol versus 5.03 without intervention. The publisher describes a lower score than placebo. The outcome is procedural pain and the exposure is a topical constituent.

fit: topical clove oil and pediatric dental injection pain
assessment: In a four-arm pediatric dental study, topical lignocaine gave lower self-rated and observer pain than clove oil. Clove oil versus ice was inconclusive.

fit: topical clove essential-oil gel and rat nociception
assessment: The gel lowered late-phase formalin pain scores. The paper found no clear early-phase composite or thermal latency effect. No ground-clove or clinical pain effect was measured.

fit: inhaled clove and postoperative headache
assessment: Overall three-arm contrasts were inconclusive at eight and 24 hours (p=.20 and .31). The study did not test ingested clove or Parkinson’s pain.

fit: topical clove oil and pediatric dental pain
assessment: Three active treatments had no statistically clear between-group difference. There was no inactive comparison or Parkinson pain outcome.

fit: injected clove distillate and experimental rat pain
assessment: The clove pharmacopuncture study evaluated a distilled injected formulation in cell and rat experiments. It increased thermal tail-flick latency and attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity after experimental inflammation. This records a local and preclinical analgesic signal with an exposure and outcome distinct from consuming ground clove for Parkinson pain.

fit: green beans in a Parkinson menu and aggregate motor scores
assessment: The Parkinson pilot offered green beans as one of many options. Aggregate motor change was inconclusive and individual facial-expression scores, steaming and participant-specific green bean intake were unreported.

fit: oral sweet basil extracts and beam motor coordination in an ischemia model
assessment: The 2009 poster and 2011 journal abstract share researchers and endpoint but differ in reported occlusion duration. Overlap unresolved. The accessible outcomes give no stride estimate or fresh-food exposure.

fit: oral sweet basil leaf extract after cerebral ischemia in mice
assessment: Author abstract reports improved motor coordination and a neurological severity score after post-ischemia treatment. Detailed results, fresh herb intake and measured stride remain open.

fit: mixed Parkinson diet and composite motor score
assessment: Appendix A lists both herbs in a multicomponent diet. Composite UPDRS III scores improved. The examination includes gait examination, but no item-level result, individual herb amount or preparation, or herb-specific contrast was reported.

fit: injected Capsicum fruit extract in a barbiturate challenge
assessment: Some extract and fraction groups showed a longer loss-of-righting interval. Natural sleep and clinical insomnia were outside this mouse assay.

fit: extract and a sleep diary in healthy athletes

fit: hot sauce and mustard mixture and sleep in healthy men
assessment: The six-person experiment reported worsened sleep-stage and wake measures after the seasoned meal. Separate spice-specific and Parkinson effects were unmeasured.

fit: paprika oleoresin in a matched cannabinol crossover
assessment: The randomized comparison varied cannabinol. The paprika colorant was listed among excipients. There is no separate ground-paprika sleep effect.

fit: clove smell identification item and Parkinson freezing phenotype
assessment: The clove odor recognition contrast between freezers and non-freezers was inconclusive (p=.212). The study did not measure change in freezing after ingesting clove.

fit: filbertone profiling in cold-pressed hazelnut oils
assessment: Table VI measures semi-quantitative filbertone signals in some cold-pressed preparations. Raw-kernel oils in this study are below the quantification limit. No systemic uptake or tremor outcome was measured.

assessment: The primary author dissertation for the same article shows behavioral task results. It supplies no oral hazelnut oil arm, human Parkinson cohort or resting-tremor comparison.

fit: isolated filbertone with biochemical endpoints in cell and mouse models
assessment: The full original gives biochemical and tissue markers. The preprint and article are one family. It provides neither a cold-pressed oil exposure nor a human resting-tremor result.

fit: whole hazelnuts offered and Parkinson motor composite includes rest tremor
assessment: The published composite motor score includes rest tremor. The menu lists whole nuts and separately lists other oils. There is no rest-tremor result by item or grade-specific exposure.

fit: cinnamon powder and honey with illustrative medication diaries
assessment: The case reported longer medication ON intervals. Both figures mark 15 minutes of dyskinesia and provide no severity rating or isolated cinnamon effect.

fit: cinnamon intake as a group-visit dietary outcome
assessment: OA15.04 reports increased cinnamon intake in a 155-person randomized group-visit dietary secondary analysis for adults with chronic pain and depression; preparation and an isolated cinnamon symptom effect are not reported. The claim seeks ground cinnamon and dyskinesia severity.

fit: cinnamon constituent and cell or tissue outcomes

fit: self-reported coconut oil use and overall PD symptom progression

fit: self-reported coconut oil frequency and total Parkinson symptom score
assessment: The cross-sectional composite association gives no refined-oil classification or listener-rated intelligibility outcome.

fit: virgin coconut oil within mixed ketogenic plan and composite motor score

fit: ketogenic diet and Parkinson patient-reported voice handicap

fit: ketogenic diet and companion report of talking; oil exposure unverified

fit: pineapple frequency and pooled urinary incontinence impact

fit: pineapple in the original-source scope for urinary urgency frequency

fit: pineapple fruit and juice as reported bladder symptom triggers
assessment: Pineapple and juice were rated as worsening bladder symptoms in a painful-bladder cohort. No assigned intake, raw preparation or separate Parkinson urgency episode counts.

fit: pineapple or juice before pelvic pain and bladder symptom flares
assessment: Case-crossover odds were inconclusive overall and in participants reporting a possible dietary trigger. The dietary item pooled fruit and juice and the endpoint was a flare, without a Parkinson urgency estimate.

fit: pineapple juice sensitivity in veterans
assessment: The symptom survey recorded pineapple juice sensitivity in 42 interstitial cystitis participants and two in each comparator. It did not measure raw pineapple or Parkinson urgency.

fit: bromelain-containing mixture in bacterial and ex vivo bladder models
assessment: The mixture altered some bacterial and inflammatory measures. It provided no voiding or urgency outcome, no raw pineapple and no Parkinson participants.

fit: grouped high-acid foods and urgency urinary incontinence
assessment: Adjusted OR 1.29 (95% CI 1.03–1.62) for grouped high-acid foods. Pineapple membership and separate estimate unverified. The endpoint includes leakage.

fit: canola vehicle and acute throat symptoms during olive challenge
assessment: Acute symptoms followed a blend containing extra-virgin olive oil. No canola-specific voice estimate or designated processing grade.

fit: canola menu and speech domains in Parkinson disease
assessment: Part II and III include speech, but no separately reported speech item, sound-pressure data or processing-specific canola contrast was available.

fit: instrumented mouse stride length with equal soybean oil in two blends
assessment: The Angelman-model gait experiment measured longer strides on standard feed and shorter strides toward control with a safflower blend. Both experimental diets contained the same soybean oil amount, and the model had no Parkinson shortened-stride phenotype.

fit: dietary soybean oil substitution and ordinal stepping and coordination in rats
assessment: After spinal cord injury, scores on an ordinal measure of stepping and coordination were lower in soybean-oil-fed animals than in menhaden-oil-fed animals. No stride distances or soybean-oil preparation grade were reported.

fit: equal soybean oil and mouse treadmill stride variability
assessment: Curcumin changed stride variability while the diet oil amount was matched. The study did not isolate soybean oil or measure shortened clinical stride.

fit: soybean-oil laboratory chow and quantified treadmill gait timing
assessment: The study found no clear differences in propulsion, swing or braking time between soy-fat chow and a coconut oil/DHA/ARA developmental feed. No stride distance, oil processing grade, or Parkinson context was reported.

fit: Cuminum fruit water extract by gavage in MPTP mice; rotarod and activity endpoints

fit: Parkinson diet trial includes pan-heated cumin in soup; diet-level motor complication score
assessment: Heating in a mixed soup is not verified toasting; individual intake and a cumin-specific dyskinesia result are unavailable.

fit: UK Parkinson survey recorded cumin use in previous month; preparation and dyskinesia outcome unreported
assessment: Individual cumin use is reported but toasting, dose and dyskinesia severity are not assessed as a cumin contrast.

fit: oral extract of dried tarragon leaves and forced-swim immobility
assessment: Both extract arms under restraint had lower immobility than restraint alone, with similar total maze arm entries. This comparison concerns a concentrated extract and stress behavior rather than a clinical depressive symptom.

fit: oral tarragon tincture and rat forced-swim behavior
assessment: The paper reports no activity for the remaining preparations including tarragon in its forced-swim test, without raw tarragon estimates. The preparation and outcome differ from dried herb and Parkinson depressive symptoms.

fit: tarragon extract in feed and behavior after mouse social defeat
assessment: Social interaction and grooming improved in the behavioral model. Sucrose preference did not differ clearly. The results do not measure depressive symptoms in people with Parkinson disease.

fit: injected tarragon extract and behavioral immobility in mice
assessment: Extract reduced immobility in forced swim and at one tail-suspension dose. These are rodent proxies and do not test clinical depression or dried culinary tarragon.

fit: refined olive oil and 1-back task activation
assessment: The activation interaction was inconclusive. Imaging does not establish a clinical attention effect.

fit: MIND meals with extra-virgin olive oil and planned flanker testing
assessment: The registered outcome covers attention, but the intervention is a whole meal pattern and the oil is extra-virgin, with no posted results.

fit: olive-oil comparator and sustained attention battery

fit: olive-oil comparator with letter cancellation and reaction times

fit: usual cooking olive oil and attention scores in a cross-sectional cohort

fit: olive oil as a shared vehicle in an attention trial

fit: refined oil taste and exploratory EEG

fit: summer savory oil and rat rotarod motor coordination
assessment: Balance after lead exposure gives no dystonia measure.

fit: food-derived polymers, fermentation, animal models and processed fiber snacks
assessment: Oat beta-glucans are discussed as fermentable plant polysaccharides. The reported outcomes concern microbes and metabolites and do not evaluate cooked oats and Parkinson rigidity.

fit: oat bran as an option within a bundled Parkinson diet
assessment: The pilot had a small, inconclusive composite motor change. It did not quantify oat intake or individual rigidity.

fit: oat-containing synbiotic in a Parkinson rat model
assessment: The rat intervention combined oats with three probiotic strains and measured tissue and microbiota outcomes rather than rigidity.

fit: common-sage extract chemistry and antiproliferative experiment
assessment: The author abstract confirms sage-derived extracts and chemical and cancer cell endpoints. P33 references this same report. It provides no culinary dose or Parkinson symptom comparison.

fit: isolated ellagic acid gavage and measured stride in rats

fit: sage leaf extract and paw-print index after sciatic injury
assessment: Footprint index improved after extract. No stride length was measured.

fit: safflower oil capsules and bowel tolerability

fit: safflower oil comparator and constipation adverse event in Glut1 deficiency

fit: safflower-containing comparator and registered bowel diaries

assessment: The adjusted composite difference was +6.8 points per frequency step (95% CI −6.8 to +20.5). No separate constipation or grade comparison is available.

fit: high-oleic safflower and canola in defined diet and stool characteristics
assessment: The blend with different fiber produced firmer stools and greater output per unit fiber. The formula varied several ingredients and did not measure Parkinson constipation.

fit: inhaled marjoram oil and resting blood pressure
assessment: In nine seated healthy adults, mean arterial pressure decreased versus plain air at the last two minutes. A separate supine comparison used baseline. Standing symptoms and oral fresh marjoram were outside the experiment.

fit: marjoram extract and aortic ring relaxation
assessment: Vascular tissue relaxation is not an orthostatic symptom measurement.

fit: filtered marjoram tea and composite nonmotor scale in Parkinson
assessment: The report gives no separate estimate for standing lightheadedness. It tested a dried-leaf tea.

fit: inhaled marjoram oil and mean arterial pressure
assessment: Rested between-group pressure change was inconclusive. No standing symptoms or food exposure.

fit: clinical allspice allergy case with limited access

fit: anise in a Parkinson honey mixture and broad sleep disturbance in an unlinked survey

assessment: Appendix A lists the oil among other foods, and supplement Figure S2 reports UPDRS III totals. The pressing process, individually consumed oil and handwriting outcomes are unreported.

fit: filtered marjoram tea and composite nonmotor scale in Parkinson
assessment: The reported NMSS total cannot identify a change in visual hallucination frequency.

fit: tested oral marjoram extract and behavioral observation in rats
assessment: The Methods specify female rats and a dried aerial-parts extract. General observation and acute mortality do not measure hallucinations. No Parkinson or fresh-leaf exposure.

fit: historical report of attempted use without verified hallucination outcome

fit: cinnamon odor identification in early-onset Parkinson
assessment: Cinnamon recognition was 43.9% in an early-onset cohort of 156, and the original figure shows about 56% errors. No item denominator, food intake or cinnamon-specific duration estimate was reported.

fit: cinnamon odor recognition across causes of hyposmia

fit: six inhaled odors and olfaction during diabetes-related cognitive impairment
assessment: Abstract reports overall olfaction difference without numeric item effects. Probable registry NCT06327633. No oral intervention or individual cinnamon contrast.

assessment: The ingredient form in the vial and participant use cannot be confirmed. The Part I composite supplies no dried-basil result on apathy severity.

fit: basil listed with other spices in a Parkinson hospital diet
assessment: The report gives a baseline Part I total and clinical motor follow-up. Basil preparation, individual consumption and apathy severity results are unavailable.

assessment: Cinnamon is named among diagnostic odor items. The cohort enrolled people with iRBD and recorded sleep-related measures independently of the odor. No dream-enactment outcome is attributed to cinnamon.

fit: combined cinnamon bark and ginger Kampo formula
assessment: Dream enactment reportedly stopped in one Parkinson case after a seven-ingredient formula. The contribution of cinnamon was not separated.

fit: tarragon versus thyme odor pair in mice
assessment: Author spreadsheets give mean pair 7 acquisition/reversal errors of 7.40/7.47 in 15 Alzheimer-model mice and 7.83/15.22 in 18 controls. Both scents were present, paired exposure was olfactory, and genotype and task order limit interpretation.

fit: odor rotation including tarragon and mouse olfactory deficit
assessment: Discrimination index after reopened naris was lower than intact controls without enrichment, with no clear difference from intact controls in the enriched group. Rotating odors and food ingestion are distinct.

fit: odor rotation including tarragon and mouse odor recognition
assessment: Enriched mice retained odor recognition through 240 minutes while controls showed it only at 30 minutes. Both conditions lacked clear recognition at 480 minutes. No tarragon arm or dietary exposure.

fit: odor rotation including tarragon and impaired mouse odor discrimination
assessment: Double knockouts discriminated two esters after enrichment p < .001, with p = .72 in empty-container animals. The study did not isolate tarragon odor or measure eating dried herb.

assessment: Bian and colleagues compared orally administered volatile fractions from raw and dry-fried huajiao in groups of ten mice.
